lessons.title: Expectation, Variance & Covariance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Expectation is `E[X]=Σx p(x)` or `∫x f(x)dx` when it exists, and linearity gives `E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c` without independence. Variance is `Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]=E[X²]−μ²`. For sums, `Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y)`; covariance vanishes for independent finite-variance variables, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence. Correlation standardizes covariance to [−1,1] when variances are positive and measures linear association, not causation. In data, distinguish population from sample estimators, use stable online/two-pass algorithms and inspect tails and drift beyond mean/variance.
keyPoints: Linearity of expectation needs no independence
Moments may not exist or characterize a distribution
Stable estimation needs denominator and weight semantics
lessons.why: Expected cost, model loss, traffic, portfolio risk, ensemble error and sample-size calculations all use moments. Common mistakes—adding standard deviations, omitting covariance, using ddof inconsistently, calculating variance by subtracting huge nearly equal values, or reading correlation causally—can materially distort decisions. Moment algebra is powerful precisely because it states what can and cannot be simplified.
lessons.intuition: Expectation is the balance point of a probability distribution. Variance is its average squared spread around that point. Covariance asks whether two variables tend to deviate from their means in the same direction. When combining uncertain quantities, aligned deviations reinforce risk; opposing deviations cancel; independent deviations add only in variance, not standard deviation.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.math: E[g(X)]=Σg(x)p(x) or ∫g(x)f(x)dx. `Var(X)=E[(X−μ)²]`; `Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−μ_X)(Y−μ_Y)]`. `Var(a^TX)=a^TΣa`. Total expectation: `E[X]=E[E[X|Y]]`. Total variance: `Var(X)=E[Var(X|Y)]+Var(E[X|Y])`.
lessons.workedExample: Each variance is 100 and covariance is `0.8×10×10=80`. Expected total is 200 by linearity regardless of dependence. Total variance is `100+100+2×80=360`, so standard deviation is about 18.97—not 20 (adding standard deviations) and not 14.14 (assuming independence). If correlation were −0.8, variance would be 40. Correlation may change during incidents, so a historical estimate can understate joint tail load. Capacity planning should inspect conditional/tail scenarios, not only Normal mean ± standard deviation.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
x=np.array([1,2,3,4])
y=np.array([2,4,5,8])
print(x.mean(), x.var(ddof=1))
print(np.cov(x,y,ddof=1)[0,1])
print(np.corrcoef(x,y)[0,1])

commonMistakes.mistake: Linearity of expectation requires independence.
commonMistakes.correction: Expectations of sums always add when defined; independence is used for products and variance simplifications.

commonMistakes.mistake: Zero correlation means independence.
commonMistakes.correction: It only rules out linear covariance; nonlinear dependence can remain unless special joint-family assumptions hold.

commonMistakes.mistake: Use `E[X²]−E[X]²` directly on huge-offset data.
commonMistakes.correction: Subtraction can catastrophically cancel; use centered two-pass or Welford algorithms.

followUps.question: Why is covariance matrix positive semidefinite?
followUps.answer: For any a, `a^TΣa=Var(a^TX)≥0`.

followUps.question: What does total variance separate?
followUps.answer: Average variance within conditioning groups and variance between their conditional means.

followUps.question: When does E[g(X)]=g(E[X])?
followUps.answer: Generally for affine g; nonlinear equality requires special circumstances. Jensen gives an inequality for convex/concave g.

lessons.production: Define population/window, units, filters, weights and ddof; use stable mergeable moment algorithms and validate against batch references. Monitor count/effective weight, means, variances, quantiles/tails, covariance conditioning and slice/time dependence. Treat missing/outlier policy explicitly, restrict sensitive aggregates, retain source lineage and checkpointed summaries, and roll back/recompute when invariants or drift thresholds fail.
lessons.description: Expectation is a probability-weighted average of a random variable; variance measures expected squared deviation from its mean; covariance measures linear co-movement. These are properties of a specified distribution, not guarantees about one observation. This chapter develops linearity of expectation, indicator variables, transformations, variance identities, covariance matrices, correlation, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds, conditional moments and laws of total expectation/variance. You will learn why expectations add without independence while variances require covariance terms, why zero covariance does not generally imply independence, and how scaling and nonlinear transformations change moments. A worked portfolio/system-load example derives aggregate variance under dependence. The lab computes exact weighted moments, merges online summaries and compares them with NumPy. Production guidance covers population versus sample denominators, weighted data, missingness, streaming algorithms, numeric cancellation, nonstationarity, tail risk, covariance regularization, privacy and rollback. The objective is to use moments as compact but limited summaries, understand precisely which algebra they support, and avoid turning correlation or an average into a causal or distributional claim.
learningObjectives: Compute expectations of functions and exploit linearity and indicator variables without requiring independence.
Derive variance/covariance rules for sums and affine transformations and interpret covariance matrices geometrically.
Estimate and operate moments with correct denominators, weights, stable streaming algorithms, drift/tail checks and explicit limits.

deepSections.title: Expectation, transformations, and indicators
deepSections.body:
For discrete X, `E[g(X)]=Σ_x g(x)p(x)`; for continuous X, integrate `g(x)f(x)`. You do not need the distribution of g(X) to compute its expectation this way. Expectation may be infinite or undefined for heavy-tailed variables, so algebra requiring finite moments needs assumptions. `E[aX+b]=aE[X]+b`, and linearity extends to sums regardless of dependence.

Indicator I_A equals one when event A occurs, zero otherwise, so `E[I_A]=P(A)`. Counts can be written as sums of indicators, making expected counts the sum of individual probabilities even when events depend. For example, expected number of collisions or occupied bins may be easy while the full count distribution is hard. Independence becomes relevant for products: if X,Y independent and integrable, E[XY]=E[X]E[Y], but the converse is not generally true.

Expectation of a nonlinear function is not generally the function of the expectation. Jensen's inequality says `g(E[X])≤E[g(X)]` for convex g, explaining why variability raises expected convex cost. Ratios, logs and thresholds need full distribution information or approximations; substituting means can bias decisions.

deepSections.title: Variance, covariance, and correlation
deepSections.body:
Variance `E[(X−μ)²]` is nonnegative and has squared units. The identity `E[X²]−E[X]²` is algebraically useful but can be numerically unstable in finite precision. Scaling gives `Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X)`. Standard deviation returns original units but does not add for sums.

Covariance `E[(X−μ_X)(Y−μ_Y)] = E[XY]−E[X]E[Y]`. Thus `Var(Σ_iX_i)=Σ_iVar(X_i)+2Σ_{i<j}Cov(X_i,X_j)`. Independence implies zero covariance for finite moments, but dependent symmetric/nonlinear relationships can have zero covariance. Correlation divides by standard deviations and lies in [−1,1] by Cauchy–Schwarz; it is undefined for constant variables and invariant to positive affine scaling.

A covariance matrix Σ has entries Cov(X_i,X_j), is symmetric positive semidefinite, and gives variance of any linear combination a^TX as `a^TΣa`. Near-singular covariance reflects redundant directions or insufficient data and destabilizes inverses. Sample covariance in high dimensions often needs shrinkage or structured assumptions. Correlation matrices remove units but do not solve confounding or nonlinear dependence.

deepSections.title: Conditional moments and decomposition
deepSections.body:
Conditional expectation `E[X|Y]` is itself a random variable/function of Y and is the best mean-squared predictor among functions of Y under suitable conditions. The tower property says `E[E[X|Y]]=E[X]`. The law of total variance splits `Var(X)=E[Var(X|Y)]+Var(E[X|Y])`: average within-group uncertainty plus variation of group means.

This decomposition explains hierarchical data and mixture variance. Overall variance can be large even if every group is tight because means differ; conversely groups can be noisy around a common mean. Aggregating correlations can produce Simpson-like reversals because group composition changes. Report within/between components and the conditioning variables.

For vector X, the law generalizes to covariance: total covariance equals expected conditional covariance plus covariance of conditional means. Uncertainty propagation through linear maps A is `Cov(AX+b)=AΣA^T`. For nonlinear maps, a Jacobian approximation can be used locally, but tail/nonlinearity may require simulation. Conditional moments are descriptive unless the conditioning/intervention distinction is justified causally.

deepSections.title: Estimating and operating moments
deepSections.body:
Population variance divides by population mass. The common unbiased sample variance for IID observations divides the sum of squared deviations by n−1 after estimating the mean; maximum-likelihood Normal variance uses n. Weighted data require clarity: frequency weights, probability weights and inverse-probability weights have different effective sample-size and denominator formulas. Library `ddof` defaults differ.

Use two-pass centered variance or Welford's recurrence rather than one-pass `mean(x²)−mean(x)²` for large offsets. Parallel/streaming summaries can merge count, mean and centered sum of squares exactly up to rounding. Missing-value deletion changes the target population when missingness is informative. Time dependence makes an IID standard error invalid; moments may drift and autocorrelation reduces effective information.

Monitor count/weight, mean, variance, quantiles/tails, covariance conditioning and slice/time changes. Robust summaries complement moments when outliers/heavy tails dominate. Cap or quarantine invalid values according to domain policy, not silently. Covariance and means can reveal sensitive attributes; restrict release and use privacy techniques when appropriate. Version window, filters, weights, units and algorithm; keep previous aggregates/checkpoints for rollback and recompute from source when invariants fail.

workedExamples.title: Variance of combined service load
workedExamples.setup: Services A and B each have mean load 100, standard deviation 10 and correlation 0.8. What is total-load uncertainty?
workedExamples.walkthrough: Each variance is 100 and covariance is `0.8×10×10=80`. Expected total is 200 by linearity regardless of dependence. Total variance is `100+100+2×80=360`, so standard deviation is about 18.97—not 20 (adding standard deviations) and not 14.14 (assuming independence). If correlation were −0.8, variance would be 40. Correlation may change during incidents, so a historical estimate can understate joint tail load. Capacity planning should inspect conditional/tail scenarios, not only Normal mean ± standard deviation.
workedExamples.conclusion: Dependence controls diversification or reinforcement; covariance terms are not optional.

exercises.solution: Catastrophic cancellation in `mean(x²)−mean(x)²` and rounding; use a stable centered algorithm and clamp only tiny roundoff after diagnosis.

lessons.title: Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem
lessons.interviewAnswer: The LLN says a sample average converges to the population expectation under conditions; it explains consistency. The IID finite-variance CLT says `√n(Ȳ−μ)/σ` converges in distribution to standard Normal; it explains approximate sampling uncertainty and `SE(Ȳ)=σ/√n`. It does not say the raw data become Normal. Approximation quality depends on skew, tails, rarity and dependence, not a universal n threshold. Clustered/time-correlated data have smaller effective sample size and need cluster-robust, block or model-based methods. Verify with design-aware simulation/bootstrap and use the estimated standard error appropriate to the sampling process.
keyPoints: Standard error shrinks as 1/√n under IID
lessons.why: Confidence intervals, experiment readouts, monitoring thresholds and Monte Carlo error often rely on asymptotics. Treating millions of events as independent when they come from thousands of users creates tiny false standard errors. Heavy tails can make variance unstable, and rare-event proportions can have poor Normal intervals. Understanding what converges and under which sampling design prevents false precision.
lessons.intuition: The LLN says repeated independent-ish measurements average away noise and settle near the balance point. The CLT zooms into the shrinking error around that point by multiplying it by √n; the shape of that scaled error often approaches a bell curve. Without the zoom, the average collapses to a point, so the two laws describe consistency and uncertainty at different scales.
lessons.deepDive: The full explanation is organized into the structured sections below.
lessons.math: LLN: `Ȳ_n→μ` in probability (or almost surely under stronger form/conditions). IID CLT with finite variance σ²>0: `√n(Ȳ_n−μ)/σ ⇒ N(0,1)`. Hence `SE(Ȳ)=σ/√n` under IID. For dependent observations, `Var(Ȳ)=n^{-2}[ΣVar(X_i)+2Σ_{i<j}Cov(X_i,X_j)]`, not generally σ²/n.
lessons.workedExample: Treating sessions IID gives approximate SE `sqrt(.05×.95/100000)=0.000689`, a very tight interval. If outcomes cluster by user, session count overstates independent information. Aggregate to user-level outcomes for the target or compute a user-cluster robust/bootstrap SE; the effective sample size might be closer to 10,000 and SE roughly three times larger, depending on cluster structure. The LLN/CLT can still apply over independent users, not sessions. If product mix or conversion propensity drifts during the window, even user independence/stationarity needs review.

commonMistakes.mistake: The CLT says observed data become Normal.
commonMistakes.correction: It concerns the centered/scaled sampling distribution of sums/means under assumptions.

followUps.question: How do LLN and CLT differ?
followUps.answer: LLN gives convergence of averages to the mean; CLT characterizes the √n-scaled error distribution.

followUps.question: What is standard error?
followUps.answer: The standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution under the specified design/model.

followUps.question: Why does dependence matter?
followUps.answer: Covariance terms change variance of the sum/mean, often reducing effective sample size far below row count.

lessons.production: Define target, independent unit, sampling/weighting, window and stopping rule. Use cluster/time/design-aware standard errors, validate with unit-aware simulation/bootstrap and monitor tail, autocorrelation, cluster/effective-size and drift signals. Report uncertainty without false precision, bound secure random resampling and roll back or abstain when assumptions/coverage fail.
lessons.description: The law of large numbers (LLN) explains convergence of sample averages to an expectation; the central limit theorem (CLT) explains why a properly centered and scaled sum often has an approximately Normal distribution. They answer different questions and require assumptions that real data can violate. This chapter develops weak/strong LLN intuition, standard error, IID CLT, finite variance, rate/quality of approximation, continuity correction and the delta method. It then examines dependence, clustering, heavy tails, rare events, bounded and non-identical variables, bootstrap connections and why “n>30” is not a theorem. You will learn to separate population size from effective sample size, distinguish the distribution of data from the sampling distribution of a statistic, and choose cluster/time-aware uncertainty. A worked conversion-rate example calculates standard error and diagnoses user-level dependence. The lab simulates Bernoulli/exponential sample means across n and verifies `1/√n` scaling and approximate coverage. Production guidance covers sampling frames, sequential looks, drift, label delay, random streams, monitoring, privacy and rollback. The objective is to use asymptotics as checked approximations, not automatic permission to attach a Normal interval to any large table.
learningObjectives: Distinguish LLN convergence from CLT distributional approximation and state the assumptions/normalization for each.
Compute standard errors for means/proportions and diagnose dependence, heavy tails, skew, rare events and effective sample size.
Validate and operate asymptotic uncertainty using simulation/resampling, design-aware estimators, monitoring and safe reporting.

deepSections.title: Law of large numbers and consistency
deepSections.body:
For IID variables with finite expectation μ, the weak LLN says the sample mean converges in probability to μ: for any ε>0, probability of an error larger than ε goes to zero. Strong LLN gives almost-sure convergence under conditions. Neither supplies a finite-sample confidence level by itself. Convergence can be slow for heavy-tailed/skewed data, and an average of biased or selected samples converges to the wrong population expectation.

Variance of an IID sample mean is σ²/n when finite, which supports Chebyshev bounds and explains noise reduction. Dependence adds covariance terms; positive correlation can keep variance much larger. Identical distribution is not always required—there are LLNs for non-identical and dependent sequences—but assumptions must match the design. Nonstationary data may converge to a moving or mixture target with little decision value.

Consistency of an estimator means convergence to the target as information grows. More rows created by duplicating events do not add information. Population target, sampling frame, weighting and observation process must be defined before invoking the LLN.

deepSections.title: CLT, standardization, and intervals
deepSections.body:
For IID finite-variance X_i, the classical CLT states `(ΣX_i−nμ)/(σ√n)=√n(Ȳ−μ)/σ` converges in distribution to N(0,1). Thus the sampling distribution of Ȳ is approximately Normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n for sufficiently suitable n. Replacing σ by a consistent estimate yields common large-sample intervals; small Normal-population samples lead to t distributions when variance is estimated.

The approximation concerns repeated samples of the statistic, not the empirical distribution of observations. A skewed Exponential population can have approximately Normal sample means. Berry–Esseen-type results show error depends on third absolute moment and √n under conditions, explaining why tail/skew matter. A continuity correction can improve Normal approximation to lattice/discrete counts.

For Bernoulli p, mean is p and variance p(1−p), but Wald intervals can fail near 0/1 or with few expected successes/failures. Wilson, exact or Bayesian methods may be better. The delta method linearizes smooth transformations g(Ȳ), giving approximate variance `(g'(μ))²σ²/n`; it fails near nonsmooth points or singular derivatives.

deepSections.title: Dependence, clustering, and heavy tails
deepSections.body:
Repeated events within a user, classroom, hospital or time block are correlated. If clusters are independent but observations within cluster are not, treat clusters as sampling units and use cluster-robust estimators or aggregate/cluster bootstrap. Time series require long-run variance including autocovariances and may use HAC, block bootstrap or explicit models. Effective sample size can be far below row count.

Heavy-tailed distributions may have finite mean but enormous/infinite variance, slowing LLN and invalidating the classical finite-variance CLT. Stable-law limits can replace Normal scaling. Outliers are then expected under the model, not necessarily data errors. Robust estimators such as trimmed means or median-of-means target related quantities/offer different guarantees and should be chosen explicitly.

Sampling without replacement from a finite population introduces dependence and finite-population corrections. Survey weights, unequal probabilities and stratification change variance. Adaptive experiments and sequential monitoring create dependence between stopping and estimates; always-valid methods or pre-specified sequential designs are needed rather than repeated fixed-horizon intervals.

deepSections.title: Validate and operate asymptotic approximations
deepSections.body:
Simulate from a plausible data-generating/design model and examine standardized statistic histograms, quantiles and interval coverage at actual n. Bootstrap resamples according to independent units, not rows by default. Compare analytic standard errors with cluster/block/bootstrap estimates and inspect sensitivity to influential units. Coverage on synthetic IID data validates implementation, not real-world assumptions.

Version target population, unit, estimator, window, weights, clustering/time rule, standard-error method and stopping policy. Monitor cluster counts/sizes, autocorrelation, tail metrics, effective sample size, label delay and composition drift. Report numerator/denominator and uncertainty together. Avoid displaying false precision or treating overlapping intervals as a complete hypothesis test.

Use reproducible independent random streams for simulation, bound resample cost and protect row/unit data. If diagnostics show poor approximation, use design-based exact/randomization methods, robust/bootstrap alternatives, larger independent sample or abstain. Keep prior metric/uncertainty implementation for rollback and backtest new methods on archived windows without peeking into active decisions.

exercises.prompt: What quantity converges to Normal in the IID CLT?

lab.goal: Simulate non-Normal sample means, verify `1/sqrt(n)` standard-error scaling and approximate CLT interval coverage with reproducible streams.
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(20260821); reps=20000
means_25=rng.exponential(1.0,size=(reps,25)).mean(axis=1)
means_100=rng.exponential(1.0,size=(reps,100)).mean(axis=1)
# independent coverage experiment
samples=rng.exponential(1.0,size=(5000,100))
covered=np.mean([lo<=1.0<=hi for lo,hi in (interval(row) for row in samples)])
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(means_25.mean()-1)<.01 and abs(means_100.mean()-1)<.01
ratio=means_25.std(ddof=1)/means_100.std(ddof=1)
assert abs(ratio-2)<.08
standardized=np.sqrt(100)*(means_100-1.0)
assert abs(standardized.mean())<.03 and abs(standardized.std(ddof=1)-1)<.03
assert .935<covered<.96
# Raw exponential data stay skewed even when means are closer to Normal.
raw=rng.exponential(1.0,size=100000)
assert np.quantile(raw,.9)>2.2

lessons.title: Confidence Intervals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A 95% frequentist confidence interval comes from a procedure that would contain the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its model and sampling assumptions. After observing one interval, the fixed parameter is either inside it or not; 95% is not its posterior probability. A useful answer states the estimand, construction, assumptions, and whether the interval excludes both the null value and business-relevant thresholds. Use design-aware, profile, score, or bootstrap intervals when a simple symmetric Wald interval is unreliable.
keyPoints: Estimate plus critical value times SE is only one construction
Bias is not represented by a narrow interval
Prediction intervals include future outcome noise
lessons.why: Point estimates conceal sampling uncertainty and invite false precision. A model may improve AUC by 0.003, a campaign may lift conversion by 0.4 points, or a latency change may save 5 ms; without an interval, readers cannot judge which alternatives remain compatible with the data. Interviews test the notorious 95% interpretation, but the deeper skill is selecting an interval that matches the estimator and design. In product decisions, an interval that crosses zero may still rule out material harm, while a statistically positive interval may lie entirely below the minimum worthwhile effect. Coverage can fail because of bias, dependence, optional stopping, post-selection, boundary parameters, or an inappropriate asymptotic approximation. Reporting more decimal places does not repair those failures. A defensible interval is tied to an estimand and a repeatable procedure, not a decorative error bar.
lessons.intuition: Imagine a machine that repeatedly samples data and draws an interval using the same recipe. Lay those intervals across a horizontal line marking the fixed true mean. A 95% procedure misses about five of every hundred lines in the long run, assuming the recipe's conditions. The individual interval does not move after it is observed; the randomness was in the data and therefore in the endpoints. Increasing confidence makes the machine draw wider lines, because it must capture the truth more often. Increasing independent information usually narrows them. Prediction is harder than parameter estimation: a future observation includes both uncertainty about the mean and its own irreducible noise, so a prediction interval is wider. Bayesian credible intervals answer a different probability question by conditioning on data and a prior. Neither language should be borrowed without its assumptions.
lessons.deepDive: Confidence intervals invert a family of tests or use a pivotal, asymptotic, likelihood, or resampling construction. The familiar estimate plus-or-minus critical-value times SE works well only when the estimator is approximately symmetric and the SE is reliable. The construction, not the label '95%', determines actual coverage.
lessons.math: For iid normal observations with unknown variance, (Xbar-mu)/(S/sqrt(n)) follows t with n-1 degrees of freedom, yielding Xbar +/- t_(1-alpha/2,n-1) S/sqrt(n). A prediction interval for a new normal observation uses S sqrt(1+1/n), which is wider. For an asymptotically normal estimator theta_hat, theta_hat +/- z_(1-alpha/2) estimated-SE is a Wald interval. Inverting a two-sided level-alpha test gives the set of theta0 values not rejected. These formulas do not include design bias or post-selection uncertainty unless explicitly modeled.
lessons.workedExample: An experiment estimates conversion lift at +1.2 percentage points with a 95% interval [-0.2, 2.6]. Zero is inside, so a matching two-sided 5% test would not reject a zero effect. But decision-making needs thresholds. If a loss greater than -0.5 points is unacceptable, the interval rules out that magnitude of harm under the procedure. If launch requires at least +1.0 point, the interval still includes effects below the threshold, so benefit is uncertain. Saying 'no effect' discards this information. The report should state randomization unit, estimator, repeated-peeking policy, confidence construction, and whether guardrail intervals are adjusted for multiplicity.
lessons.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
x=np.array([10,11,12,9,13,12,11])
mean=x.mean(); se=stats.sem(x)
print(stats.t.interval(.95, df=len(x)-1, loc=mean, scale=se))
commonMistakes: Assigning 95% posterior probability to a fixed frequentist parameter.
Treating failure to reject as proof of equality or no effect.
Using symmetric Wald intervals for bounded or strongly skewed quantities without checking coverage.
Ignoring clustering, repeated peeking, model selection, or multiple reported intervals.
Confusing a confidence interval for a mean with a prediction interval for a future observation.

followUps.question: Why does a 99% interval tend to be wider than a 95% interval?
followUps.answer: The procedure must capture the target in a larger fraction of repeated samples, so the critical value moves farther into the reference distribution's tails while the data and SE stay fixed.

followUps.question: What does it mean when a 95% interval includes zero?
followUps.answer: A matching two-sided 5% test does not reject zero. It does not prove zero, and it does not answer whether material harm or useful benefit has been ruled out. Inspect the full interval against predefined thresholds.

followUps.question: When is a bootstrap interval appropriate?
followUps.answer: When the sample represents the repetition mechanism and analytic uncertainty is difficult. Resampling must preserve clusters, pairs, time blocks, stratification, and refitting steps. It cannot repair selection bias or an unrepresentative sample.

lessons.production: Store interval method and assumptions with every metric definition: estimand, unit, confidence level, sidedness, variance estimator, resampling unit, stopping rule, and multiplicity family. Run coverage simulations before deploying important decision thresholds, including boundary rates and realistic cluster sizes. Monitor effective sample size, missingness, variance, weight concentration, and interval width. Do not suppress wide intervals; they are evidence of limited information. Use sequential confidence sequences for continuous monitoring rather than repeatedly recomputing fixed-horizon intervals. Limit small-slice output for privacy and stability. Version random seeds and software APIs for bootstrap results. If a pipeline changes attribution or unit grain, invalidate old intervals. Roll back the estimator and uncertainty method together. Dashboards should show point estimate, interval, sample window, and practical thresholds, with plain-language caveats rather than a green/red significance badge.
lessons.description: A confidence interval is the output of a procedure designed to cover an unknown target at a stated long-run rate under specified assumptions. This chapter builds that sentence into a practical workflow. It derives a t interval for a mean, explains the duality between two-sided tests and intervals, distinguishes confidence intervals from credible and prediction intervals, and compares normal, t, Wilson, profile-likelihood, and bootstrap constructions. It emphasizes that confidence level is a property of the procedure before data are observed—not a posterior probability assigned to a fixed frequentist parameter afterward. You will learn why interval width responds to standard error and confidence level, how bias and optional stopping destroy nominal coverage, why a symmetric Wald interval can be absurd near boundaries, and how to communicate compatibility without reducing inference to “significant” or “not significant.” The worked example treats a conversion lift whose interval crosses both zero and a business threshold. The lab verifies repeated-sample coverage and shows that one observed interval either covers or does not.
learningObjectives: Interpret frequentist confidence intervals through repeated-sample coverage without assigning probability to a fixed parameter.
Construct and diagnose t, proportion, bootstrap, and prediction intervals under their assumptions.
Connect interval width to standard error, confidence level, sample design, and multiplicity.
Use intervals to reason about practical thresholds, equivalence, and uncertainty rather than binary significance.

deepSections.title: Coverage and the repeated-sampling statement
deepSections.body: Let C(X) be a random set computed from data X. A 1-alpha confidence procedure satisfies P_theta(theta in C(X)) at least or approximately 1-alpha under a model for each relevant theta. Probability ranges over hypothetical datasets. After X=x is observed, C(x) is fixed in frequentist analysis. Saying '95% probability theta lies here' silently changes frameworks unless a posterior distribution has been defined. Coverage may be exact, conservative, or asymptotic. An exact binomial interval can overcover because discreteness prevents every nominal level; an asymptotic interval may undercover in small samples. Simulation across plausible parameter values is an effective coverage audit.

deepSections.title: Choosing a construction instead of defaulting to Wald
deepSections.body: For a normal mean with unknown variance and iid normal observations, Xbar plus-or-minus t critical times s/sqrt(n) has exact model-based coverage. Large-sample estimators often use a normal Wald interval. Wald intervals can extend outside valid ranges for probabilities or rates and can perform poorly with skewness, separation, weak identification, or boundaries. Score/Wilson intervals for proportions, likelihood-ratio/profile intervals, transformations such as log scale, and bootstrap intervals can behave better. Bootstrap percentile intervals inherit bias and skewness issues; basic and BCa variants make different corrections. The method must preserve pairing, clusters, stratification, and the estimator's complete fitting pipeline.

deepSections.title: Intervals, tests, equivalence, and practical thresholds
deepSections.body: For a two-sided level-alpha test and a matching 1-alpha interval, a candidate null value is rejected exactly when it falls outside the interval. The interval communicates more because it shows a range of compatible effect sizes. Failure to exclude zero is not proof of no effect. To support practical equivalence, predefine a smallest effect of interest and use an equivalence procedure such as two one-sided tests; the interval must lie within the equivalence bounds. For noninferiority, direction and margin must be set before data. Inspect whether the interval excludes material harm, excludes the minimum worthwhile benefit, or remains decision-ambiguous. These questions connect inference to loss and action.

deepSections.title: Why nominal coverage fails
deepSections.body: Coverage is conditional on design and analysis discipline. Selection bias shifts the estimator without widening its standard error. Repeated peeking and stopping when an interval becomes favorable change its coverage unless sequential methods are used. Selecting the best model, subgroup, or metric and then reporting its ordinary interval ignores selection. Autocorrelation and clustering make iid SEs too small. Weak instruments, rare outcomes, heavy tails, and small samples can make asymptotic shapes poor. Missing data and measurement error introduce additional assumptions. Run design-aware simulations, negative controls, sensitivity analyses, and specification checks; no interval summarizes unmodeled uncertainty automatically.

deepSections.title: Marginal, conditional, and simultaneous coverage
deepSections.body: Nominal coverage is often marginal over the sampling distribution. It need not provide 95% coverage within every covariate slice, after selecting extreme estimates, or simultaneously across many parameters. A model may have correct average coverage while severely undercovering rare segments. Conditional intervals seek validity given relevant features but are harder to obtain without assumptions. Simultaneous confidence regions or bands protect an entire family of parameters or a function, and are wider than pointwise intervals. When users inspect whichever subgroup looks most interesting, ordinary pointwise intervals no longer describe that selection. Decide whether the consumer needs one prespecified parameter, all time points on a curve, or a selected winner, then choose the corresponding inferential target and verify coverage by scenario.

workedExamples.title: Conversion lift against two decision thresholds
workedExamples.body: Interpret the same interval relative to the null, a harm boundary, and a minimum worthwhile benefit. The conclusion changes with the decision question even though the statistical evidence does not.

exercises.prompt: Interpret a 95% interval [2, 8] for a mean difference.
exercises.solution: Under repeated use of the stated procedure and its assumptions, 95% of intervals cover the fixed true difference. This observed interval excludes zero and contains effect sizes from 2 through 8; it is not a 95% posterior probability statement.

exercises.prompt: A mean has SE 3. Approximately how does quadrupling independent n affect SE?
exercises.solution: SE scales approximately as 1/sqrt(n), so quadrupling n halves SE to about 1.5, assuming the same variance and independent information.

exercises.prompt: Why can a narrow interval be misleading in a convenience sample?
exercises.solution: The interval typically represents sampling variability under its model, not selection bias. A large convenience sample can concentrate tightly around the wrong population target.

visuals.title: Repeated intervals and fixed truth
visuals.caption: Conceptual: intervals vary across samples while the target remains fixed; nominal coverage describes the procedure.

visuals.title: Interval families answer different questions
visuals.caption: Use the language belonging to the construction and probability model.

lab.goal: Verify long-run coverage of a t interval and show why an observed confidence interval is not a posterior probability statement.
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import t
rng_np = np.random.default_rng(11)
x = rng_np.normal(mu, 2.0, size=80)
se = x.std(ddof=1)/np.sqrt(x.size)
critical = t.ppf(0.975, df=x.size-1)
scipy_interval = (x.mean()-critical*se, x.mean()+critical*se)
lab.verifyIt:
coverage = sum(lo <= mu <= hi for lo,hi in intervals)/len(intervals)
assert 0.93 < coverage < 0.97
assert scipy_interval[0] < scipy_interval[1]
assert isinstance(scipy_interval, tuple)
lab.shipIt: Attach estimand, unit, interval construction, confidence level, stopping rule, and practical thresholds to every reported interval; audit coverage with design-faithful simulation.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing & p-values
lessons.interviewAnswer: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null model and test assumptions, of obtaining a statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability the null is true, not the false-positive probability of this result, and not effect size. A complete test specifies the estimand, null and alternative, statistic, reference distribution, sidedness, alpha, and stopping rule before looking. Then report the estimate and interval, check assumptions and multiplicity, and interpret the result against practical costs.
keyPoints: The null is a complete enough data-generating claim to calibrate a statistic
p-values are conditional tail areas, not posterior probabilities
Alpha controls a procedure's Type I error under valid use
Power depends on a specific alternative
Evidence, effect magnitude, and action utility are distinct
lessons.why: Tests influence experiments, model comparisons, quality monitoring, medical evidence, and policy. Misinterpretation can ship useless features, suppress real harm, or manufacture discoveries by trying many analyses. A p-value can be numerically correct while answering the wrong question because the unit, outcome, subgroup, or null was chosen after inspection. Conversely, rigidly banning tests discards a useful calibration tool. Interviews focus on p-values because they expose conditional-probability reasoning and experimental discipline. The practical skill is to design a procedure whose error behavior matches the decision, then communicate what the result does and does not establish. The ASA explicitly warns against basing conclusions only on a threshold and against treating significance as effect importance. That principle belongs in analytics systems, not only academic papers.
lessons.intuition: Assume a card shuffler is fair and choose a score that grows when the observed sequence looks suspicious. Run the fair shuffler many times and see how often its score is at least as extreme. That frequency is a simulation picture of the p-value. A rare score says the data and the fair-shuffler model are in tension; it does not identify which assumption failed or calculate the probability of cheating. Alpha is a rule chosen before play that limits false alarms when the model holds. Power asks how often the rule detects a particular kind and size of cheating. If you inspect many scores and report only the strangest, the original calibration no longer applies. The same logic governs product tests: define the metric and analysis before observing treatment labels, respect assignment, and separate evidence from business value.
lessons.deepDive: A test maps data to a decision or evidence measure with known behavior under a null model. Validity comes from the sampling or randomization distribution, not from the vocabulary of significance. Parametric, permutation, and exact tests differ in how that reference distribution is obtained.
lessons.math: For statistic T and observed t, an upper-tail p-value is P_H0(T>=t); a two-sided definition must specify how both tails are ordered. A level-alpha test has sup over theta in H0 of P_theta(reject)<=alpha. At alternative theta1, power is P_theta1(reject)=1-beta(theta1). For a normal mean with known sigma, Z=(Xbar-mu0)/(sigma/sqrt(n)); reject a two-sided H0 at level alpha when |Z|>z_(1-alpha/2). The matching interval excludes mu0 exactly when the test rejects. These probabilities describe repeated procedure behavior.
lessons.code:
from scipy import stats
# Example: compare two independent sample means
a = [10, 11, 9, 12, 10]
b = [13, 14, 12, 13, 15]
stat, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b, equal_var=False)
print(stat, p)
commonMistakes: Saying p=0.03 means a 97% probability the alternative is true.
Treating p>=0.05 as evidence of equality or no effect.
Choosing a one-sided test after seeing the effect direction.
Ignoring repeated peeking, multiple metrics, subgroup search, or model-selection attempts.
Reporting significance without effect size, interval, assumptions, or practical threshold.

followUps.question: What is the difference between alpha and a p-value?
followUps.answer: Alpha is a prechosen operating threshold for a procedure's Type I error. The p-value is a data-dependent tail area under H0. Comparing them implements a rule, but they are not the same probability.

followUps.question: Does p=0.001 prove the alternative?
followUps.answer: No. It indicates strong incompatibility with the specified null model for the chosen statistic, assuming the design and analysis are valid. It does not rule out bias, misspecification, multiplicity, or data errors.

followUps.question: How should continuous experiment monitoring be handled?
followUps.answer: Use a prespecified group-sequential design, alpha-spending rule, confidence sequence, or other always-valid method. Fixed-horizon tests repeatedly inspected without adjustment lose their nominal error control.

lessons.production: Create an experiment or inference specification before data access: owner, population, unit, estimand, hypotheses, sidedness, primary and guardrail metrics, exclusions, covariance adjustment, alpha, power target, stopping rule, and multiplicity family. Validate sample-ratio balance, exposure logging, missing outcomes, cluster dependence, novelty effects, and implementation integrity. Store all attempted analyses and immutable code/data versions. Dashboards should display estimates, intervals, practical thresholds, and sequential status; avoid binary green labels. Restrict small-cell data and secure sensitive subgroup results. Monitor repeated-test false-alert rates with simulations. If analysis code changes after results, label it exploratory and obtain fresh confirmation. Rollback decisions should consider guardrail harm and reversibility, while preserving the original audit trail. A centralized metric registry prevents silent redefinition across teams.
lessons.workedExample: A feature raises conversion from 10.00% to 10.08% in a very large experiment and produces p=0.004. The result is difficult to reconcile with an exact zero-effect model under the planned analysis, but the estimated lift is only 0.08 percentage points. If engineering and support costs require at least 0.30 points, statistical significance does not justify launch. Report the 95% interval, guardrail effects, assignment diagnostics, sample-ratio checks, and the predefined minimum detectable and worthwhile effects. If the team inspected the result daily using a fixed-horizon test, p=0.004 may not retain its advertised calibration; use the planned sequential method or re-run a confirmatory experiment.

lab.goal: Build an exact sign-flip randomization test, compare its tail count with SciPy, and verify null calibration by construction.
lab.useIt:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import permutation_test
result = permutation_test((np.asarray(diffs),), lambda x: np.mean(x), permutation_type='samples', alternative='two-sided', n_resamples=np.inf)
lab.verifyIt:
assert len(null_stats) == 2**len(diffs)
assert 0.0 <= p_value <= 1.0
assert abs(p_value-result.pvalue) < 1e-12
assert sign_flip_pvalue([1.0,-1.0,2.0,-2.0])[0] == 1.0
lab.shipIt: Prespecify the statistic and exchangeability/randomization mechanism, log every analysis, use sequentially valid monitoring, and report effect estimates and intervals with the p-value.

lessons.description: Hypothesis testing is a calibrated procedure for measuring how incompatible observed data are with a specified null model, not a machine for assigning truth probabilities to hypotheses. This chapter connects the scientific question, estimand, null and alternative, test statistic, reference distribution, p-value, decision rule, Type I error, Type II error, power, effect size, and confidence interval. It contrasts Fisher-style evidence with Neyman–Pearson decision rules without pretending that one p-value settles a scientific or product decision. You will learn how sidedness, optional stopping, model assumptions, randomization, and multiple testing alter validity; why “fail to reject” is not “accept”; and why a tiny p-value may accompany a negligible effect in a huge dataset. The worked example separates statistical evidence from launch utility. The lab implements a one-sample randomization test and verifies its tail count against SciPy. Production guidance covers preregistration, metric governance, sequential monitoring, audit trails, privacy, and reporting estimates with uncertainty rather than threshold badges.
learningObjectives: Translate a domain question into an estimand, explicit null/alternative, statistic, and valid reference distribution.
Interpret p-values, Type I/II errors, and power without common probability reversals.
Choose sidedness and stopping rules before observing results and diagnose assumption violations.
Report effect estimates, intervals, practical thresholds, and multiplicity context alongside test results.

deepSections.title: From question to calibrated statistic
deepSections.body: Start with the target population and estimand, such as the intention-to-treat difference in 14-day retention. State H0 and a scientifically meaningful alternative. Choose a statistic sensitive to that alternative. Derive or simulate its distribution under H0 while preserving the design. Define one- or two-sided extremeness and alpha before inspecting results. A two-sided test spends error in both directions; a one-sided test is justified only when the opposite direction would not trigger a claim and was excluded in advance. Nuisance parameters may be estimated, conditioned out, or handled through asymptotics. Every choice affects calibration.

deepSections.title: p-values, alpha, and the two error types
deepSections.body: The p-value P_H0(T at least as extreme as t_obs) conditions on H0. It does not provide P(H0|data), which would require prior odds and likelihoods. Alpha is the maximum or nominal probability of rejection under H0 for a fixed procedure. A Type I error rejects a true null. A Type II error fails to reject under a specified alternative; beta and power 1-beta depend on effect size, variance, design, and sample size. A p-value above alpha does not prove H0, because the study may be underpowered or the statistic insensitive. The observed p-value is not the achieved Type I error rate or the probability the decision is wrong.

deepSections.title: Assumptions, optional stopping, and researcher degrees of freedom
deepSections.body: A t test relies on independence and a reference model or approximation; a randomization test relies on assignment and a sharp or otherwise specified null; a permutation test relies on exchangeability for the chosen shuffle. Repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon p-value and stopping below 0.05 inflates false positives. Trying transformations, exclusions, subgroups, outcomes, and covariates until one passes does the same. Pre-specification, held-out confirmation, sequential tests, alpha-spending, or always-valid evidence processes restore calibration for their settings. Log every analysis attempt, not only the successful query. Model diagnostics matter because a small p-value may reflect outliers, dependence, or misspecification rather than the intended alternative.

deepSections.title: Evidence is not effect size or utility
deepSections.body: With enough independent observations, a negligible deviation can yield a tiny p-value; with few observations, a valuable effect can remain uncertain. Report the estimate and interval against minimum worthwhile benefit and maximum acceptable harm. Decision theory adds costs, opportunity, reversibility, and prior information. Equivalence and noninferiority tests answer targeted absence-of-material-difference questions; ordinary failure to reject does not. Multiple outcomes require a defined family and error criterion. Replication and external validity matter after internal calibration. A test is one input to a decision record, not an automatic launch switch.

deepSections.title: Exact, conservative, and asymptotic validity
deepSections.body: A level claim can be exact for every finite sample under a design, conservative because discreteness prevents using all alpha, or asymptotic as sample size grows. The label p-value does not reveal which. Small cell counts, boundary parameters, weak identification, or estimated nuisance quantities can make an asymptotic reference inaccurate. Exact conditioning may protect size but lose power or target a narrower null. Parametric bootstrap and permutation calibration can improve finite-sample behavior when their models are credible. Before deployment, simulate the complete procedure at several null parameter settings, not only one convenient point. The maximum false-rejection rate across relevant nulls is the operating characteristic that a composite-null level claim must control.

workedExamples.title: A precise but economically negligible lift
workedExamples.body: Separate incompatibility with an exact-zero null from the magnitude and value of the estimated effect. Then audit stopping and multiplicity before using the nominal p-value.

exercises.prompt: Define a p-value in one conditional-probability sentence.
exercises.solution: It is the probability, under the specified null model and assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

exercises.prompt: A test returns p=0.20 with 20% power for the effect of interest. Can you conclude no effect?
exercises.solution: No. The procedure frequently fails to reject when that effect exists. Report the interval and acknowledge that the data are weakly informative; consider a better-powered study.

exercises.prompt: Why is choosing one-sidedness after seeing the sign invalid?
exercises.solution: It uses the data twice and changes the tail rule to favor the observation, so the claimed Type I error calibration no longer matches the procedure actually used.

visuals.title: A defensible test
visuals.caption: Calibration begins before results are visible and ends with a decision richer than a threshold.

visuals.title: Null reference and observed tail
visuals.caption: Conceptual: the p-value is the reference-model tail at least as extreme as the observed statistic.

sourceNotes.contribution: Provides authoritative principles for interpreting and reporting p-values without threshold misuse.
Provides formal test construction, error rates, power, and likelihood-based inference foundations.
Documents current exact, permutation, and Monte Carlo testing interfaces used in the lab.

lessons.title: A/B Testing & Statistical Power
lessons.interviewAnswer: An A/B test randomly assigns eligible units to control or treatment, so treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes in expectation. The intention-to-treat effect is the difference in arm means using every assigned unit under a prespecified analysis. Before launch I define the unit, population, primary metric, guardrails, alpha, power, MDE, duration, and stopping rule. During analysis I check assignment and exposure integrity, especially SRM, then report effect size and interval alongside p-value. I do not treat nonsignificance as no effect, peek with a fixed-horizon test, or ship a statistically significant but operationally harmful result.
keyPoints: Randomization identifies a causal intention-to-treat contrast
The randomization unit determines independence and effective sample size
Power depends on variance, baseline, allocation, alpha, and decision-relevant MDE
Effect size and uncertainty matter more than a significance label
Trust checks and guardrails precede launch interpretation
lessons.why: Observational product metrics confound feature exposure with who chose, qualified for, or successfully loaded the feature. Random assignment breaks that systematic link and enables a transparent causal comparison. Small product effects can be worth millions, but large samples can make trivial changes significant, while underpowered tests routinely miss useful changes. A/B testing also fails when instrumentation differs by variant, users switch identities, or one user's treatment affects another. Interviews test whether candidates understand design and decision quality, not only a z-test formula. In production, trustworthy experimentation is a platform capability involving assignment, logging, metrics, inference, alerting, review, and safe deployment.
lessons.intuition: Each eligible user has two potential outcomes: what would happen under control and under treatment, but only one is observed. Randomization creates two groups that are comparable before treatment, so their average outcome difference estimates the missing counterfactual contrast. Sampling noise means the estimate moves across repeated experiments; an interval describes compatible effect sizes under assumptions. Power is the chance that the planned rule detects a chosen true effect. A smaller MDE demands more information. The result should answer a decision: whether benefits exceed a practical threshold while guardrails remain safe, not merely whether exact zero can be rejected.
lessons.deepDive: The experiment is a chain from causal estimand through randomized assignment, measurement, statistical estimator, and decision rule. Breaking any link can produce precise evidence about the wrong population or outcome.
lessons.math: Let p_T=x_T/n_T and p_C=x_C/n_C. Estimated absolute effect d=p_T-p_C. An unpooled standard error for an interval is sqrt(p_T(1-p_T)/n_T+p_C(1-p_C)/n_C); a null z-test often uses pooled p=(x_T+x_C)/(n_T+n_C). Approximate equal-arm sample per group for a mean effect delta is 2 sigma^2(z_{1-alpha/2}+z_{1-beta})^2/delta^2. Relative lift is d/p_C when p_C>0. These formulas assume independent units and the stated fixed-horizon plan.
lessons.workedExample: Checkout conversion is 10%, and the smallest worthwhile absolute improvement is 0.5 percentage points. With two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power, planning uses baseline variance and a two-proportion calculation, then inflates for exclusions defined before assignment and a complete weekly cycle. Observed control is 10.1% and treatment 10.45%, an effect of +0.35 points with a 95% interval from -0.05 to +0.75. The result is compatible with small harm and a worthwhile gain, so it is inconclusive for the +0.5-point decision threshold despite a positive point estimate. Guardrail latency also worsened; the team does not ship and instead diagnoses performance before a new test.
lessons.code:
# Conceptual experiment checklist
experiment = {
  "unit": "user",
  "primary_metric": "conversion",
  "alpha": 0.05,
  "power": 0.80,
  "guardrails": ["latency", "error_rate"]
}

commonMistakes.mistake: Interpreting p>0.05 as no effect
commonMistakes.correction: It means the planned test did not reject its null; inspect the interval to see which harms and benefits remain compatible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Powering for any detectable effect
commonMistakes.correction: Choose a decision-relevant MDE using value and risk; arbitrary tiny effects create impractical sample demands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Analyzing only exposed users
commonMistakes.correction: Exposure is post-assignment and may be treatment-dependent; ITT preserves randomization unless a valid triggered design was specified.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring guardrails after a primary win
commonMistakes.correction: A primary metric does not compensate for unacceptable reliability, safety, fairness, or cost harm.

followUps.question: What is the difference between statistical and practical significance?
followUps.answer: Statistical significance concerns evidence against a null under a procedure; practical significance asks whether the magnitude justifies action given costs, thresholds, and risks.

followUps.question: Why is 50/50 allocation common?
followUps.answer: For equal per-unit variance and cost, balanced arms minimize variance for a fixed total sample. Risk, capacity, or multi-arm designs can justify another ratio.

followUps.question: What does randomization guarantee?
followUps.answer: In expectation it balances pre-treatment potential-outcome determinants under a correct assignment mechanism. It does not fix missing data, interference, broken logging, or chance imbalance in one realization.

lessons.production: Version the hypothesis, estimand, eligibility query, unit, allocation, assignment salt, variants, power inputs, primary and guardrail metric contracts, analysis windows, multiplicity and stopping rules before launch. Log assignment and exposure separately with immutable timestamps. Ramp gradually behind kill switches. Monitor SRM, invariant metrics, crashes, latency, data loss, cross-variant contamination, and delayed outcomes without applying invalid fixed-horizon inference. Reproduce results from raw events and an independent assignment snapshot. Protect user privacy and small slices. Publish effect, interval, denominator, exclusions, diagnostic status, and decision. Rollback treatment serving immediately on guardrail breach while retaining assignment and evidence; never rewrite experiment history.

lab.goal: Implement a two-proportion A/B estimate, interval, null z-test, and approximate power calculation, then compare with statsmodels and verify invariants.
lab.useIt:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest
stat,pvalue=proportions_ztest([1045,1010],[10000,10000])
lab.verifyIt:
effect,interval,z,p=report
assert abs(effect-0.0035)<1e-12
assert interval[0]<effect<interval[1]
assert abs(z-stat)<1e-10 and abs(p-pvalue)<1e-10
assert planned_n>0
assert mean_sample_per_arm(sqrt(0.1*0.9),0.0025)>3*planned_n
reverse=ab_proportions(1010,10000,1045,10000)
assert abs(reverse[0]+effect)<1e-12
assert 0<=p<=1
lab.shipIt: Bind calculations to immutable assignment and metric snapshots, validate SRM and analysis-unit independence first, version alpha/MDE/stopping rules, monitor guardrails, and publish effects with intervals and denominators rather than significance labels alone.

lessons.description: A/B testing estimates the causal effect of a product or policy change by randomly assigning eligible experimental units to variants and comparing prespecified outcomes. This chapter connects potential outcomes, randomization, difference-in-means and difference-in-proportions estimators, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, Type I and II errors, statistical power, minimum detectable effect (MDE), practical significance, multiple metrics, heterogeneous effects, and decision rules. You will learn why randomization identifies an intention-to-treat effect, why exposure logging and unit choice matter, how baseline rate and variance determine sample size, and why a nonsignificant result is not proof of equivalence. A worked checkout experiment translates a business threshold into power, duration, and interpretation. The lab implements a two-proportion effect estimate, standard error, interval, z-test, and approximate sample-size calculation; compares with statsmodels; and verifies invariants using deterministic data. Production guidance covers assignment, sample-ratio mismatch, novelty, interference, sequential monitoring, data quality, privacy, guardrails, rollout, and rollback. The aim is a trustworthy decision process, not a ritual that converts every p-value below 0.05 into a launch.
learningObjectives: Define the estimand, eligible population, randomization unit, variants, outcomes, and decision threshold before observing results.
Compute and interpret treatment effects, uncertainty, p-values, power, and MDE for common independent-arm metrics.
Distinguish statistical significance, practical significance, equivalence, noninferiority, and inconclusive evidence.
Audit an online test for assignment, exposure, SRM, multiplicity, interference, and post-randomization bias.

deepSections.title: Population, unit, assignment, and estimand
deepSections.body: Specify eligibility before assignment, the experimental unit, allocation ratio, assignment mechanism, treatment versions, exposure semantics, and analysis population. User randomization fits persistent user experiences; session or request randomization may create carryover and correlated observations; cluster randomization protects shared treatment but reduces effective sample size. The intention-to-treat (ITT) estimand compares outcomes by assigned arm regardless of actual exposure and preserves randomization. Treatment-on-treated needs additional assumptions because exposure is post-randomization. Define analysis windows, delayed outcomes, triggered analyses, and exclusions without conditioning on treatment consequences. Persist assignment before serving and make it deterministic for stable identities.

deepSections.title: Effects, standard errors, intervals, and tests
deepSections.body: For independent arms, estimate a mean effect as mean(Y_T)-mean(Y_C), or a proportion effect as p_T-p_C. Its standard error combines arm variances divided by arm counts. A confidence interval is estimate plus or minus a critical value times standard error; it describes a procedure's repeated-sampling coverage, not a posterior probability that the fixed effect lies inside. A null test compares a statistic to its reference distribution under H0. Use the analysis unit implied by randomization, cluster-robust methods when assignment or dependence is clustered, and robust or bootstrap methods for heavy-tailed metrics. Report absolute and relative changes with denominators.

deepSections.title: Power, MDE, allocation, and duration
deepSections.body: Type I error alpha is the probability of rejecting a true null under the planned procedure; Type II error beta is missing a specified alternative, and power is 1-beta. MDE is a design input tied to the smallest effect worth reliably detecting, not a magical post-hoc boundary. Required sample grows roughly with variance and inverse squared effect. For proportions it depends on baseline rate; for clustered data it grows with the design effect. Equal allocation maximizes precision at equal per-unit cost, while asymmetric allocation can reflect treatment risk or capacity. Convert sample to duration using eligible traffic, weekday cycles, ramp plan, attrition, and delayed outcomes, not raw site traffic.

deepSections.title: From evidence to a launch decision
deepSections.body: Separate the null of exactly zero from practical hypotheses such as effect above a benefit threshold, noninferiority above an acceptable loss, or equivalence within a margin. A narrow interval entirely below the business threshold can support rejection even if statistically positive. A wide interval crossing harm and benefit is inconclusive, not no effect. Consider primary metric, prespecified guardrails, costs, risk, heterogeneity, novelty, and external validity. Multiple outcomes or segments require a family-wise or false-discovery plan when claims depend on searching. Report all prespecified metrics and analysis changes. A launch may still be staged because the experiment population, scale, or duration differs from full deployment.

deepSections.title: Trust checks and common experiment failures
deepSections.body: Before reading effects, verify assignment proportions, covariate balance appropriate to the design, mutually exclusive variants, stable identity, exposure delivery, event completeness, timestamps, and invariant metrics. Sample-ratio mismatch is a symptom requiring diagnosis, not a nuisance p-value to waive. Bots, duplicate users, missing events, cache behavior, or treatment-dependent logging can bias results. Peeking with fixed-horizon p-values inflates false positives. Network spillovers violate no-interference assumptions. Novelty and learning can make early effects transient. Run an A/A test and synthetic controls for the platform, but remember that passing checks does not prove every experiment valid.

workedExamples.title: A positive estimate that is not decision-ready
workedExamples.body: Translate a practical threshold into power, report the absolute effect interval, compare it with benefit and harm regions, and include guardrail evidence before deciding.

exercises.prompt: An interval is [-1%, +3%]. Can you claim no effect?
exercises.solution: No. The data remain compatible with meaningful harm and benefit; the experiment is inconclusive for many practical thresholds.

exercises.prompt: What happens to sample size if MDE is halved?
exercises.solution: Under the usual approximation it grows by about four because sample is proportional to 1/delta^2.

exercises.prompt: Why analyze at user level when users were randomized?
exercises.solution: Repeated events within a user are correlated; treating events as independent overstates information and understates uncertainty.

visuals.title: Trustworthy A/B test lifecycle
visuals.caption: Inference is one stage in a larger causal and operational control system.

visuals.title: Three evidence regions
visuals.caption: A p-value alone cannot distinguish these operationally different outcomes.

sourceNotes.contribution: Provides a peer-reviewed practical foundation for online randomization, power, variance reduction, pitfalls, and trustworthy causal interpretation.
Documents current power, sample-size, and proportion-test implementations used for idiomatic verification.
Provides university-level hypothesis testing, confidence interval, multiple-testing, and power foundations.
Provides large-scale platform experience on assignment, metrics, trust checks, and operational decision making.

lessons.title: MLE vs MAP
lessons.interviewAnswer: MLE maximizes p(data|theta), treating the observed data as fixed and theta as the optimization variable. MAP maximizes p(data|theta)p(theta), equivalently log likelihood plus log prior. A zero-mean Gaussian prior often yields an L2 penalty and a Laplace prior an L1 penalty, with scaling determined by noise and prior parameters. Both return point estimates; MAP is not full Bayesian inference and is not invariant to arbitrary reparameterization. Validate the model, identifiability, optimization, and predictive calibration separately.
keyPoints: Likelihood is a function of parameters, not a normalized parameter probability
Logs turn products into stable sums
MAP adds prior information and can regularize weak data
A converged optimizer can fit a wrong or unidentified model
lessons.why: MLE connects probability assumptions to losses used throughout statistics and machine learning. Squared error follows from Gaussian observation noise; cross-entropy follows from Bernoulli or categorical likelihoods. MAP explains one source of regularization and makes prior commitments explicit. Without this foundation, practitioners treat losses as arbitrary functions and misread penalties as universally equivalent priors. In interviews, likelihood questions test conditional reasoning and optimization. In production, a misspecified likelihood can yield poor tail probabilities or calibration even when predictive ranking looks good. A prior chosen for numerical convenience may dominate low-volume segments. Conversely, unregularized MLE can diverge under complete separation or overfit sparse categories. Estimation is therefore both a mathematical objective and an engineering contract about data generation.
lessons.intuition: Suppose a coin produced eight heads and two tails. MLE asks: which head probability would make this exact outcome pattern most plausible? The answer is 0.8. MAP adds a prior belief, perhaps that extreme probabilities are uncommon, then finds the peak after combining evidence and prior. With little data, the prior moves the estimate; with abundant regular data, the likelihood usually dominates. The posterior mean averages parameter values under the posterior, while MAP selects only its highest point, so they need not match. In a multimodal posterior the MAP may describe one narrow peak while ignoring substantial mass elsewhere. In high-dimensional models, a penalty can stabilize the optimizer, but it also encodes geometry and scale. Standardizing features changes what an isotropic coefficient prior means.
lessons.deepDive: A statistical model is a family p(x|theta). After observing x, the likelihood L(theta;x) is that same expression viewed as a function of theta. It need not integrate to one over theta. Bayes' rule normalizes likelihood times prior to obtain a posterior density when a prior is defined.
lessons.math: For Bernoulli data with k successes in n trials, log L(p)=k log p+(n-k)log(1-p), whose MLE is k/n for 0<k<n. With Beta(a,b) prior, the posterior is Beta(a+k,b+n-k). For a+k>1 and b+n-k>1, MAP=(a+k-1)/(a+b+n-2), while posterior mean=(a+k)/(a+b+n). For Gaussian linear regression y=Xw+epsilon, epsilon~N(0,sigma^2 I), plus w~N(0,tau^2 I), negative log posterior is ||y-Xw||^2/(2sigma^2)+||w||^2/(2tau^2)+constant, so MAP is ridge with lambda=sigma^2/tau^2 under an unnormalized squared-error convention.
lessons.workedExample: A segment has 1 conversion in 2 visits. Bernoulli MLE is 0.5, a volatile estimate. With Beta(2,8) prior, posterior is Beta(3,9). MAP=(3-1)/(3+9-2)=0.20 and posterior mean=3/12=0.25. The different values are not contradictions: they optimize different loss or density criteria. A predictive probability for the next Bernoulli trial equals the posterior mean 0.25, not necessarily the mode. The prior represents eight pseudo-observations only under this conjugate interpretation and must be justified using prior data or domain knowledge, not chosen after seeing the segment outcome.
lessons.code:
# Negative log-likelihood + L2 prior (schematic)
loss = data_negative_log_likelihood + lambda_ * (weights**2).sum()
commonMistakes: Calling L(theta;x) a probability distribution over theta without a prior and normalization.
Saying MAP is full Bayesian inference or always equals the posterior mean.
Claiming L2 always means the same Gaussian prior without tracking objective scaling and feature units.
Trusting optimizer convergence without checking identifiability, boundaries, local modes, or misspecification.
Using an outcome-informed prior or regularization search on the final evaluation data.

followUps.question: Why maximize log likelihood?
followUps.answer: Log is monotone, so the maximizer is unchanged; products become sums, gradients are simpler, and numerical underflow is reduced. Stable implementations still use log-sum-exp and distribution-specific log-probability functions.

followUps.question: When do MLE and MAP become similar?
followUps.answer: When regular, highly informative data make the likelihood sharply concentrated relative to a smooth positive prior near the optimum. This is not guaranteed with weak identification, boundaries, high dimension, or a prior that excludes the likelihood optimum.

followUps.question: Why is MAP not invariant to reparameterization?
followUps.answer: A posterior density acquires a Jacobian under transformation, and the highest density point can move beyond simply transforming the old mode. Posterior probabilities transform consistently, but density modes depend on coordinates.

lessons.production: Define support, parameterization, likelihood, censoring/missingness assumptions, prior source, feature scaling, and hyperparameter-selection data. Use distribution log-probability functions, stable transforms, gradient checks, multiple initializations, and convergence diagnostics. Test analytic estimates on synthetic data with known parameters and on boundary cases. Monitor calibration, residuals, tail scores, parameter drift, condition numbers, prior-to-data influence, and optimizer failures. Persist software, seed, initialization, data snapshot, objective scaling, and convergence status. Protect sensitive priors and small-segment estimates. Set fallback estimates for sparse groups and abstain when identification is weak. Rollback must restore preprocessing and prior settings alongside parameters. For high-stakes decisions, propagate uncertainty through posterior predictive or validated frequentist procedures rather than treating a MAP point as certainty.
lessons.description: Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameter values that make the observed data most likely under a specified statistical model. Maximum a posteriori estimation multiplies that likelihood by a prior density and chooses the posterior mode. This chapter carefully distinguishes probability of data given parameters from a probability distribution over parameters, derives log-likelihood objectives for Bernoulli and Gaussian models, connects Gaussian and Laplace priors to common regularizers, and explains why MAP remains a point estimate rather than full Bayesian inference. You will learn how identifiability, constraints, reparameterization, boundary solutions, weak data, and misspecified likelihoods affect both methods; why maximizing a density is coordinate-sensitive; and why optimization convergence does not prove statistical validity. The worked example derives smoothed Bernoulli estimates and contrasts MLE, MAP, and posterior mean. The lab implements them from first principles and verifies against an analytic Beta–Binomial result. Production guidance covers numerical stability, calibration, prior governance, reproducibility, monitoring, and rollback when data or likelihood assumptions shift.
learningObjectives: Write likelihood and log-likelihood objectives without reversing their conditioning.
Derive MLE and MAP estimates for simple models and connect priors to regularization penalties.
Distinguish MAP, posterior mean, posterior predictive inference, and full posterior uncertainty.
Diagnose identifiability, numerical, boundary, prior, and misspecification failures in estimation.

deepSections.title: Likelihood, log-likelihood, and sufficient information
deepSections.body: For independent observations, L(theta)=product_i p(x_i|theta). Maximizing log L=sum_i log p(x_i|theta) gives the same optimizer because log is monotone, while avoiding underflow and exposing additive contributions. The score is the gradient of log likelihood; observed or expected information describes curvature and often determines asymptotic uncertainty. Sufficient statistics compress the sample without losing likelihood information about theta for a model—for a Bernoulli sample, the head count is sufficient. Likelihood compares parameter values conditional on the observed data; it is not P(theta|x). Likelihood ratios are invariant to parameter-independent constants, but absolute densities require careful units and support.

deepSections.title: MLE behavior: invariance, consistency, and failure modes
deepSections.body: Under regularity, identifiability, and correct specification, MLEs are often consistent and asymptotically normal with covariance related to inverse Fisher information. The MLE is invariant under one-to-one transformations: if eta=g(theta), eta_hat=g(theta_hat). Finite-sample bias can remain. Nonidentifiability creates ridges or multiple equivalent optima. Mixture likelihoods can be singular; logistic MLE can diverge under separation; variance estimates can hit boundaries. Local optimization may find a poor mode. Under misspecification, the MLE targets the closest model in a Kullback–Leibler sense rather than truth, and model-based standard errors may be wrong. Sandwich uncertainty and diagnostics may be needed.

deepSections.title: MAP, priors, and regularization scaling
deepSections.body: MAP maximizes log L(theta)+log pi(theta). A Gaussian N(0,tau squared) prior contributes -||theta|| squared/(2 tau squared); Gaussian observation variance also scales the data term, so the resulting ridge coefficient is not simply 'the prior' without conventions. An independent Laplace prior contributes an L1 penalty and may produce zeros at a posterior mode. Priors can encode signs, monotonicity, plausible scales, or hierarchical sharing more meaningfully than generic shrinkage. Hyperparameters must be chosen without outcome leakage and documented. MAP is sensitive to parameterization because a density transforms with a Jacobian; posterior probabilities are invariant when transformed correctly, but the location of a density mode need not be.

deepSections.title: A point is not a posterior or a predictive distribution
deepSections.body: MAP discards posterior width, correlation, skewness, and multimodality. Posterior mean minimizes squared-error loss for the parameter; posterior median minimizes absolute error; MAP has a local density interpretation. A posterior predictive distribution integrates p(y_new|theta) over posterior uncertainty, whereas plugging in theta_MAP ignores that uncertainty. In sparse or safety-critical settings the difference matters for tail risk and abstention. Laplace approximation, variational inference, MCMC, bootstrap, and profile likelihood capture different uncertainty approximations. Choose an estimator and uncertainty method based on the decision loss, not because one optimizer is convenient.

deepSections.title: Curvature, profile likelihood, and uncertainty
deepSections.body: At a regular interior optimum, negative Hessian curvature of the log likelihood approximates observed information; its inverse gives an asymptotic covariance estimate. Flat directions signal weak identification and large uncertainty even when optimization reports convergence. Profile likelihood fixes a parameter of interest, reoptimizes nuisance parameters, and uses likelihood-ratio contours that can capture asymmetry better than a Wald interval.
