visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Super-resolution & Reconstruction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Super-resolution infers a higher-resolution signal from limited observations. The central tension is recovering detail without hallucinating unsupported structure, so downstream/domain validation is often essential.
lessons.why: Super-resolution/reconstruction interviews test whether you distinguish resolution enhancement, hallucination risk, paired/unpaired data and task-specific validation.
lessons.intuition: The model maps a low-information input to a higher-resolution output. Because multiple high-resolution images can correspond to one low-resolution input, the problem is inherently ambiguous.
lessons.deepDive: Classical interpolation is deterministic and smooth but cannot invent missing high-frequency content. Supervised SR learns from aligned LR/HR pairs with pixel/perceptual/adversarial losses. Generative SR can create realistic texture but may hallucinate details. Scientific reconstruction therefore needs downstream structural/physical validation. 3D SR adds volumetric consistency and heavy compute constraints.
lessons.workedExample: A GAN can make SEM-like texture visually sharp while altering pore boundaries; PSNR/perceptual metrics alone cannot prove porosity correctness.
commonMistakes: Equating visually sharp output with ground-truth recovery.
Calling interpolation learned super-resolution.
Ignoring whether LR/HR pairs are aligned.
followUps: Pixel loss vs perceptual loss?
Why can GAN SR lower PSNR?
How do you validate scientific SR?
2D slice vs 3D model?
lessons.production: Choose output acceptance metrics tied to downstream use, version preprocessing/scale factors, and use batch/GPU jobs for large 3D outputs.

lessons.title: Embeddings
lessons.interviewAnswer: Embeddings map discrete objects such as words, products or code into dense vectors where geometry captures learned relationships. They support similarity search, retrieval and neural-network inputs.
lessons.why: Embeddings power semantic search, transformers, recommenders and graph/text systems. Interviewers expect both geometric intuition and awareness of retrieval limitations.
lessons.intuition: An embedding maps an object—word, document, image, user, PR—into a vector so that useful relationships become geometric, often measured by cosine similarity or dot product.
lessons.deepDive: Embeddings can be learned through supervised, self-supervised or contrastive objectives. Similarity reflects the training objective and domain, not universal semantic truth. Vector magnitude may carry information for dot-product retrieval; cosine normalizes it away. Retrieval systems need compatible query/document encoders, appropriate chunking and an index such as HNSW/IVF for scale.
lessons.workedExample: CodeBERT maps PR text into vectors where semantically related software changes can be closer even when they do not share exact words, which is useful for reviewer recommendation.
commonMistakes: Assuming nearest embedding means factually correct or causally related.
Mixing embeddings produced by incompatible models/spaces.
Using cosine and dot product interchangeably when vector norms differ.
followUps: Cosine vs dot-product similarity?
How are embeddings trained?
What is an ANN index?
How do you evaluate embedding retrieval?
lessons.production: Track embedding model/version with the index. Re-embedding can be expensive, and model changes can make old vectors incompatible with new queries.

visual.title: Embedding space
visual.caption: Embeddings place items with similar learned meaning near each other according to a training objective.

lessons.title: Tokenization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Tokenization converts text into a sequence of discrete token IDs. Subword methods balance vocabulary size and sequence length and must match the model’s training tokenizer exactly.
lessons.why: Tokenization defines the units language models operate on and directly affects context length, multilingual/code behavior and cost.
lessons.intuition: A tokenizer converts raw text into integer token IDs from a finite vocabulary. Modern subword tokenizers balance whole-word efficiency with the ability to represent unseen words.
lessons.deepDive: BPE/WordPiece/Unigram learn subword vocabularies from corpora. The same visible string can tokenize differently across models. Token count—not character/word count—drives context usage and inference cost. Special tokens encode boundaries/control signals. Byte-level schemes guarantee coverage but may use more tokens for some languages/domains.
lessons.workedExample: A rare technical identifier may split into many subword tokens, consuming context and potentially weakening semantic representation compared with common words.
lessons.code:
tokens=tokenizer("microstructure reconstruction", return_tensors="pt")
print(tokens.input_ids)
commonMistakes: Assuming one token equals one word.
Using a tokenizer from a different model than the embedding/LLM weights.
Hard-coding character limits when the real constraint is tokens.
followUps: BPE intuition?
Why special tokens?
Why tokenization differs by language?
How does token count affect cost?
lessons.production: Estimate/request limits in tokens, version tokenizer with the model, and handle truncation/chunking explicitly.

visual.title: Tokenization
visual.caption: Tokenization converts text into discrete units that map to model vocabulary IDs.

lessons.title: Self-Attention: Q, K, V
lessons.interviewAnswer: Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent representation by comparing its query with other tokens’ keys and taking a weighted combination of their values.
lessons.why: Attention is the central operation behind modern transformers and many multimodal/generative systems.
lessons.intuition: Think of each token asking a question (query), advertising what it contains (key), and carrying information to share (value). Query–key similarity determines how much of each value is mixed into the output.
lessons.deepDive: For matrices Q, K and V, scaled dot-product attention computes QKᵀ/√d, applies softmax row-wise, and multiplies by V. Multiple heads learn different projection subspaces. Causal language models additionally mask future positions.
lessons.math: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V
lessons.code:
import torch
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / (Q.size(-1) ** 0.5)
weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)
out = weights @ V
commonMistakes: Saying attention “finds the most important word” as if it were one fixed interpretation.
Forgetting the √d scaling or causal mask.
Assuming attention weights are guaranteed explanations.
followUps: Why multi-head attention?
Why is attention O(n²) in sequence length?
What are cross-attention and self-attention?
What is KV caching?
lessons.production: Long contexts create memory/latency pressure; serving systems use KV caches, efficient attention kernels and sometimes alternative architectures.
lessons.workedExample: In a sentence, the representation of “bank” can attend differently to “river” versus “loan”, producing context-dependent meaning.

lab.goal: Implement scaled dot-product self-attention with explicit tensor shapes.
lab.buildIt:
import torch, math
B,T,D=2,4,8
x=torch.randn(B,T,D); Wq=torch.randn(D,D); Wk=torch.randn(D,D); Wv=torch.randn(D,D)
Q,K,V=x@Wq,x@Wk,x@Wv
scores=Q@K.transpose(-2,-1)/math.sqrt(D)
weights=scores.softmax(-1); out=weights@V
print(Q.shape,scores.shape,out.shape)
lab.useIt:
from torch.nn.functional import scaled_dot_product_attention
out2=scaled_dot_product_attention(Q,K,V)
print(out2.shape)
lab.verifyIt:
assert torch.allclose(weights.sum(-1),torch.ones(B,T),atol=1e-5)
assert out.shape==(B,T,D)

visual.title: Self-attention weight map
visual.caption: Each query token assigns a normalized weight distribution over key tokens; the weighted values form the output.

lessons.title: Transformer Architecture
lessons.interviewAnswer: Transformers combine attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections and normalization. Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants serve different tasks.
lessons.why: Transformers are central to modern NLP, vision and generative AI; you should be able to explain the block, not only self-attention.
lessons.intuition: Each token first gathers context through attention, then independently passes through a feed-forward network. Residual connections and normalization stabilize deep stacks.
lessons.deepDive: A transformer block typically contains multi-head attention, position-wise feed-forward layers, residual connections and normalization. Attention projects hidden states to Q/K/V, computes compatibility and mixes values. Multiple heads learn different subspaces. Encoders use bidirectional attention; autoregressive decoders apply causal masks. Positional information is required because plain attention has no inherent sequence order.
lessons.math:
Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V
FFN(x)=W₂ φ(W₁x+b₁)+b₂
lessons.workedExample: In a causal language model, token t can attend to positions ≤t but not future tokens; the causal mask enforces next-token prediction semantics.
lessons.code:
# PyTorch concept
layer = torch.nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d_model=512,nhead=8,batch_first=True)
commonMistakes: Explaining a transformer as “just attention” and omitting FFN/residual/norm.
Forgetting causal masking in decoder-only language models.
Saying attention gives order without positional information.
followUps: Why divide by sqrt(d_k)?
Encoder vs decoder-only transformer?
What does multi-head attention buy?
Why LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm?
lessons.production: Transformer inference cost grows with sequence length; batching, KV cache, quantization and context management are major serving concerns.

visual.title: Transformer block
visual.caption: Transformer layers alternate attention-based context mixing with position-wise feed-forward computation.

lessons.title: BERT vs GPT-style Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: BERT-style models are typically encoder-only and learn bidirectional contextual representations; GPT-style models are decoder-only and autoregressively predict the next token. Their pretraining objectives drive different strengths.
lessons.why: BERT vs GPT tests whether you understand encoder-style bidirectional representation learning versus causal autoregressive generation.
lessons.intuition: BERT-style encoders can look both left and right to understand a token in context. GPT-style decoder-only models predict the next token using only earlier tokens.
lessons.deepDive: BERT is pretrained with masked-token objectives and is strong for embeddings/classification/extraction with task heads. GPT-style models use causal masks and next-token prediction, naturally supporting generation and in-context prompting. Modern systems blur categories with encoder-decoder and instruction-tuned variants, so choose based on task rather than brand.
lessons.workedExample: For semantic classification of a complete PR description, an encoder such as CodeBERT/BERT can produce contextual features. For generating an explanation, a causal LLM is more natural.
commonMistakes: Calling BERT generative in the same autoregressive sense as GPT.
Saying GPT has no bidirectional information at all—later tokens integrate all earlier context, but cannot see future tokens during causal prediction.
Assuming one family always has better embeddings.
followUps: What is causal masking?
Why masked language modeling?
Encoder-decoder transformer use case?
How would you get sentence embeddings from BERT?
lessons.production: Encoder models are often cheaper for embeddings/classification; generative LLMs add latency/cost and should be used only when generation/reasoning is needed.

visual.title: BERT vs GPT training
visual.caption: The attention mask and training objective shape what the model learns to do.

lessons.title: Positional Information
lessons.interviewAnswer: Attention itself is permutation-invariant, so transformers need positional information. Systems may use learned embeddings, sinusoidal encodings or relative/rotary approaches such as RoPE.
lessons.why: Attention alone is permutation-equivariant, so transformers need a way to represent order or relative position.
lessons.intuition: Without position information, the same set of token embeddings in a different order would look equivalent to pure self-attention.
lessons.deepDive: Absolute learned/sinusoidal embeddings add a position vector to each token. Relative position methods encode pairwise distance; rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) rotate query/key dimensions based on position and support relative-phase behavior. Position methods affect length extrapolation and long-context performance.
lessons.math: Sinusoidal PE uses sin/cos at different frequencies; RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to Q/K pairs.
lessons.workedExample: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” contain the same words but different order; position information lets attention distinguish them.
commonMistakes: Saying attention inherently knows sequence order.
Treating all positional encodings as interchangeable for arbitrary context extension.
Changing maximum context without checking positional-training limits.
followUps: Absolute vs relative position?
What is RoPE?
Why sin/cos?
How does long-context extension interact with position encodings?
lessons.production: Long-context serving must respect the model’s positional method/training range; naive extension can degrade quality even if memory allows more tokens.

visual.title: Position information
visual.caption: Attention alone is permutation-invariant; positional information tells the model where tokens occur in the sequence.

lessons.title: Language Modeling & Next-token Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: A causal language model estimates the probability of each next token conditioned on previous tokens and trains using cross-entropy over sequences. Generation repeatedly samples or selects from the predicted distribution.
lessons.why: Next-token prediction is the central training objective behind decoder-only LLMs and connects probabilities, cross-entropy, perplexity and inference.
lessons.intuition: Given previous tokens, predict a probability distribution for the next token. Repeating this process autoregressively produces text.
lessons.deepDive: Training uses teacher forcing: the model sees ground-truth previous tokens and minimizes token-level cross-entropy. The likelihood of a sequence factorizes as a product of conditional next-token probabilities. At inference, the model feeds generated tokens back into context and samples/decodes from logits. Exposure to broad data plus scale produces useful representations/behaviors, but the objective optimizes predictive likelihood—not truthfulness.
lessons.math:
p(x_1...x_T)=Π_t p(x_t | x_{<t})
NLL = -Σ_t log p(x_t|x_{<t})
Perplexity = exp(mean NLL per token)
lessons.workedExample: If the correct next token gets probability 0.8, its loss is -log(0.8); if probability is 0.01, the loss is much larger.
lessons.code:
# CrossEntropyLoss over shifted logits/labels is the common training pattern
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[:, :-1].reshape(-1,V), ids[:,1:].reshape(-1))
commonMistakes: Saying next-token training explicitly teaches factual truth or reasoning steps.
Confusing teacher forcing with autoregressive inference.
Comparing perplexity across incompatible tokenizers without caution.
followUps: What is perplexity?
Why causal mask?
Teacher forcing?
Why can next-token prediction lead to broad capabilities?
lessons.production: Inference cost depends on context/prefill plus token-by-token decoding; KV cache avoids recomputing all prior attention states each step.

lessons.title: Autoencoders & VAEs
lessons.interviewAnswer: A standard autoencoder learns a compressed code for reconstruction. A VAE regularizes the latent distribution and samples from it, enabling generation but introducing a reconstruction–regularization trade-off.
lessons.why: VAEs introduce probabilistic latent-variable models, reconstruction–regularization trade-offs and the reparameterization trick.
lessons.intuition: An encoder predicts a distribution over latent codes rather than one fixed code. Sample a latent, decode it, and regularize the latent distribution so nearby codes form a usable generative space.
lessons.deepDive: The VAE maximizes an evidence lower bound: expected reconstruction log-likelihood minus KL divergence between approximate posterior q(z|x) and prior p(z). Reparameterization z=μ+σ⊙ε makes sampling differentiable with respect to μ/σ. Strong KL pressure can cause posterior collapse; weak pressure yields poor prior sampling. Output likelihood determines the reconstruction term.
lessons.math:
ELBO = E_{q(z|x)}[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x)||p(z))
z=μ+σ⊙ε, ε~N(0,I)
lessons.workedExample: A VAE can interpolate smoothly between latent codes and sample from a known prior, but reconstructions may be blurrier than adversarial/perceptual models.
lessons.code:
mu, logvar = encoder(x)
std=(0.5*logvar).exp(); z=mu+std*torch.randn_like(std)
xhat=decoder(z)
commonMistakes: Calling a VAE deterministic.
Forgetting the KL term/why it exists.
Using MSE reconstruction blindly without considering data likelihood.
followUps: Why reparameterization?
What is KL divergence doing?
VAE vs autoencoder?
What is posterior collapse?
lessons.production: VAEs provide compact latent representations and uncertainty-friendly generation, but validate latent stability and reconstruction quality under domain shift.

visual.title: Variational autoencoder
visual.caption: A VAE learns a structured latent distribution by combining reconstruction quality with a KL regularization term.

lessons.title: VQ-VAE / VQGAN & Vector Quantization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vector quantization maps continuous encoder features to entries in a discrete codebook. VQGAN combines discrete compression with perceptual/adversarial objectives to improve reconstructed visual quality.
lessons.why: Vector quantization connects compression, discrete representations and generative modeling, and it is directly relevant to tokenizer/bottleneck-based microstructure work.
lessons.intuition: The encoder produces continuous feature vectors, but the quantizer replaces each with the nearest learned codebook vector. The image is therefore represented by discrete code indices rather than full pixels/features.
lessons.deepDive: VQ-VAE uses an encoder, discrete codebook and decoder with a commitment/codebook objective; straight-through estimation passes gradients around the non-differentiable nearest-neighbor lookup. VQGAN adds perceptual/adversarial training to improve high-frequency realism and enables stronger compression. Codebook collapse/dead codes are common issues, addressed with usage monitoring, EMA updates or resets.
lessons.math:
z_q(x)=e_k where k=argmin_j ||z_e(x)-e_j||₂
Typical objective = reconstruction + codebook/commitment terms (+ perceptual/adversarial terms in VQGAN)
lessons.workedExample: A 256×256 image compressed to a 16×16 grid uses 256 discrete positions. If the codebook has 1024 entries, each index can be represented with 10 bits before entropy coding, which makes bitrate reasoning possible.
lessons.code:
# conceptual nearest-code lookup
dist=((z[...,None,:]-codebook)**2).sum(-1)
idx=dist.argmin(-1)
z_q=codebook[idx]
commonMistakes: Calling quantization lossless compression.
Ignoring codebook utilization/dead codes.
Confusing the number of latent tokens with the actual number of bits required to encode them.
followUps: Why straight-through estimation?
What is commitment loss?
How do you measure compression in bits?
VAE vs VQ-VAE vs VQGAN?
lessons.production: Track codebook version, utilization and bitrate as well as reconstruction metrics. Domain-specific tokenizers may outperform natural-image tokenizers when structural statistics differ.

lab.goal: Implement the core vector-quantization operation: map continuous latent vectors to nearest codebook entries.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
z=np.array([[.1,.9],[.8,.2],[.45,.55]])
codebook=np.array([[0.,1.],[1.,0.],[.5,.5]])
d=((z[:,None,:]-codebook[None,:,:])**2).sum(-1)
idx=d.argmin(1); quantized=codebook[idx]
print(idx,quantized)
lab.useIt:
# Framework implementations add encoder/decoder training, commitment loss,
# EMA or gradient-based codebook updates and a straight-through estimator.
recon_error=((z-quantized)**2).mean(); print(recon_error)
lab.verifyIt: assert idx.tolist()==[0,1,2]

visual.title: Vector-quantized autoencoder
visual.caption: Vector quantization replaces continuous latents with discrete codebook entries; adversarial/perceptual losses improve visual fidelity.

lessons.title: GAN Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A GAN trains a generator to fool a discriminator while the discriminator learns to distinguish real from generated samples. This adversarial game can produce sharp images but may be unstable.
lessons.why: GAN fundamentals are needed to explain CycleGAN/VQGAN and to compare adversarial training with diffusion/flow matching.
lessons.intuition: The generator tries to create samples that look real; the discriminator tries to tell real from generated. Training improves both in a game rather than optimizing one fixed supervised target.
lessons.deepDive: The original minimax GAN objective can suffer from saturated gradients and unstable dynamics because generator/discriminator objectives change together. Variants such as non-saturating loss, Wasserstein objectives, gradient penalty, spectral normalization and architectural constraints improve behavior. Mode collapse occurs when the generator covers only part of the data distribution.
lessons.math: min_G max_D E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1-D(G(z)))]
lessons.workedExample: If a generator produces only one realistic-looking grain pattern regardless of noise input, the discriminator may be fooled locally but diversity is poor—classic mode collapse.
lessons.code:
# training alternates conceptually:
# 1) update D on real and detached fake samples
# 2) update G so D scores generated samples as real
commonMistakes: Saying GAN loss values alone directly measure image quality.
Training G and D without controlling detach/update boundaries.
Assuming adversarial realism guarantees semantic or physical correctness.
followUps: What is mode collapse?
Why are GANs unstable?
WGAN-GP intuition?
GAN vs diffusion?
lessons.production: GAN inference can be fast, but training reproducibility and validation are difficult. Store checkpoints/metrics and evaluate diversity plus task-specific correctness, not only discriminator loss.

lab.goal: See the two-player GAN objective with a minimal discriminator score and generator target.
lab.buildIt:
import math
def sigmoid(x): return 1/(1+math.exp(-x))
real_logit=2.0; fake_logit=-1.0
D_real,D_fake=sigmoid(real_logit),sigmoid(fake_logit)
d_loss=-(math.log(D_real)+math.log(1-D_fake))
g_loss=-math.log(D_fake)
print(D_real,D_fake,d_loss,g_loss)
lab.useIt:
# In PyTorch, use BCEWithLogitsLoss rather than applying sigmoid manually.
import torch
loss=torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()(torch.tensor([fake_logit]),torch.ones(1))
print(loss.item())
lab.verifyIt:
assert D_real>D_fake
assert g_loss>0

visual.title: GAN training game
visual.caption: The generator learns to fool the discriminator while the discriminator learns to distinguish generated from real samples.

lessons.title: CycleGAN & Unpaired Translation
lessons.interviewAnswer: CycleGAN learns mappings between two unpaired image domains using adversarial losses plus cycle consistency. The cycle constraint encourages content preservation but does not guarantee physical correctness or eliminate hallucination.
lessons.why: CycleGAN is important when paired examples do not exist and is directly relevant to unpaired scientific/image translation projects.
lessons.intuition: Learn A→B and B→A together. Adversarial losses make outputs look like each target domain; cycle consistency encourages translating there and back to recover the original content.
lessons.deepDive: Two generators G:A→B and F:B→A plus discriminators D_A/D_B are trained jointly. Adversarial objectives match marginal domain appearance; cycle loss ||F(G(a))-a|| and ||G(F(b))-b|| constrains mappings. Identity loss is sometimes added. Cycle consistency reduces arbitrary mappings but does not guarantee semantic/physical correctness or prevent hallucination.
lessons.math: L = L_GAN(G,D_B)+L_GAN(F,D_A)+λ_cyc L_cyc (+ λ_id L_id)
lessons.workedExample: Two microscopy or imaging modalities can form unpaired domains when exact aligned source/target pairs do not exist. Cycle consistency encourages content preservation, but generated target-style texture still requires domain-specific validation.
lessons.code:
# inference typically uses only the desired generator
with torch.no_grad():
    translated = G(source)
commonMistakes: Saying CycleGAN needs paired images.
Saying cycle loss guarantees no hallucinations.
Using discriminator/generator training losses as the only quality metric.
followUps: Why two generators/discriminators?
What is cycle consistency?
What is used at inference?
Why not supervised SR?
lessons.production: Store only required inference generators/checkpoints, but retain training configs. Monitor output artifacts and domain-specific validity, especially under input-domain drift.

visual.title: CycleGAN
visual.caption: Cycle consistency encourages an unpaired translation A→B→A to preserve information from the original sample.

lessons.title: Diffusion Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: Diffusion models learn to reverse a progressive corruption process. During generation they start from noise and iteratively move toward a sample from the learned data distribution.
lessons.why: Diffusion appears frequently in modern image generation and connects naturally to denoising, score/velocity prediction and latent models.
lessons.intuition: Training creates noisy versions of real data and teaches the model how to move them toward clean data. At inference, start from noise and repeatedly apply the learned reverse dynamics.
lessons.deepDive: Different formulations predict noise ε, clean data x₀, velocity v or a score. The forward corruption process is known, while the neural network approximates the reverse process. Latent diffusion runs this process in a compressed representation to reduce compute.
lessons.math: One common forward form: xₜ = √ᾱₜ x₀ + √(1-ᾱₜ) ε,  ε~N(0,I)
lessons.code:
# Pseudocode
for x0 in data:
    t = sample_timestep()
    eps = randn_like(x0)
    xt = add_noise(x0, eps, t)
    pred = model(xt, t, condition)
    loss = mse(pred, eps)
commonMistakes: “Diffusion just removes Gaussian noise.” It learns conditional reverse dynamics across noise levels.
Assuming lower pixel MSE always means better generative quality.
followUps: Diffusion vs GAN?
What is classifier-free guidance?
Why latent diffusion?
What is v-prediction?
lessons.production: Sampling latency can be significant because inference uses multiple model evaluations; distillation, better solvers and latent-space models reduce cost.
lessons.workedExample: A conditioned reconstruction model can start from noise and use a compact semantic representation to guide the reverse process toward a compatible microstructure.

lab.goal: Train intuition with the forward noising equation and a tiny denoising target.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
x0=torch.randn(8,3,32,32); eps=torch.randn_like(x0)
alpha_bar=torch.tensor(.6)
xt=alpha_bar.sqrt()*x0+(1-alpha_bar).sqrt()*eps
# A diffusion network would receive (xt,t,condition) and predict eps/v/x0.
print(x0.std().item(),xt.std().item())
lab.verifyIt:
assert xt.shape==x0.shape
assert torch.isfinite(xt).all()

visual.title: Diffusion generation
visual.caption: Training learns the reverse of a gradual corruption process; sampling repeatedly removes noise from an initial random state.

lessons.title: Latent Diffusion
lessons.interviewAnswer: Latent diffusion performs the generative process in a compressed latent space rather than pixels, reducing compute while a decoder maps the final latent back to the image domain.
lessons.why: Latent diffusion explains how systems such as Stable Diffusion reduce image-generation compute by denoising compressed representations instead of pixels.
lessons.intuition: First compress an image into a smaller latent grid with an autoencoder. Run the diffusion process in that latent space, then decode the final latent back to pixels.
lessons.deepDive: A pretrained encoder/decoder defines the latent representation. The denoiser operates on lower-resolution/multi-channel latents, reducing spatial compute while retaining semantic content. Conditioning enters via cross-attention/other pathways. The autoencoder is a bottleneck: if it loses details, the diffusion model cannot reconstruct them exactly. Latent scaling/distribution must match training.
lessons.workedExample: An image may be encoded from 1024×1024 pixels to a much smaller latent tensor; denoising that tensor is dramatically cheaper than operating on every RGB pixel.
commonMistakes: Saying latent diffusion is just image compression without a generative denoising model.
Ignoring reconstruction limits of the autoencoder.
Mixing latent scales/codecs from incompatible checkpoints.
followUps: Why latent instead of pixel diffusion?
What does the VAE do in Stable Diffusion?
How does conditioning enter?
What information can the bottleneck lose?
lessons.production: Cache/optimize autoencoder and denoiser separately, version latent codec with the model, and benchmark decode quality plus end-to-end latency.

visual.title: Latent diffusion
visual.caption: Moving diffusion from pixel space into a compressed latent space reduces compute while preserving generative capacity.

lessons.title: Flow Matching
lessons.interviewAnswer: Flow matching trains a model to predict a continuous velocity field that transports samples from a simple distribution such as noise toward the data distribution. Inference integrates that learned vector field over time.
lessons.why: Flow matching is increasingly important in modern generative modeling because it offers a direct vector-field view of transporting simple noise distributions into complex data distributions.
lessons.intuition: Instead of learning “what noise should I remove?”, imagine learning a velocity arrow at every intermediate point that tells the sample how to move from a simple source distribution toward real data.
lessons.deepDive: Choose a probability path connecting source noise x₀ to target data x₁. Sample an intermediate xₜ and train a network vθ(xₜ,t) to match the target velocity field. At inference, solve the ODE dx/dt=vθ(x,t) from source to data. Rectified-flow variants choose simple paths that can make trajectories easier to integrate.
lessons.math: For a simple straight interpolation xₜ=(1-t)x₀+t x₁, the target conditional velocity is x₁-x₀ (details vary by formulation/path).
lessons.code:
# Conceptual pseudocode
x0 = sample_noise()
x1 = sample_data()
t = uniform(0, 1)
xt = (1-t)*x0 + t*x1
target_v = x1 - x0
pred_v = model(xt, t, condition)
loss = mse(pred_v, target_v)
commonMistakes: Treating every flow-matching implementation as exactly the straight-line formula above; practical paths/objectives vary.
Saying flow matching and MMDiT are synonyms: one is a training/generative formulation, the other is an architecture family.
followUps: How is flow matching different from diffusion?
What ODE solver is used at inference?
What is rectified flow?
How does conditioning enter the velocity network?
lessons.production: Inference speed depends on number of function evaluations and solver choice; deployment still needs benchmarking rather than assuming flow matching is always faster.
lessons.workedExample: For conditioned microstructure reconstruction, the velocity network can use bottleneck embeddings while transporting noise toward a sample consistent with those embeddings.

lab.goal: Implement a rectified-flow training target on toy points.
lab.buildIt:
import torch
x0=torch.randn(256,2); x1=torch.randn(256,2)+torch.tensor([3.,0.])
t=torch.rand(256,1); xt=(1-t)*x0+t*x1; target=x1-x0
model=torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(3,64),torch.nn.Tanh(),torch.nn.Linear(64,2))
opt=torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(),1e-3)
for _ in range(300):
    pred=model(torch.cat([xt,t],1)); loss=((pred-target)**2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(loss.item())
lab.useIt:
# Euler integration at inference: x <- x + dt * v_theta(x,t)
x=torch.randn(32,2); dt=.05
for i in range(20):
    tcur=torch.full((32,1),i/20)
    with torch.no_grad(): x += dt*model(torch.cat([x,tcur],1))
lab.verifyIt:
assert torch.isfinite(loss)
assert x.shape==(32,2)

visual.title: Flow matching
visual.caption: Flow matching learns a continuous vector field that transports noise toward the data distribution.

lessons.title: Conditioning & Classifier-Free Guidance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Conditioning provides control information such as text, labels, embeddings or structural inputs. Classifier-free guidance combines conditioned and unconditioned predictions to strengthen adherence to the condition.
lessons.why: Conditioning is how generative models become controllable rather than producing arbitrary samples.
lessons.intuition: Give the generative model extra information—text, labels, image features, edges, compressed tokens—so the denoising/flow trajectory is guided toward outputs consistent with that signal.
lessons.deepDive: Conditioning can enter by concatenation, adaptive normalization, cross-attention, added residual branches or timestep/pooled embeddings. Classifier-free guidance trains conditional and dropped-condition cases, then combines conditional/unconditional predictions at inference to strengthen adherence. Higher guidance can improve prompt/condition alignment but reduce diversity or create artifacts.
lessons.math: CFG example: ε_guided = ε_uncond + s(ε_cond - ε_uncond)
lessons.workedExample: A compressed microstructure latent can condition the decoder so generated grains follow input structure, while a Canny ControlNet condition preserves boundaries.
commonMistakes: Calling all conditioning “prompting.”
Assuming stronger guidance always improves quality.
Using conditioning signals that leak target information during training but are unavailable at inference.
followUps: Cross-attention vs ControlNet conditioning?
What is classifier-free guidance?
Why drop conditions during training?
How do you evaluate controllability?
lessons.production: Validate condition availability/quality at serving time, expose guidance controls safely, and monitor whether users can induce out-of-distribution conditions.

visual.title: Conditional generation
visual.caption: Conditioning steers generation using text, labels, images, structural signals or learned embeddings.

lessons.title: ControlNet
lessons.interviewAnswer: ControlNet adds a trainable conditioning branch to a pretrained diffusion model so structural signals such as edges, depth or poses can guide generation while preserving much of the pretrained backbone.
lessons.why: ControlNet is a practical way to add structural conditioning to pretrained diffusion models while preserving much of the base model capability.
lessons.intuition: Create a trainable branch that processes a control signal such as edges, depth or pose, then inject its features into a mostly frozen diffusion backbone.
lessons.deepDive: ControlNet copies/augments parts of the pretrained network and uses zero-initialized connections so the added branch starts with minimal disturbance to the base model. The control encoder learns spatial guidance aligned with the denoising network. It is useful when text/semantic embeddings are insufficient to preserve geometry.
lessons.workedExample: Canny edges from a microstructure can guide boundary layout while SDXL provides realistic texture/style variation.
commonMistakes: Saying ControlNet guarantees exact geometry.
Assuming the whole base diffusion model must be retrained.
Using noisy/incorrect control maps without evaluating sensitivity.
followUps: Why zero convolutions?
ControlNet vs cross-attention?
What control signals can be used?
How do you balance control strength and diversity?
lessons.production: Control preprocessing becomes part of the serving contract; version edge/depth extraction settings with the model and monitor failures when controls are sparse/noisy.

visual.title: ControlNet conditioning
visual.caption: ControlNet injects spatial control into a pretrained diffusion backbone while preserving the original generative model.

lessons.title: GAN vs Diffusion vs Flow Matching
lessons.interviewAnswer: GANs use adversarial training and usually sample in one/few passes; diffusion learns a reverse corruption process; flow matching learns a transport velocity field. Compare them by stability, sample quality/diversity, inference speed and controllability—not by a single winner.
lessons.why: Modern GenAI interviews often ask you to compare model families based on objective, sampling, diversity, stability and controllability rather than declaring one universally best.
lessons.intuition: GANs learn through a discriminator game, diffusion learns to reverse corruption, and flow matching learns a continuous velocity field transporting noise to data.
lessons.deepDive: GANs often provide fast one-pass generation but can be unstable and mode-collapse. Diffusion uses a known corruption path and iterative denoising; training is generally stable but sampling may require many network evaluations. Flow matching trains a vector field along chosen probability paths and generates by integrating an ODE; path/solver choices influence efficiency. Architecture and training paradigm are separate: a DiT-like transformer can be used with diffusion or flow-matching objectives.
lessons.workedExample: For interactive low-latency image generation, a GAN can be attractive if quality/diversity are sufficient. For high-fidelity controllable generation, diffusion/flow models may be easier to train and condition but cost more inference compute.
commonMistakes: Saying MMDiT and flow matching are the same concept.
Assuming diffusion never has mode-coverage issues or GANs are obsolete.
Comparing generation speed without fixing hardware, steps and resolution.
followUps: Why is diffusion sampling slower?
What does flow matching predict?
Can a transformer be used in both diffusion and flow matching?
When would you choose a GAN today?
lessons.production: Choose the family from latency, controllability, data, hardware and quality constraints. Profile end-to-end serving cost rather than comparing model families abstractly.

visual.title: GAN vs Diffusion vs Flow Matching
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering
lessons.interviewAnswer: Good prompting specifies the task, context, constraints and output format, then evaluates prompts on representative examples. Prompting should be treated as an engineering artifact with tests, not magic wording.
lessons.why: Prompting is the lowest-cost control surface for LLM behavior and often the first thing an interviewer expects you to reason about before fine-tuning or adding agents.
lessons.intuition: A prompt specifies the task, relevant context, constraints and desired output format. Good prompting reduces ambiguity rather than relying on clever wording tricks.
lessons.deepDive: Useful prompts separate instructions from data, define the role/task clearly, provide examples only when they add signal, constrain output structure and state what to do when evidence is insufficient. System/developer instructions generally have higher priority than user content in modern chat APIs. Prompt engineering should be evaluated with a test set because changes can improve some cases while degrading others.
lessons.workedExample: For a support classifier, specify the allowed labels and output JSON schema instead of asking for “a helpful classification.” Add representative few-shot examples only if zero-shot performance is insufficient.
commonMistakes: Treating prompt wording as a substitute for missing retrieval/tools/data.
Stuffing huge irrelevant context into every request.
Changing prompts without regression evaluation.
followUps: Zero-shot vs few-shot?
When would you use structured output?
Prompting vs fine-tuning?
How do you handle prompt injection?
lessons.production: Version prompts like code, evaluate them before release, log prompt/model versions and sanitize/segregate untrusted retrieved content so it cannot silently override application instructions.

lessons.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
lessons.interviewAnswer: RAG retrieves relevant external context and supplies it to the model at generation time. A reliable RAG system depends on ingestion, chunking, embeddings, retrieval, reranking, context construction and evaluation—not only the LLM.
lessons.why: RAG is one of the most common AI-engineering interview topics because it combines information retrieval, LLMs, data pipelines and evaluation.
lessons.intuition: Instead of asking the model to remember all facts, retrieve relevant evidence at query time and put that evidence into the context. The model then answers using current, domain-specific material.
lessons.deepDive: A robust pipeline includes ingestion → parsing → chunking → embedding/indexing → query transformation → retrieval → optional reranking → context assembly → generation → citation/evaluation. Retrieval quality and generation quality must be diagnosed separately.
lessons.math: A common semantic score is cosine(q,d) = (q·d)/(||q|| ||d||). Retrieval is usually approximate nearest-neighbor search at scale.
lessons.code:
# Conceptual pipeline
chunks = chunk_documents(docs)
index.add(embed(chunks))
q = embed(user_query)
candidates = index.search(q, k=20)
context = rerank(user_query, candidates)[:5]
answer = llm(user_query, context)
commonMistakes: Calling any prompt with pasted text “RAG” without a retrieval system.
Evaluating only final answers and never measuring retrieval recall.
Ignoring access control and document freshness.
followUps: RAG vs fine-tuning?
How do you choose chunk size?
Why rerank?
What if retrieval returns conflicting documents?
lessons.production: Production RAG needs document versioning, ACL-aware retrieval, caching, observability, evaluation sets, latency/cost budgets and safe handling of untrusted retrieved text.
lessons.workedExample: For internal engineering manuals, index approved documents, retrieve relevant sections for each question, cite the source, and evaluate whether the correct evidence was retrieved before judging the final response.

lab.goal: Build a minimal semantic retriever, then show where generation would plug in.
lab.buildIt:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
chunks=['refund policy is 30 days','shipping takes 3 days','enterprise SSO uses SAML']
vec=TfidfVectorizer().fit(chunks); X=vec.transform(chunks)
q=vec.transform(['how long can I return an item?'])
idx=cosine_similarity(q,X).ravel().argsort()[::-1][:2]
context=[chunks[i] for i in idx]; print(context)
lab.useIt:
# Production replacement: embeddings/vector DB -> optional reranker -> LLM with cited context.
prompt='Answer only from context:\n'+'\n'.join(context)+'\nQuestion: return window?'
print(prompt)
lab.verifyIt: assert context[0]=='refund policy is 30 days'

visual.title: RAG pipeline
visual.caption: RAG separates knowledge retrieval from generation so answers can use external, updateable evidence.

lessons.title: Embedding Search & Vector Databases
lessons.interviewAnswer: Convert documents and queries to embeddings, compare them using a similarity metric, and retrieve nearest items. Production retrieval often adds metadata filters, hybrid lexical search and reranking.
lessons.why: Vector retrieval is the core of modern semantic search and many RAG systems, so interviews probe embeddings, similarity, indexing and evaluation together.
lessons.intuition: Encode documents and queries into the same vector space, then retrieve nearby vectors. At small scale brute-force comparison works; at large scale approximate nearest-neighbor indexes trade exactness for speed/memory.
lessons.deepDive: Chunking determines retrieval granularity. Embedding model choice determines what similarity means. Vector databases/indexes commonly use cosine, dot product or Euclidean distance and ANN structures such as HNSW or IVF. Metadata filtering narrows candidates. Hybrid search combines dense semantic retrieval with lexical BM25. Rerankers can improve precision after a broad first-stage retrieval.
lessons.workedExample: For planning-policy RAG, chunk by coherent policy sections, embed chunks, retrieve top candidates by semantic similarity, optionally rerank, then pass only grounded chunks to the LLM.
commonMistakes: Assuming the nearest vector is necessarily relevant enough to answer.
Using huge chunks that retrieve broad documents but bury the needed sentence.
Changing the embedding model without rebuilding/revalidating the index.
followUps: Cosine vs dot product?
HNSW intuition?
Dense vs sparse/hybrid retrieval?
How do you evaluate retrieval separately from generation?
lessons.production: Monitor recall/precision on a labeled query set, index freshness, embedding version, latency and filter correctness. Keep source IDs/metadata so answers can cite provenance.

lab.goal: Build cosine-similarity retrieval over a tiny vector index and return top-k items.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
docs=np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[.8,.2],[-1.,0.]])
q=np.array([1.,.1])
def norm(x): return x/np.linalg.norm(x,axis=-1,keepdims=True)
scores=norm(docs)@norm(q)
rank=np.argsort(-scores)
print(rank,scores[rank])
lab.useIt:
top_k=2
print('retrieved ids',rank[:top_k].tolist())
lab.verifyIt:
assert rank[0] in (0,2)
assert scores[rank[0]]>scores[rank[-1]]

visual.title: Embedding retrieval
visual.caption: Semantic retrieval compares learned vector representations rather than exact term overlap.

lessons.title: RAG Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval metrics ask whether relevant evidence was found; generation metrics assess faithfulness, relevance and task success. Human or domain evaluation remains important.
lessons.why: RAG can fail in retrieval or generation, so one end-to-end “answer quality” score is insufficient for debugging.
lessons.intuition: Ask two separate questions: did we retrieve the right evidence, and did the model use that evidence correctly?
lessons.deepDive: Retrieval evaluation uses metrics such as Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR/nDCG depending on labels/ranking needs. Generation evaluation checks faithfulness/groundedness, answer correctness, relevance and citation support. Build a representative evaluation set with answerable and unanswerable queries. LLM-as-judge can scale evaluation but should be calibrated against human judgments and protected from reference leakage.
lessons.workedExample: If the correct policy paragraph never appears in top-5 retrieval, prompting cannot fix the answer. If it is retrieved but the answer contradicts it, the generation/prompt/model stage is the problem.
commonMistakes: Evaluating only final answer fluency.
Using the same LLM-generated synthetic questions as the only evaluation benchmark.
Treating an LLM judge as unquestionable ground truth.
followUps: How do you evaluate retrieval?
What is faithfulness?
How do you evaluate unanswerable queries?
When is LLM-as-judge appropriate?
lessons.production: Maintain regression suites of real user queries, trace retrieved chunks and model outputs, monitor citation/grounding failures, and rerun evaluation when chunking, embeddings, prompts or models change.

visual.title: RAG Evaluation
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Tool / Function Calling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Tool calling lets the model choose structured actions while deterministic code performs calculations, database access or external operations. The model orchestrates; the tool remains the source of truth for precise operations.
lessons.why: Tool calling is how LLM systems interact reliably with calculators, databases, APIs and deterministic business logic instead of hallucinating actions or numbers.
lessons.intuition: The model does not execute arbitrary code by itself. It selects a named tool and produces structured arguments; the application validates and executes the tool, then returns the result to the model.
lessons.deepDive: Define narrow tool schemas, validate types/ranges, authenticate separately from the model, enforce permission boundaries and treat tool outputs as untrusted external data. The control loop can be one-shot or agentic. Use deterministic tools for calculations, state changes and source-of-truth retrieval. Add idempotency for side effects and require confirmation for high-impact actions.
lessons.workedExample: For a supply-chain copilot, the LLM calls a forecast/reorder function that returns numbers from a deterministic model; it then explains those values rather than inventing them.
commonMistakes: Letting the model directly perform sensitive actions without application-side authorization.
Using free-form text arguments instead of validated schemas.
Calling an LLM for deterministic arithmetic the tool can compute exactly.
followUps: Tool calling vs RAG?
How do you prevent unsafe side effects?
What if the model calls the wrong tool?
How do you evaluate tool-use accuracy?
lessons.production: Log tool choice, arguments, result, latency and errors. Add retries/timeouts, permission checks, idempotency keys and human confirmation where consequences matter.

lab.goal: Treat tool calling as structured input validation, not free-form execution.
lab.useIt:
call={'name':'weather','args':{'city':'Hamburg'}}
print(validate(call))

visual.title: Tool calling
visual.caption: The LLM orchestrates; deterministic systems remain responsible for calculations, database access or side effects.

lessons.title: Agents & LangGraph
lessons.interviewAnswer: An agent repeatedly observes state, chooses an action/tool, updates state and decides whether to continue. Graph-based orchestration makes control flow, retries and state transitions explicit.
lessons.why: Agent questions test whether you know when an LLM should orchestrate multi-step tool use and when a deterministic workflow is safer.
lessons.intuition: An agent is an LLM-controlled loop: observe state, choose an action/tool, execute it, inspect the result, and continue until a stopping condition is met.
lessons.deepDive: Agent frameworks such as LangGraph represent state and transitions explicitly, enabling branching, retries, checkpoints and human approval. The model should choose among bounded tools rather than have unrestricted system access. Use deterministic workflows when the sequence is known; use agentic control when tool choice/order depends on intermediate results. Memory, termination and error recovery must be designed deliberately.
lessons.workedExample: A planning assistant first decides whether the question needs a forecast tool or policy retrieval; after getting the result, it may call a second tool or answer. A fixed “forecast→summarize” workflow does not need an agent.
commonMistakes: Calling every multi-step pipeline an agent.
Allowing unlimited loops/tool calls without budgets or termination.
Giving the agent broad write permissions by default.
followUps: Agent vs workflow?
Why LangGraph?
How do you persist agent state?
How do you evaluate an agent?
lessons.production: Set step/time/cost limits, trace every tool call, make side effects idempotent, require confirmation for high-impact actions and provide deterministic fallbacks for critical paths.

visual.title: Agent loop
visual.caption: An agent repeatedly chooses actions based on intermediate observations instead of producing one fixed response.

lessons.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
lessons.interviewAnswer: MCP standardizes how AI applications discover and invoke external tools/resources through a common protocol, reducing one-off integrations between assistants and services.
lessons.why: MCP is increasingly relevant for AI engineering because it standardizes how compatible AI clients discover and interact with external tools/resources.
lessons.intuition: Instead of writing a custom integration separately for every AI client, an MCP server exposes capabilities through a common protocol that clients can discover and invoke.
lessons.deepDive: MCP separates clients from servers that expose tools/resources/prompts through a standardized interface. It does not replace authorization, business logic or tool safety; those still belong in the server/application. Transport and deployment details can vary. The value is interoperability and a consistent contract, not making LLM outputs inherently more reliable.
lessons.workedExample: A forecasting application can expose “get_forecast” and “get_reorder_point” through MCP so multiple compatible assistants can use the same deterministic backend tools.
commonMistakes: Describing MCP as a model or vector database.
Assuming MCP automatically grants safe access to every tool.
Exposing internal tools without authentication/permission checks.
followUps: MCP vs normal REST API?
What does an MCP server expose?
Where does authorization live?
Why use MCP for an internal tool ecosystem?
lessons.production: Treat MCP servers as production APIs: authenticate clients, validate arguments, rate-limit, log tool calls and version capability contracts.

visual.title: MCP architecture
visual.caption: MCP standardizes how AI clients discover and invoke external capabilities through a common protocol.

lessons.title: LLM Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Define task-specific datasets and success criteria, then combine deterministic checks, model-based judges where appropriate, and human review. Track quality, latency, cost and safety together.
lessons.why: LLM systems are stochastic and task-dependent, so “it looked good in a few prompts” is not an engineering evaluation strategy.
lessons.intuition: Turn the application goal into measurable dimensions: correctness, groundedness, usefulness, safety, latency and cost. Build a stable test set and compare changes against it.
lessons.deepDive: Use exact/programmatic checks where possible, model-based judges for subjective dimensions, and human review for calibration/high-risk cases. Evaluate components separately: retrieval, tool selection, structured output, final response. Include adversarial and edge cases. Report distributions and failure categories rather than one aggregate score. Version prompts, models and datasets so regressions are reproducible.
lessons.workedExample: For a tool-using planning assistant, evaluate whether it chooses the correct function and arguments, whether the numerical result matches the tool output, whether the explanation is useful, and total latency/cost.
commonMistakes: Using only BLEU/ROUGE for open-ended assistant quality.
Changing the test set every time a model changes.
Trusting one LLM judge without human calibration or pairwise consistency checks.
followUps: How would you build an eval set?
LLM-as-judge pros/cons?
How do you evaluate agents?
What metrics matter in production?
lessons.production: Run evals in CI before prompt/model releases and online monitoring after deployment. Keep failure traces so qualitative regressions can be diagnosed, not just counted.

visual.title: LLM Evaluation
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: LLM Inference: Temperature, Top-p, KV Cache
lessons.interviewAnswer: Temperature and top-p affect sampling randomness; the KV cache reuses attention keys/values from previous tokens to avoid recomputing the entire prefix during autoregressive generation.
lessons.why: Inference controls explain output randomness and runtime cost. Temperature/top-p affect token sampling, while KV cache and batching affect performance.
lessons.intuition: The model produces logits for the next token. Decoding converts logits to probabilities and selects a token; caching reuses attention states from previous tokens so generation does not recompute the whole history.
lessons.deepDive: Temperature rescales logits before softmax: lower values sharpen the distribution; higher values flatten it. Top-p samples from the smallest token set whose cumulative probability reaches p. Greedy decoding chooses the max token. KV cache stores prior key/value projections for autoregressive attention, reducing repeated compute but consuming memory proportional to layers, sequence length, batch and head dimensions.
lessons.math: p_i = softmax(z_i / T). Lower T → sharper distribution.
lessons.workedExample: For deterministic structured extraction, use low temperature and schema constraints. For creative generation, moderate sampling may help. Large context + many concurrent requests can become KV-cache-memory bound even if model weights fit comfortably.
lessons.code:
# conceptual generation settings
generate(temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9, max_new_tokens=300)
commonMistakes: Saying temperature changes model knowledge.
Treating top-p and temperature as equivalent controls.
Ignoring KV-cache memory when estimating serving capacity.
followUps: Temperature 0 vs greedy decoding?
What does top-p do?
Why KV cache speeds decoding?
Prefill vs decode?
lessons.production: Monitor time-to-first-token, tokens/sec, context length, KV-cache utilization and batching efficiency. Decode settings should be task-specific and regression-tested.

visual.title: LLM inference path
visual.caption: Serving separates prompt prefill from token-by-token decode; KV caching avoids recomputing past attention states.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning, LoRA & Quantization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Fine-tuning changes model behavior through training; LoRA learns low-rank adapter updates instead of all parameters; quantization reduces numerical precision to lower memory/compute, usually with some quality trade-off.
lessons.why: Fine-tuning/LoRA/quantization questions test whether you can choose between behavior adaptation, retrieval and serving optimization.
lessons.intuition: Fine-tuning changes model weights. LoRA changes a small low-rank set of trainable adapters instead of all weights. Quantization stores/computes weights or activations with fewer bits to reduce memory/cost.
lessons.deepDive: Full fine-tuning can adapt deeply but is expensive and risks catastrophic changes. LoRA represents weight updates as low-rank matrices, greatly reducing trainable parameters and optimizer memory. Quantization may be post-training or quantization-aware and trades precision for memory/throughput. RAG should usually handle changing external knowledge; fine-tuning is better for behavior/style/task patterns.
lessons.math: LoRA update: W' = W + BA, with rank r ≪ min(d_in,d_out)
lessons.workedExample: For an internal assistant that needs company facts updated weekly, use RAG. If it consistently fails to follow a specialized structured reasoning/output pattern, LoRA may be worth evaluating.
lessons.code:
# conceptual PEFT
# freeze base weights; train low-rank adapter matrices on target examples
commonMistakes: Fine-tuning to “teach” frequently changing facts that retrieval could provide.
Assuming 4-bit quantization has zero quality trade-off.
Comparing LoRA ranks without considering which layers are adapted.
followUps: RAG vs fine-tuning?
Why LoRA saves memory?
What is QLoRA?
Post-training vs quantization-aware training?
lessons.production: Version base model, adapters, tokenizer and quantization config together. Re-run safety/task evals after any fine-tune or quantization change.

visual.title: LoRA adaptation
visual.caption: LoRA learns a low-rank update while keeping the large pretrained weight matrix frozen.

lessons.title: Graph ML Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A graph represents entities as nodes and relationships as edges. ML on graphs combines node/edge features with graph structure to predict node labels, links, graph properties or rankings.
lessons.why: Graph ML starts with representing entities and relationships explicitly; interviews expect you to know nodes, edges, direction, heterogeneity and graph-specific leakage.
lessons.intuition: A graph stores objects as nodes and relationships as edges. Features live on nodes/edges, while topology itself provides information that ordinary tabular models may miss.
lessons.deepDive: Graphs may be directed/undirected, weighted, homogeneous or heterogeneous with multiple node/edge types. Degree, neighborhoods, paths and connected components describe structure. Adjacency matrices/lists encode connectivity. In ML, splits require care: edges/nodes from the future can leak information, and message passing can indirectly expose validation/test structure depending on the setup.
lessons.math: Adjacency A_ij=1 (or weight) when an edge connects i→j. Degree d_i=Σ_j A_ij for a simple directed-out degree.
lessons.workedExample: A developer–PR graph has two node types and “authored”/“reviewed” edges. The same PR text alone misses historical reviewer relationships that graph structure captures.
commonMistakes: Treating graph rows as independent samples.
Ignoring edge direction/type.
Randomly splitting temporal interaction graphs without leakage analysis.
followUps: Homogeneous vs heterogeneous graph?
Directed vs undirected?
What is node degree?
How do you split graph data?
lessons.production: Graph freshness, edge timestamps and entity resolution matter as much as the GNN. Build reproducible snapshot logic for training and online updates.

visual.title: Graph representation
visual.caption: Graphs represent entities as nodes and relationships as edges; node/edge features add attributes.

lessons.title: Message Passing in GNNs
lessons.interviewAnswer: GNN layers aggregate information from neighbors and combine it with the current node representation. Repeating layers expands the receptive field over graph hops.
lessons.why: Message passing is the core abstraction behind many GNNs and explains how local graph structure becomes learned node representations.
lessons.intuition: Each node receives summaries from neighbors, combines them with its own state, and repeats this for several layers so information travels multiple hops.
lessons.deepDive: A generic layer computes messages from neighbors, aggregates them with a permutation-invariant function such as sum/mean/max, then updates the node representation. After k layers, a node typically depends on k-hop neighborhoods. Too many layers can lead to over-smoothing or over-squashing; high-degree neighborhoods may require sampling.
lessons.math: m_v = AGG_{u∈N(v)} M(h_v,h_u,e_uv); h_v' = U(h_v,m_v)
lessons.workedExample: In reviewer recommendation, a developer embedding can incorporate the PRs they reviewed; another layer can indirectly incorporate relationships from nearby developers/PRs.
commonMistakes: Thinking neighbor order should affect a permutation-invariant graph aggregator.
Adding many layers without considering oversmoothing.
Ignoring edge features/types when they carry semantics.
followUps: What is over-smoothing?
Why must aggregation be permutation invariant?
How many hops does k layers see?
What is neighbor sampling?
lessons.production: Bound neighborhood expansion for memory/latency and monitor degree skew; giant hubs can dominate compute and representation quality.

visual.title: GNN message passing
visual.caption: GNN layers repeatedly aggregate information from local neighborhoods.

lessons.title: GraphSAGE
lessons.interviewAnswer: GraphSAGE learns aggregation functions that combine sampled neighbor features, enabling inductive embeddings for nodes that were not present during training.
lessons.why: GraphSAGE is a key inductive GNN architecture and directly supports reviewer/recommendation systems where new nodes appear over time.
lessons.intuition: Instead of learning one embedding per node, GraphSAGE learns how to combine a node’s features with sampled neighbor features. That learned aggregator can be applied to unseen nodes.
lessons.deepDive: At each layer, sample/aggregate neighbor representations and combine them with the node’s current representation, often followed by nonlinear transformation/normalization. Mean, pooling and LSTM-style aggregators are possible. Sampling makes training scalable on large graphs, while inductive parameter sharing allows embeddings for new nodes if their features/neighborhood are available.
lessons.math: h_v^(k)=σ(W^(k) · CONCAT(h_v^(k-1), AGG({h_u^(k-1):u∈N(v)})))
lessons.workedExample: For a new PR, its CodeBERT features plus learned transformations/graph context can place it near developers with relevant historical expertise without retraining a free embedding for that exact PR node.
lessons.code:
# Conceptual PyG layer
from torch_geometric.nn import SAGEConv
conv=SAGEConv(in_channels=768,out_channels=768)
commonMistakes: Saying GraphSAGE requires every test node to exist during training.
Ignoring neighbor-sampling bias/variance.
Confusing graph structure with text similarity alone.
followUps: GraphSAGE vs GCN?
Why is GraphSAGE inductive?
How do you handle no-neighbor cold-start nodes?
How do you use it for link prediction?
lessons.production: Refresh graph edges/features incrementally, bound neighbor sampling for latency, monitor cold-start quality and separate candidate generation from final ranking/business constraints.

lab.goal: Implement one GraphSAGE-style neighbor aggregation step with mean aggregation.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
X=np.array([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,1.]])
neighbors={0:[1,2],1:[0],2:[0]}
out=[]
for i in range(len(X)):
    agg=X[neighbors[i]].mean(0)
    out.append(np.concatenate([X[i],agg]))
out=np.stack(out)
print(out)
lab.verifyIt:
assert out.shape==(3,4)
assert H.shape==(3,2)

visual.title: GraphSAGE
visual.caption: GraphSAGE is inductive because the aggregation function can embed previously unseen nodes from features and neighborhoods.

lessons.title: Link Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Link prediction scores whether an edge should exist between two nodes. Candidate node embeddings are combined with a scoring function and trained against positive and negative edges.
lessons.why: Link prediction is a natural formulation for reviewer recommendation, social connections and knowledge-graph completion.
lessons.intuition: Learn node representations, then score whether a pair of nodes should have an edge. Training uses observed positive edges plus sampled negative pairs.
lessons.deepDive: Scores can be dot products, bilinear functions or neural decoders over node embeddings. Negative sampling matters because the number of non-edges is enormous and random negatives may be too easy. Temporal splits are important when predicting future links. Ranking evaluation often fits better than binary accuracy because the real task is choosing top candidates.
lessons.math: s(u,v)=h_uᵀh_v (simple dot-product decoder); p(edge)=σ(s)
lessons.workedExample: For each PR, historical reviewer edges are positives. Candidate developers not reviewing that PR can be negatives, but avoid sampling impossible/inactive reviewers that make training unrealistically easy.
commonMistakes: Treating every missing edge as a true negative.
Using random train/test edges when future recommendation is the goal.
Evaluating only AUC when production returns top-K candidates.
followUps: How do you sample negatives?
Dot-product vs MLP decoder?
Why chronological split?
How does cold start affect link prediction?
lessons.production: Candidate generation, eligibility/availability filters and ranking constraints often sit around the learned link score. Log impressions/acceptance for online evaluation.

lab.goal: Score candidate graph links with embedding similarity and evaluate whether a true edge ranks highly.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
pr=np.array([1.,.2])
reviewers=np.array([[.9,.1],[0.,1.],[.5,.5],[-1.,0.]])
scores=reviewers@pr
rank=np.argsort(-scores)
print(rank,scores[rank])
lab.useIt:
true_reviewer=0; k=2
recall_at_k=float(true_reviewer in rank[:k]); print('Recall@2',recall_at_k)
lab.verifyIt:
assert rank[0]==0
assert recall_at_k==1.0

lessons.title: Recall@K & Ranking Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Recall@K asks whether relevant items appear in the top K recommendations. It fits reviewer/recommender systems better than plain classification accuracy because users receive ranked candidates.
lessons.why: Ranking systems are judged by whether relevant items appear near the top, so Recall@K is often more meaningful than classification accuracy.
lessons.intuition: For each query, look only at the first K recommendations and ask what fraction of the relevant items were recovered.
lessons.deepDive: Recall@K ignores ordering within the top K; Precision@K penalizes irrelevant returned items; MRR emphasizes the rank of the first relevant result; nDCG handles graded relevance and position discounts. Metric choice depends on how many relevant items exist and what users actually inspect. Offline labels may be incomplete—unobserved does not always mean irrelevant.
lessons.math: Recall@K = (# relevant items in top K)/(# relevant items)
lessons.workedExample: If the true reviewer set contains 2 people and one appears in the top 10, Recall@10=0.5 for that PR. In a single-label formulation, the metric becomes whether the one known reviewer appears in top K.
commonMistakes: Saying Recall@10=77% means 77% of the top 10 suggestions are correct.
Ignoring multiple relevant reviewers.
Comparing ranking metrics without matching candidate sets/label definitions.
followUps: Precision@K vs Recall@K?
What is MRR?
Why nDCG?
How do incomplete labels affect offline evaluation?
lessons.production: Track ranking quality by query cohort and candidate availability; online acceptance/merge latency may be better business metrics than offline Recall@K alone.

lessons.title: Popularity Bias in Recommenders
lessons.interviewAnswer: Highly active/popular entities can dominate recommendations even when niche specialists are more relevant. Mitigation can include debiasing, re-ranking, diversity constraints or separating expertise from activity.
lessons.why: Recommenders often over-recommend popular items/users because historical interactions are heavily skewed, reducing personalization and specialist discovery.
lessons.intuition: If one maintainer reviews almost everything, the model can learn “recommend the maintainer” and score well without learning topic-specific expertise.
lessons.deepDive: Bias comes from exposure and label imbalance: popular candidates have more training edges and more chances to be selected. Mitigations include candidate normalization, degree-aware features/losses, debiasing embeddings, diversity constraints and separating expertise from activity. Improvements should be validated against relevance, not just forced equal exposure.
lessons.workedExample: Centroid subtraction can remove a generic “core team” direction so niche PR text surfaces specialists rather than the same high-degree maintainer every time.
commonMistakes: Assuming popularity is always bad—high activity may be a valid reliability signal.
Forcing equal recommendation rates regardless of relevance.
Evaluating only aggregate Recall@K and missing long-tail quality.
followUps: How would you measure popularity bias?
What is exposure bias?
How do you balance expertise and activity?
Could debiasing hurt accuracy?
lessons.production: Monitor recommendation concentration, long-tail coverage, acceptance and workload distribution. Provide business controls when activity/availability is operationally important.

visual.title: Popularity bias
visual.caption: Interaction data is often dominated by popular items, which can cause recommenders to over-recommend the head unless corrected.

lessons.title: ETL vs ELT
lessons.interviewAnswer: ETL transforms data before loading it into the target system; ELT loads raw data first and transforms within a powerful warehouse/lakehouse. Choice depends on governance, scale, latency and platform.
lessons.why: ETL vs ELT tests whether you understand where transformations happen and how modern data platforms trade control, scalability and governance.
lessons.intuition: ETL transforms data before it reaches the analytical destination. ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse/lakehouse using its compute.
lessons.deepDive: ETL is useful when destination constraints, privacy or standardization require processing before load. ELT preserves raw data and exploits scalable warehouse compute, improving reprocessing/flexibility. Real systems are often hybrid. The important design questions are lineage, schema evolution, idempotency, data quality, cost and whether transformations need to support both batch and near-real-time consumers.
lessons.workedExample: An ADF pipeline can extract relational tables, apply SQL transformations and load curated outputs—ETL. A lakehouse workflow might first land raw files, then use Spark/SQL models inside the platform—ELT.
commonMistakes: Saying ELT is always newer/better.
Ignoring governance and sensitive fields when landing raw data.
Treating ETL/ELT as only a tool choice rather than a data-flow architecture choice.
followUps: When would you prefer ETL?
Why is ELT common in cloud warehouses?
How do you make pipelines idempotent?
How do you handle schema changes?
lessons.production: Track lineage, source timestamps, row counts, checksums and quality expectations at each stage. Backfills and retries should not duplicate or corrupt downstream data.

visual.title: ETL vs ELT
visual.caption: The choice depends on compute location, governance, latency and how many downstream consumers need raw data.

lessons.title: Batch vs Streaming
lessons.interviewAnswer: Batch processing handles bounded datasets on a schedule; streaming processes events continuously or in small increments. Choose based on freshness requirements, complexity, cost and correctness needs.
lessons.why: Batch vs streaming is a core architecture trade-off for data and ML systems: freshness, complexity, cost and correctness all change.
lessons.intuition: Batch waits and processes a bounded collection. Streaming processes an unbounded flow continuously or in small micro-batches.
lessons.deepDive: Batch is simpler, cheaper and easier to reproduce when minute/hour/day freshness is sufficient. Streaming is justified when decisions need low event-to-action latency. Stream processing introduces ordering, event time, late data, state, checkpoints and delivery semantics. Many systems combine a streaming serving path with batch recomputation/backfills.
lessons.workedExample: Daily model-feature recomputation is naturally batch. Fraud detection at payment time requires streaming/online features because waiting until tomorrow is useless.
commonMistakes: Choosing streaming because it sounds modern without a latency requirement.
Confusing Kafka ingestion with stream processing.
Ignoring late/out-of-order events and state recovery.
followUps: Event time vs processing time?
When is micro-batching enough?
How do you replay data?
What is the operational cost of streaming?
lessons.production: Define freshness SLOs first. Use the simplest architecture that meets them, and design replay/backfill paths so real-time state can be recovered after bugs or outages.

visual.title: Batch vs streaming
visual.caption: Many systems combine both: streaming for freshness and batch for recomputation/backfills.

lessons.title: Kafka Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kafka is a distributed event log. Producers write records to partitioned topics; consumers read offsets, often in consumer groups for parallelism and fault tolerance.
lessons.why: Kafka appears in data-engineering and ML-platform interviews because it cleanly separates event producers from many downstream consumers.
lessons.intuition: A topic is split into partitions. Producers append records; consumers read records by offset. Consumer groups divide partitions among members so processing can scale horizontally.
lessons.deepDive: Kafka is a durable distributed log rather than a simple message queue. Ordering is guaranteed within a partition, not across an entire multi-partition topic. Delivery semantics depend on producer, broker and consumer processing/commit behavior.
lessons.math: Key relationship: one partition is actively consumed by at most one consumer in the same consumer group at a time.
lessons.code:
# Conceptual Python producer/consumer
# producer.send('radiation-events', value=event)
# consumer = Consumer({'group.id': 'flink-job', ...})
# consumer.subscribe(['radiation-events'])
commonMistakes: Saying Kafka itself performs arbitrary stream analytics—that is typically handled by stream processors/consumers.
Assuming global ordering across partitions.
Confusing consumer groups with broadcast to independent applications.
followUps: Why partitions?
What happens when a consumer fails?
At-least-once vs exactly-once?
Kafka vs RabbitMQ?
lessons.production: Monitor lag, throughput, partition balance, broker health and schema compatibility. Choose partition keys carefully because they define ordering and load distribution.
lessons.workedExample: In a radiation-monitoring pipeline, a producer publishes measurements to Kafka while a Flink job consumes and processes them independently.

visual.title: Kafka data flow
visual.caption: Kafka decouples producers and consumers through durable ordered partition logs.

lessons.title: Flink & Stateful Stream Processing
lessons.interviewAnswer: Flink processes unbounded streams with state, event-time semantics, windows and checkpointing. It is designed for continuous computations where correctness across time and failures matters.
lessons.why: Flink questions test stateful stream processing, event-time reasoning and recovery beyond simply consuming Kafka messages.
lessons.intuition: Flink continuously processes events while maintaining state. Checkpoints make that state recoverable, and event-time/watermarks let windows reason about when events actually occurred.
lessons.deepDive: Operators transform streams; keyed streams partition state by key. Stateful operators snapshot state/checkpoint metadata to durable storage. Event time handles out-of-order events; watermarks estimate event-time progress; windows group events over time intervals. Exactly-once guarantees require source/state/sink coordination and depend on the full pipeline, not Flink alone.
lessons.workedExample: Radiation readings keyed by sensor can maintain rolling state and classify risk; a watermark allows late readings within a tolerated delay to update event-time windows.
commonMistakes: Confusing processing time with event time.
Claiming exactly-once without considering the sink.
Ignoring checkpoint size/recovery cost for large state.
followUps: Watermarks?
Keyed state?
Checkpoint vs savepoint?
How does Flink recover after failure?
lessons.production: Monitor checkpoint duration/failures, backpressure, watermark lag, state size and Kafka consumer lag; tune parallelism from bottlenecks.

visual.title: Stateful stream processing
visual.caption: Flink processes unbounded streams with state, event-time semantics and fault-tolerant checkpoints.

lessons.title: Spark / PySpark
