Provides university-level randomization, blocking, causal comparison, and experimental design foundations.
Provides large-scale operational lessons on assignment systems, treatment delivery, trust checks, ramps, and analysis.
Provides deployed evidence on cluster randomization and interference-aware design in large connected systems.

lessons.title: Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM)
lessons.interviewAnswer: SRM means the observed variant counts are inconsistent with the planned allocation beyond ordinary random fluctuation. I test assignment-unit counts against expected proportions, usually with a chi-square goodness-of-fit check, before looking at effects. A very small p-value is a smoke alarm, not an effect adjustment: I investigate assignment, eligibility, exposure delivery, missing telemetry, identity changes, redirects, filters, joins, bots, and time of onset. I also distinguish all-assigned SRM from triggered-population SRM. Until the root cause is explained and shown not to bias the estimand, I quarantine the result and normally fix and restart the experiment.
keyPoints: SRM tests allocation integrity, not treatment impact
Expected counts come from the actual design and ramp history
Assignment, exposure, and analysis populations need separate checks
The chi-square p-value detects a symptom but not its cause
A failed SRM gate blocks causal interpretation until diagnosed
lessons.why: A missing telemetry event can occur more often in one variant precisely because that variant crashes, redirects, or changes the code path. An analysis then drops affected units and turns harm into an apparent win. Duplicate identifiers, stale assignment cookies, inconsistent eligibility, or faulty joins can cause the same symptom. Because treatment effects are often small, even modest selective loss can dominate the signal. Microsoft's SRM taxonomy describes the diagnostic as analogous to fever: easy to detect, diverse in cause, and dangerous to ignore. Interviews ask SRM because it reveals whether a candidate trusts the experimental data-generating process before running inference.
lessons.intuition: If a fair assignment service sends half of a large eligible population to each arm, arm counts wobble around fifty-fifty by chance. A difference of a few users is ordinary; a difference of thousands is not. The SRM statistic scales each squared deviation by its expected count, then asks how surprising the total would be under the design. But the alarm cannot tell whether the randomizer, treatment delivery, event logging, identity resolution, or analysis filter caused the loss. Build a chain of counts from eligible to assigned to delivered to exposed to measured, and find the first stage where arms diverge.
lessons.deepDive: SRM is a model check on the experiment's allocation process. Its value comes from coupling a simple global test with stage-wise accounting and operational forensics, not from mechanically applying a significance threshold.
lessons.workedExample: A 50/50 test records 510,000 assigned users per arm, so assignment SRM passes. The analysis table contains 505,000 control but only 482,000 treatment users. Stage reconciliation shows equal delivery but treatment users on app version 8.2 crash before emitting the exposure and purchase events. An inner join to exposure silently removed them; surviving treatment users appear to convert better. The correct response is not to scale treatment counts upward. The team quarantines the causal result, fixes crash and event parity, adds a left-join missingness guardrail, and restarts under a new version. The broken run remains evidence of treatment harm and platform failure.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking event counts instead of randomized units
commonMistakes.correction: Repeated activity differs by treatment; deduplicate the actual assignment unit for the allocation check.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring SRM because baseline covariates look balanced
commonMistakes.correction: Observed balance cannot rule out selective loss on unmeasured potential outcomes or broken telemetry.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reweighting to 50/50
commonMistakes.correction: Count weights do not recover selectively missing outcomes; diagnose the generating defect first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Testing only the final analysis table
commonMistakes.correction: Reconcile eligible, assigned, delivered, exposed, measured, and analyzed stages to localize the break.

followUps.question: Does unequal arm size always mean SRM?
followUps.answer: No. Compare observed counts with the planned allocation, including ramp changes and capacity rules. SRM is implausible deviation from design, not inequality itself.

followUps.question: Can an experiment with SRM still be analyzed?
followUps.answer: Only after the cause is fully understood and a defensible estimand and correction are established. The safe default is quarantine, fix, and restart.

followUps.question: Why can assignment SRM pass while analysis SRM fails?
followUps.answer: Treatment-dependent delivery, event loss, filtering, identity, or joins can selectively remove units after correct assignment.

lessons.production: Compute stage-wise unique-unit counts from immutable eligible, assignment, delivery, exposure, metric, and analysis snapshots. Derive expected counts from versioned allocation and ramp history. Alert with minimum-count and repeated-monitoring logic; route to an owner with experiment, slice, onset, residual, and lineage evidence. Automatically hide treatment effects behind a trust gate when SRM fails. Retain raw IDs under strict access and privacy controls for forensic joins, then aggregate incident artifacts. Version fixes and restart under a new experiment identifier. Monitor assignment-library versions, identifier churn, event parity, late arrival, and join attrition. Rollback treatment serving on correlated reliability harm, but never delete the malformed run that exposed the defect.
lessons.description: Sample ratio mismatch (SRM) occurs when observed experiment allocation counts differ implausibly from the proportions specified by the randomization design. It is one of the highest-value trust diagnostics in online experimentation because many assignment, eligibility, exposure, identity, and logging defects first appear as unexpected arm counts. This chapter derives the multinomial chi-square check, explains its assumptions and scale sensitivity, distinguishes assignment-level from triggered-analysis SRM, and builds a root-cause taxonomy across randomization, delivery, telemetry, filtering, bots, joins, and time. You will learn why SRM is a symptom rather than a correction target, why balanced outcomes cannot rescue a failed trust check, how to localize onset and affected slices, and when unequal counts are expected by design. A worked redirect bug shows how treatment-dependent loss reverses an apparent effect. The lab implements the SRM statistic and p-value, compares it with SciPy, and diagnoses a time-slice failure using invariants. Production guidance covers continuous alerting, multiple looks, minimum counts, ownership, forensic snapshots, restart criteria, and rollback. The rule is simple: do not interpret treatment effects until the mismatch is understood and the causal sample is trustworthy.
learningObjectives: Compute an SRM goodness-of-fit statistic for arbitrary planned allocation proportions and interpret it as a trust diagnostic.
Separate valid random allocation fluctuation from assignment, delivery, exposure, logging, filtering, identity, and join failures.
Localize an SRM by event stage, time, platform, geography, eligibility, and identifier without outcome-driven fishing.
Define automated alert, investigation, restart, and evidence-preservation procedures for an experimentation platform.

deepSections.title: Expected counts and the goodness-of-fit test
deepSections.body: For K variants with observed counts O_k, planned shares pi_k summing to one, and total N, expected counts are E_k=N*pi_k. Pearson's statistic is sum_k (O_k-E_k)^2/E_k and is approximately chi-square with K-1 degrees of freedom under independent assignment and sufficiently large expected counts. Use the assignment unit, not events or sessions, unless that is truly the randomized unit. Compute expectations from the allocation schedule when ramps changed over time. Tiny p-values are common for meaningful defects at scale, but fixed universal thresholds and repeated monitoring require an alerting design. Exact multinomial methods can handle small counts.

deepSections.title: Assigned, exposed, triggered, and analyzed populations
deepSections.body: Run SRM first on all eligible assigned units from the authoritative assignment log. Then reconcile treatment delivery, exposure, outcome telemetry, and the final analysis population. A triggered analysis can legitimately change arm proportions only if triggering is pre-treatment or unaffected by assignment; treatment-dependent triggering is post-randomization selection. Counts of exposure events can differ because users generate repeated events, so deduplicate at the unit level. A test that passes at assignment but fails after a metric join points downstream. A test that fails at assignment points toward eligibility, randomizer, identity, namespace, or ramp logic.

deepSections.title: Root-cause taxonomy
deepSections.body: Assignment causes include incorrect weights, inconsistent hashing libraries, overlapping experiments, missing salts, nonsticky IDs, and variant-specific eligibility. Delivery causes include redirects, caching, fail-open behavior, platform version gating, and capacity rejection. Instrumentation causes include variant-specific event paths, crashes before logging, schema drift, blocked scripts, and late events. Analysis causes include inner joins, asymmetric bot rules, timezone windows, deduplication, post-treatment filters, and incompatible snapshots. Identity causes include cookie deletion, device switching, merging, duplicate IDs, and logged-out users. External causes include crawlers or campaigns routed differently. The correction follows the first broken stage, not the final count table.

deepSections.title: Localizing onset and affected slices
deepSections.body: Plot cumulative observed-minus-expected counts over assignment time and annotate ramps, releases, schema changes, outages, and redirects. Test coarse prespecified slices such as platform, app version, country, data center, eligibility path, and identifier type to locate concentration, while controlling alert multiplicity and avoiding outcome-driven selection. Reconstruct the same units through raw assignment, exposure, and outcome tables with left joins and reason-coded attrition. Compare treatment and control missingness at each stage. Validate a suspected root cause by reproducing it on affected records and showing that the divergence begins where predicted, not merely by finding a correlated slice.

deepSections.title: Quarantine, repair, restart, and prevention
deepSections.body: Do not reweight arm counts to the planned ratio and declare the bias solved; missing units may differ in outcomes. If the cause is fully known and independent of potential outcomes under a defensible estimand, a planned correction may be possible, but this is exceptional and documented. Usually stop or quarantine, fix the system, choose whether old evidence is unusable, and restart with a new experiment version. Preserve the broken run for platform learning. Add prevention through shared assignment libraries, immutable exposure contracts, left-join analyses, event parity tests, A/A tests, ramp gates, automated stage-wise reconciliation, and incident owners. A passed rerun does not retroactively validate contaminated data.

lessons.math: Given planned probabilities pi_1,...,pi_K and N observed assignment units, E_k=N*pi_k and X^2=sum_k(O_k-E_k)^2/E_k. Under the null and regularity, X^2 is approximately chi-square_{K-1}; p=P(ChiSq>=X^2). For two 50/50 arms this is equivalent to checking a binomial count. Standardized cell residuals (O_k-E_k)/sqrt(E_k) show direction but are dependent. Repeated looks or many slice tests require an alert policy; a small p-value does not quantify outcome bias.

workedExamples.title: A downstream SRM that manufactures a conversion win

lessons.title: Variance Reduction & CUPED
lessons.interviewAnswer: CUPED reduces experiment variance by subtracting the predictable part of an outcome from a pre-treatment covariate. With outcome Y and centered covariate X, define Y_adj=Y-theta(X-E[X]), where theta=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X). Because treatment is randomized and X is measured before treatment, arm means of X are equal in expectation, so the treatment contrast stays unbiased while residual variance falls; with an optimal single covariate the ideal reduction is rho squared. I freeze the pre-period cutoff, estimate theta without outcome-driven selection, handle missing X explicitly, preserve ITT, and verify the adjusted effect against the raw estimate and historical simulations.
keyPoints: CUPED removes outcome variation predictable before treatment
Pre-treatment timing protects the causal contrast
Ideal single-covariate variance reduction is governed by squared correlation
Regression adjustment generalizes CUPED but needs design-aware specification
Precision gains never excuse SRM, leakage, or post-treatment selection
lessons.why: User-level revenue, sessions, and engagement are heterogeneous: a small group of naturally heavy users creates large variance even after randomization balances groups in expectation. Historical behavior predicts much of that variation but cannot be affected by today's treatment. Removing it can detect the same decision-relevant effect with fewer units or a narrower interval at the same sample size. The original CUPED paper demonstrated the value of pre-experiment data for online experiments. However, a covariate contaminated by treatment, a cutoff tied to exposure, or post-hoc selection among many adjustments can bias or overstate gains. Production implementations therefore treat temporal lineage and analysis governance as first-class requirements.
lessons.intuition: Two randomized arms may contain slightly different numbers of naturally high-spending users by chance. If last month's spend predicts this month's spend, subtract each user's expected baseline tendency before comparing arms. The adjusted outcome asks whether a user did unusually well relative to their pre-treatment pattern. Centering preserves the overall scale, and randomization means neither arm should receive systematically different baseline adjustments. Stronger pre-to-post correlation removes more noise. A user with no history requires a prespecified representation; silently keeping only returning users changes the target population.
lessons.deepDive: CUPED is a control-variate estimator embedded in a randomized design. It exploits known zero treatment contrast for pre-treatment variables to reduce estimator variance while retaining the original causal estimand.
lessons.workedExample: A revenue test has raw user-level standard deviation $40 and an effect estimate of +$0.60. Pre-period revenue correlates 0.7 with experiment-period revenue. Ideal residual variance is about 1-0.49=51% of raw variance, so standard error falls by roughly sqrt(0.51), subject to estimation and missing history. CUPED produces +$0.58 with a substantially narrower interval; the small point-estimate change is compatible with random baseline imbalance, not evidence that CUPED created revenue. New users are retained using a missing-history indicator. Raw and adjusted conclusions, theta, cutoff, missingness, and interval are all published.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a covariate measured after assignment
commonMistakes.correction: Treatment may change it, so subtraction can remove part of the effect or induce selection bias; enforce a pre-treatment cutoff.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping users without history
commonMistakes.correction: That changes the population and can bias a triggered analysis; handle missing history explicitly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting CUPED to fix a broken test
commonMistakes.correction: It reduces random variance under a trustworthy design; it does not repair SRM, logging loss, or interference.

commonMistakes.mistake: Selecting the best covariate after reading results
commonMistakes.correction: Prevalidate and version adjustment choices to avoid analysis multiplicity and overstated gains.

followUps.question: Why does CUPED remain unbiased?
followUps.answer: The centered covariate has zero expected arm contrast under randomization and is unaffected by treatment, so subtracting a fixed multiple does not change the expected treatment difference.

followUps.question: How much variance can it remove?
followUps.answer: For the optimal single linear covariate, the ideal outcome variance reduction is rho squared; treatment-effect variance also depends on allocation and estimation details.

followUps.question: What if theta is estimated from the experiment?
followUps.answer: Treatment-blind pooled estimation is common and often asymptotically valid, but fully interacted regression, robust errors, and historical validation improve protection under heterogeneity and finite samples.

lessons.production: Create a covariate contract with source, unit, historical window, absolute cutoff, transformation, missingness handling, and owner. Enforce that no input timestamp reaches the assignment or treatment period. Version theta or model artifacts and compute them treatment-blind. Persist raw and adjusted outcomes, effects, intervals, covariance, correlation, variance reduction, sample inclusion, and balance. Monitor cutoff violations, missing-history drift, feature availability, theta instability, residual variance, raw-adjusted divergence, and coverage on A/A traffic. Limit access to historical user behavior and minimize retention. If the adjustment pipeline fails, publish the valid raw estimator with wider uncertainty. Rollback the CUPED artifact without changing assignments, outcomes, or the prespecified causal target.
lessons.description: Controlled-experiment variance reduction uses pre-treatment information to make treatment-effect estimates more precise without changing the randomized causal contrast. CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) adjusts an outcome by a centered covariate measured before assignment, typically the same user metric in a historical window. This chapter derives the optimal linear coefficient, variance reduction factor, unbiasedness under randomization, cross-fitting and regression adjustment, missing pre-period data, triggered metrics, ratio metrics, multiple covariates, heterogeneity, and failure modes. You will learn why correlation determines precision gain, why post-treatment covariates create bias, why centering and a treatment interaction matter, and how to estimate gains on historical A/A-style data rather than selecting a favorable adjustment after seeing outcomes. A worked revenue experiment shows a large variance reduction with unchanged effect expectation. The lab implements CUPED from first principles, compares it with an OLS treatment coefficient, and verifies unbiased effect recovery plus reduced variance over repeated randomized trials. Production guidance covers cutoff enforcement, leakage checks, coefficient versioning, missingness, metric lineage, monitoring, fallback, and rollback. CUPED creates information by removing predictable noise; it cannot repair broken randomization or measurement.
learningObjectives: Derive the CUPED adjustment coefficient and variance reduction from covariance and correlation.
Choose covariates that are predictive, pre-treatment, consistently available, and unaffected by assignment or exposure.
Connect CUPED to regression adjustment, interactions, cross-fitting, and robust analysis for complex metrics.
Implement and validate an adjustment using unbiasedness, variance, leakage, missingness, and reproducibility checks.

deepSections.title: Control-variate derivation
deepSections.body: Let X be a pre-treatment covariate with mean mu_X and define Y_cv=Y-theta(X-mu_X). Its expectation equals E[Y] for any fixed theta because the centered term has mean zero. Its variance is Var(Y)+theta^2 Var(X)-2 theta Cov(Y,X), minimized at theta*=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X) when Var(X)>0. Substitution gives Var(Y_cv)=Var(Y)(1-rho^2), where rho is correlation between X and Y. In an experiment, comparing adjusted arm means retains ITT because assignment is independent of pre-treatment X in expectation. Finite-sample estimates of theta add uncertainty, usually small at scale but still part of method validation.

deepSections.title: Choosing and constructing covariates
deepSections.body: Good covariates predict the outcome, are available before assignment for the target units, have stable semantics, and cannot be altered by treatment. The same metric in a comparable pre-period is common; multiple historical periods, geography, device, or model predictions can add signal. Freeze an absolute cutoff before any unit could receive treatment, not a user-relative window starting from exposure. Do not use post-treatment clicks, survival, session count, or eligibility consequences. Avoid selecting covariates solely because they maximize precision in the current treatment comparison. Evaluate expected gains on historical periods, A/A splits, or cross-validation and keep a versioned covariate contract.

deepSections.title: Regression adjustment, interactions, and cross-fitting
deepSections.body: CUPED with one linear control is equivalent to residualizing outcomes or including a centered covariate in a treatment regression under corresponding specification. With treatment effects heterogeneous by X, include treatment-by-covariate interactions or use a fully interacted estimator so adjustment does not impose a common slope across arms. Robust standard errors protect heteroskedasticity. Flexible machine-learning predictions can serve as control variates when trained without treatment-period leakage; cross-fitting separates prediction training from residual evaluation and supports modern covariate adjustment. The target remains the randomized marginal effect, not the regression coefficient's associational interpretation outside the design.

deepSections.title: Missing history, new users, and nonlinear metrics
deepSections.body: New users have no pre-period metric. Complete-case CUPED changes the estimand to returning users and can interact with eligibility. Instead predefine zero plus a missingness indicator, group-specific centering, or a prediction model that accepts available features, then verify balance and effect interpretation. Heavy tails may need winsorization defined independently of treatment and applied consistently. Ratio metrics require unit-level definitions, delta-method or influence-function adjustment, or numerator and denominator treatment that preserves the estimand; subtracting a covariate from an already aggregated ratio is generally invalid. Triggered analyses must ensure the trigger is pre-treatment or assignment-invariant.

deepSections.title: Validating gains and guarding failure modes
deepSections.body: Always compute raw and adjusted effects: material divergence beyond expected noise suggests leakage, imbalance, implementation error, or estimand change. On historical null periods, verify centered adjusted effects and interval calibration. Measure covariance, theta, raw and residual variance, empirical reduction, missingness, and gains by prespecified platform or cohort. Re-estimate or version theta when behavior drifts, but do not tune repeatedly on live treatment effects. CUPED does not fix differential logging, SRM, interference, or noncompliance. If the covariate pipeline is late or invalid, fall back to the prespecified unadjusted estimator rather than blocking safety decisions or imputing from treatment-period outcomes.

lessons.math: For centered X_c=X-mu_X, Y_cuped=Y-theta X_c. E[Y_cuped]=E[Y]. The variance-minimizing theta*=Cov(Y,X)/Var(X), yielding Var(Y_cuped)=Var(Y)-Cov(Y,X)^2/Var(X)=Var(Y)(1-rho^2). Estimate the treatment effect as mean(Y_cuped|Z=1)-mean(Y_cuped|Z=0). In a sample, center X using a treatment-blind population mean and compute uncertainty for the adjusted outcome at the randomization unit, with robust or cluster-aware methods matching the design.

workedExamples.title: Reducing revenue noise without changing the target
workedExamples.body: Use a frozen historical revenue covariate, derive theta, retain new users with explicit missingness handling, compare raw and adjusted effects, and validate empirical variance reduction on historical splits.

exercises.prompt: If pre/post correlation is 0.6, what ideal variance fraction remains?
exercises.solution: 1-rho^2=1-0.36=0.64, so ideal variance reduction is 36% and standard error scales by sqrt(0.64)=0.8.

exercises.prompt: Why center X?
exercises.solution: Centering keeps the adjusted outcome mean on the original scale and makes the control-variate expectation zero; arm contrasts would cancel a common constant, but centering clarifies interpretation and numerics.

exercises.prompt: Can treatment-period session count be a CUPED covariate?
exercises.solution: No if treatment can affect sessions. It is post-treatment and adjustment could remove the treatment pathway or create selection bias.

lab.goal: Implement CUPED adjustment, compare it with regression adjustment, and verify effect unbiasedness plus variance reduction over repeated randomized experiments.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def cuped(y,x):
    x=np.asarray(x,float); y=np.asarray(y,float)
    xc=x-x.mean(); theta=float(np.dot(xc,y-y.mean())/np.dot(xc,xc))
    return y-theta*xc,theta
rng=np.random.default_rng(7); n=4000
x=rng.normal(10,3,n); z=rng.integers(0,2,n)
y=5+0.8*x+1.5*z+rng.normal(0,2,n)
y_adj,theta=cuped(y,x)
def arm_effect(values,z): return values[z==1].mean()-values[z==0].mean()
raw_effect=arm_effect(y,z); adjusted_effect=arm_effect(y_adj,z)
lab.useIt:
import statsmodels.api as sm
design=sm.add_constant(np.column_stack([z,x-x.mean()]))
fit=sm.OLS(y,design).fit(cov_type='HC1')
regression_effect=float(fit.params[1])
lab.verifyIt:
assert abs(theta-0.8)<0.05
assert abs(adjusted_effect-regression_effect)<1e-10
assert np.var(y_adj)<np.var(y)
assert abs(adjusted_effect-1.5)<0.12
raw=[]; adjusted=[]
for seed in range(200):
    local=np.random.default_rng(seed); zz=local.integers(0,2,n); yy=5+0.8*x+1.5*zz+local.normal(0,2,n); aa,_=cuped(yy,x)
    raw.append(arm_effect(yy,zz)); adjusted.append(arm_effect(aa,zz))
assert abs(np.mean(adjusted)-1.5)<0.03
assert np.var(adjusted)<0.6*np.var(raw)
lab.shipIt: Freeze covariate cutoff and missingness semantics, version theta/model, publish raw and adjusted estimates, monitor leakage and realized variance reduction, and fall back to the unadjusted ITT estimator if the covariate pipeline is invalid.

lessons.title: Sequential Testing, Peeking & Early Stopping
lessons.interviewAnswer: A fixed-horizon test controls Type I error only for its planned sample and analysis. If I repeatedly peek and stop when p<0.05, I give noise multiple chances to cross the threshold and inflate false positives. Valid options include prespecified group-sequential looks with alpha spending, a sequential probability ratio test for specified alternatives, or anytime-valid p-values, e-values, and confidence sequences. I define the stopping rule, information times, minimum duration, primary metric, multiplicity, and delayed-outcome handling before launch. Safety kill switches can stop exposure immediately, but confirmatory efficacy claims still follow their declared evidence procedure.
keyPoints: Optional stopping changes the sampling distribution
Monitoring schedule and stopping rule are part of the design
Group-sequential methods spend a finite error budget across planned looks
Confidence sequences provide simultaneous coverage over time
Safety stopping and efficacy inference answer different questions
lessons.why: Teams naturally watch experiments daily, want to stop losing variants early, and want to ship obvious wins without waiting. Traditional fixed-horizon reports tempt users to treat today's p-value as if no earlier looks occurred. Under a true null, enough looks make a threshold crossing increasingly likely. Valid sequential tools reconcile monitoring with error control, but their intervals are often wider early and their assumptions still depend on assignment, dependence, and metric construction. Interviews ask peeking because it exposes whether a candidate understands a procedure rather than a one-time formula. Experiment platforms must encode the rule so dashboards cannot silently change inferential meaning.
lessons.intuition: A fixed-horizon threshold is like one finish-line photograph. Peeking takes many photographs and keeps the most flattering one. Even when treatment does nothing, a noisy estimate wanders and may briefly look significant. Alpha spending divides a finite false-positive budget across planned checkpoints; early evidence must be stronger because more opportunities remain. A confidence sequence is a sequence of intervals constructed so the true value is covered simultaneously at all times with high probability, allowing observation at an arbitrary stopping time. Flexibility is paid for through wider early boundaries, not obtained for free.
lessons.deepDive: Sequential validity is a property of the entire stochastic evidence process. Calendar time, sample size, information, pending outcomes, and decision actions must be connected to the same prespecified filtration and stopping logic.
lessons.workedExample: A team views a null A/A conversion test at 10 equally spaced looks and stops at the first ordinary p<0.05. Simulation shows false launches far above 5%. They replace this with a prespecified five-look design using alpha/5 at each checkpoint, require two full weekly cycles, and keep a separate immediate crash kill switch. At the third look an ordinary p-value is 0.03: interesting, but above the 0.01 sequential boundary, so no efficacy claim is made. The test reaches its final planned look with a narrow interval excluding the practical benefit threshold and stops for lack of value, not because exact zero was proven.

commonMistakes.mistake: Peeking but claiming looks are highly correlated
commonMistakes.correction: Correlation reduces but does not remove inflation; calibrate the entire planned or anytime-valid procedure.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using an anytime-valid p-value with an ordinary interval
commonMistakes.correction: Inference objects must be matched; use the corresponding confidence sequence for time-uniform interval claims.

commonMistakes.mistake: Requiring statistical harm before stopping crashes
commonMistakes.correction: Operational safety can stop exposure immediately; statistical evidence governs later causal interpretation, not user protection.

commonMistakes.mistake: Restarting and combining p-values informally
commonMistakes.correction: A restart changes assignment, treatment, or evidence history; define a new experiment or a valid continuation rule.

followUps.question: What is a confidence sequence?
followUps.answer: A sequence of intervals designed to cover the fixed parameter simultaneously over all times with probability at least 1-alpha, enabling valid inspection at a data-dependent time.

followUps.question: What is alpha spending?
followUps.answer: A rule allocating cumulative Type I error across information times, with boundaries calibrated so total false-rejection probability remains controlled.

followUps.question: Can you always stop an experiment for harm?
followUps.answer: Yes operationally when users are at risk. Whether the resulting data support a formal harm claim depends on the prespecified monitoring and multiplicity procedure.

lessons.production: Store the inference mode, primary hypothesis, alternative or practical margin, maximum sample, minimum duration, information-time definition, planned looks, alpha-spending or e-process version, metric contracts, and delayed-outcome cutoff. The dashboard reads this immutable plan and cannot expose fixed-horizon significance at interim looks. Persist each look with data snapshot, counts, estimate, boundary, remaining budget, trust status, and action. Monitor SRM and invariants before sequential evidence. Simulate platform-wide false-positive behavior, including correlated metrics and overlapping tests. Safety alerts bypass efficacy gates but are audited. On invalid data or code, freeze claims, stop risky treatment, and restart under a new version; rollback must preserve the complete evidence path.
lessons.description: Sequential experimentation allows data-dependent monitoring or stopping while preserving a declared error guarantee. Repeatedly applying a fixed-horizon p-value whenever new data arrive does not do this: optional stopping selects unusually favorable noise and inflates false positives. This chapter develops fixed-horizon designs, group-sequential looks, alpha spending, sequential probability ratio tests, always-valid p-values, e-values, confidence sequences, futility, harm stopping, minimum run constraints, delayed outcomes, and decision-theoretic trade-offs. You will learn why stopping rules are part of the statistical procedure, how time-uniform intervals differ from ordinary intervals, how to choose between planned looks and continuous monitoring, and why operational kill switches should not be confused with efficacy claims. A worked product experiment contrasts naive peeking with an anytime-valid rule. The lab simulates false-positive inflation from fixed-horizon peeking and verifies control from a Bonferroni group-sequential design using SciPy. Production guidance covers dashboards, information time, alpha budgets, metric multiplicity, late data, restarts, safety escalation, audit logs, and rollback. Sequential methods provide flexibility only when the monitoring rule and evidence process are designed together.
learningObjectives: Explain mathematically and through simulation why optional stopping invalidates repeatedly viewed fixed-horizon p-values.
Choose and interpret fixed-horizon, group-sequential, alpha-spending, confidence-sequence, and e-value procedures.
Separate efficacy, futility, harm, operational, and business stopping rules with their distinct guarantees.
Implement and validate a planned-look design using family-wise error simulations and an immutable monitoring schedule.

deepSections.title: Why naive repeated testing fails
deepSections.body: A p-value is calibrated under a null distribution and an analysis rule. At each independent or correlated look, the estimate has another opportunity to produce an extreme statistic. The probability of ever crossing 0.05 exceeds 5%, even though adjacent looks reuse data and are dependent. Stopping at a favorable crossing also biases the reported effect upward, known as the winner's curse. Continuing after an unfavorable result but stopping after a favorable one is asymmetric optional stopping. A final ordinary interval calculated at that selected time no longer has its nominal fixed-horizon coverage. Simulation under the complete pipeline is a powerful audit of the actual rule.

deepSections.title: Planned looks and alpha spending
deepSections.body: Group-sequential designs specify interim information times and efficacy boundaries so the probability of any false rejection stays at alpha. Bonferroni can allocate alpha/K across K looks and is simple but conservative. Pocock-like boundaries spend more evenly; O'Brien-Fleming-like boundaries demand very strong early evidence and approach conventional thresholds later. Alpha-spending functions allow looks at flexible information times while tracking cumulative budget. Information time should reflect precision, not merely calendar days, especially with uneven traffic or delayed outcomes. Correlated endpoints and multiple variants consume an additional multiplicity budget.

deepSections.title: SPRT, e-values, and confidence sequences
deepSections.body: Wald's sequential probability ratio test accumulates a likelihood ratio between specified simple hypotheses and stops at evidence boundaries. Always-valid p-values remain valid at any stopping time under their construction. An e-process is a nonnegative process with null expectation controlled over time; a large e-value supplies evidence, and Ville's inequality bounds the probability its running maximum crosses 1/alpha. Confidence sequences invert sequential tests to provide intervals with simultaneous coverage across time. Modern nonparametric confidence sequences handle means and treatment effects under stated boundedness or variance assumptions. These objects are not ordinary p-values or confidence intervals with a new label; use matched estimators and implementations.

deepSections.title: Efficacy, futility, harm, and operational stopping
deepSections.body: Efficacy stopping claims benefit under the confirmatory rule. Futility stops when the chance or value of reaching a useful conclusion is low; nonbinding futility can preserve some guarantees more easily than binding rules. Harm stopping may use asymmetric thresholds and multiple safety metrics because protecting users outweighs power. Operational kill switches respond to crashes, latency, security, or data corruption and need no permission from an efficacy test, but the stopped run may not support a causal product claim. Minimum runtime covers novelty, weekly cycles, and delayed outcomes. Maximum runtime prevents indefinite underpowered tests. Define whether restarts create new evidence or continue a valid sequence.

deepSections.title: Information, delayed data, and platform validation
deepSections.body: Assign each unit once and define when its outcome becomes observable. If recent units have incomplete windows, naive daily means compare arms with different maturity or repeatedly revise history. Use cohort-complete information sets, lag-aware estimators, or explicitly modeled delayed outcomes. Persist every look, sample, metric version, cumulative alpha or e-value, boundary, and action. Backtest and simulate null, alternative, heavy-tailed, clustered, missing, and late-event scenarios using the exact production code. Never let a dashboard toggle between fixed and sequential inference after seeing results. If assumptions fail, quarantine evidence and use safety behavior, not an improvised threshold.

lessons.math: For K planned looks, Bonferroni rejects if any p_k<=alpha/K, guaranteeing family-wise error at most alpha without independence. An alpha-spending design chooses cumulative A(t)<=alpha and boundaries consistent with increments. A confidence sequence {C_t} satisfies P(theta in C_t for all t)>=1-alpha. An e-process E_t under H0 satisfies E[E_tau]<=1 for suitable stopping times; Ville gives P(sup_t E_t>=1/alpha)<=alpha. Exact formulas depend on metric, dependence, variance assumptions, and assignment design.

workedExamples.title: A tempting early p-value that does not cross the sequential boundary
workedExamples.body: Contrast naive repeated 0.05 testing with a finite alpha budget, preserve a separate harm switch, and use the final interval relative to a practical threshold.

exercises.prompt: Why is p=0.03 at an interim look not automatically a win?
exercises.solution: Its meaning depends on the planned boundary or anytime-valid construction; an ordinary fixed-horizon threshold is invalid after optional monitoring.

exercises.prompt: What is information time?
exercises.solution: The fraction of planned statistical information accumulated, often related to inverse variance, not necessarily the fraction of calendar duration.

exercises.prompt: Why are early group-sequential boundaries often stricter?
exercises.solution: They reserve error budget for later looks and prevent weak early noise from triggering a high false-positive rate.

lab.goal: Simulate false-positive inflation from naive peeking and verify family-wise control from a planned Bonferroni group-sequential design.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from math import erf,sqrt
def pvalue(x,y):
    n=len(x); effect=x.mean()-y.mean(); se=sqrt(x.var(ddof=1)/n+y.var(ddof=1)/n)
    z=effect/se; return 2*(1-0.5*(1+erf(abs(z)/sqrt(2))))
def simulate(rule,runs=3000,seed=7):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed); rejected=0; looks=(40,80,120,160,200)
    for _ in range(runs):
        x=rng.normal(size=looks[-1]); y=rng.normal(size=looks[-1])
        if any(pvalue(x[:n],y[:n])<=rule(len(looks),i) for i,n in enumerate(looks,1)):rejected+=1
    return rejected/runs
naive=simulate(lambda k,i:0.05)
controlled=simulate(lambda k,i:0.05/k)
lab.useIt:
from scipy.stats import norm
bonferroni_z=float(norm.ppf(1-0.05/(2*5)))
fixed_z=float(norm.ppf(1-0.05/2))
lab.verifyIt:
assert naive>0.10
assert controlled<0.065
assert controlled>0
assert bonferroni_z>fixed_z
assert abs(simulate(lambda k,i:0.05,seed=7)-naive)<1e-12
assert 0<=naive<=1 and 0<=controlled<=1
lab.shipIt: Encode the monitoring method and information schedule immutably, record every look and remaining alpha/evidence, simulate production false positives, separate safety kills from efficacy claims, and restart rather than improvise after invalid data.

lessons.title: Metric Design: North Star, Driver & Guardrail Metrics
lessons.interviewAnswer: I start from the decision and long-term user/business objective, then create an OEC or primary metric whose direction is credibly aligned with that objective. I add driver metrics for the causal mechanism and guardrails for reliability, safety, fairness, cost, and ecosystem harm. Every metric has a contract: population, unit, numerator, denominator, time window, attribution, aggregation, missingness, direction, and version. I validate sensitivity on historical experiments and directionality against long-term outcomes and known bad changes. I avoid arbitrary composites and average-of-averages, report uncertainty, and treat metric changes like schema migrations because they alter historical and experimental meaning.
keyPoints: OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails serve different roles
Directionality and sensitivity must both be validated
Population, unit, denominator, and window define the estimand
Metric versions and lineage are part of scientific reproducibility
lessons.why: Teams optimize what dashboards reward. A click metric can encourage clickbait, time spent can reward confusion, short-term revenue can damage retention, and an average can improve by losing low-performing users. Even perfect randomization estimates the causal effect on the metric that was defined, not the value stakeholders intended. Research on online experimentation emphasizes directionality and sensitivity and documents recurring interpretation pitfalls. Interviews test whether a candidate can turn a vague goal into measurable components without laundering value judgments. In production, metrics are shared software artifacts whose bugs propagate to experiments, alerts, forecasts, and executive decisions.
lessons.intuition: Think of a metric system as an instrument panel. The primary gauge answers whether the product is moving toward durable value. Driver gauges reveal how the change worked. Guardrails light up when the route creates unacceptable damage. A single speedometer cannot show overheating, fuel, or collision risk; a wall of gauges without a decision hierarchy is equally useless. Each gauge needs calibration: it should move when the underlying property changes, stay stable when nothing changes, and not reward a shortcut that violates the real objective. Its denominator decides who counts and can change the story as much as its numerator.
lessons.deepDive: Metric design is measurement theory plus causal and operational reasoning. A metric is a versioned estimand computed from event data, not merely a SQL expression or a label on a chart.
lessons.workedExample: A recommender team proposes watch time as its North Star. A new ranker increases watch time 4% but also increases autoplay, complaint rate, and creator concentration while seven-day satisfied return falls. The metric tree is revised: satisfied sessions per assigned user is primary; successful content discovery and completion are drivers; complaints, latency, diversity, creator supply, and compute cost are guardrails. Raw watch time remains diagnostic. Each metric uses assignment-unit denominators and fixed windows. Long-term holdouts validate that satisfied return predicts retention better than minutes alone. The scorecard blocks the ranker despite its attractive engagement number.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing the easiest metric to move
commonMistakes.correction: Sensitivity without directionality rewards proxy gaming; validate relationship to durable user and business value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Averaging pre-aggregated rates
commonMistakes.correction: Preserve numerators and denominators or define the intended unit weights; average-of-averages usually changes the estimand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Making every metric a success criterion
commonMistakes.correction: Use a hierarchy: primary/OEC, drivers, diagnostics, and guardrails with prespecified decision roles.

commonMistakes.mistake: Silently changing a denominator
commonMistakes.correction: Definition changes are versioned migrations and invalidate direct historical or experimental comparison unless dual-run and reconciled.

followUps.question: What makes a good OEC?
followUps.answer: It is directionally aligned with long-term value, sensitive within experiment duration, computable and reliable, difficult to game, and paired with explicit guardrails.

followUps.question: Why can per-active-user metrics mislead?
followUps.answer: Treatment can change who becomes active, so conditioning on activity is post-treatment selection and denominator composition can drive the result.

followUps.question: Should guardrails be included in a composite?
followUps.answer: Usually severe noncompensable harms are clearer as constraints or decision gates; a composite can let primary gains conceal unacceptable damage.

lessons.production: Store metrics in a governed semantic layer with source lineage, SQL or transformation version, population, unit, windows, numerator/denominator, attribution, missingness, direction, owner, tests, and access policy. Materialize additive components so totals reconcile across slices. Validate schema, uniqueness, coverage, lateness, denominator positivity, range, and invariant relationships. Dual-run definition changes and compare experiment decisions before migration. Monitor drift, sensitivity, correlation with long-term outcomes, guardrail breach rate, and metric gaming signals. Restrict sensitive user and fairness slices. On a bug, freeze affected decisions, identify every dashboard and experiment version, backfill under a new label, publish corrections, and roll back the semantic model without erasing historical definitions.
lessons.description: Metric design translates a product objective into a measurable, sensitive, directionally trustworthy decision system. A North Star or Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC) should predict long-term value closely enough to guide short experiments, driver metrics explain mechanisms, and guardrails prevent unacceptable harm. This chapter develops metric contracts, populations, units, numerators, denominators, windows, attribution, directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, gaming, ratio estimands, heavy tails, missingness, delayed outcomes, composite scores, proxy risk, and metric lifecycle governance. You will learn why more activity is not always better, why per-user and per-event averages answer different questions, how denominator changes can reverse a result, and how to validate short-term proxies against long-term outcomes and known interventions. A worked recommendation-system scorecard separates engagement from satisfaction and ecosystem health. The lab builds a semantic metric contract and ratio-of-sums calculator, rejects grain and denominator errors, and verifies invariants against pandas. Production guidance covers lineage, versioning, backfills, dashboards, experiment inference, access control, alerts, deprecation, correction, and rollback. The goal is not one magical number; it is an auditable map from user and business value to decisions under uncertainty.
learningObjectives: Define a metric through population, unit, event, numerator, denominator, window, attribution, direction, and missingness semantics.
Construct primary, driver, diagnostic, and guardrail metrics that map to a causal product theory rather than a dashboard inventory.
Evaluate directionality, sensitivity, validity, reliability, robustness, gaming risk, and long-term proxy quality.
Implement and test ratio metrics with grain, denominator, reconciliation, and versioning invariants.

deepSections.title: From objective to OEC, drivers, and guardrails
deepSections.body: Write the long-term objective and stakeholder before choosing observables. The OEC combines or selects near-term measures believed to causally predict that objective and must have a clear preferred direction. Driver metrics correspond to mechanisms in a product theory: discoverability, activation, task success, or repeat value. Diagnostic metrics explain implementation and segments but do not automatically become claims. Guardrails encode noncompensable or constrained outcomes such as crashes, latency, complaints, fairness gaps, creator supply, privacy incidents, and cost. Draw edges between intervention, drivers, primary outcome, guardrails, and long-term value; mark assumptions and expected time lags. Avoid adding metrics simply because data exist.

deepSections.title: The semantic metric contract
deepSections.body: Specify metric name and version; target population and eligibility; analysis unit; observation and attribution windows; event sources and accepted versions; numerator and denominator; aggregation order; deduplication and identity; timezone; late-data policy; missingness; outlier treatment; direction; owner; and quality tests. A conversion rate among exposed users differs from ITT conversion among assigned eligible users. Sessions per active user conditions on activity and can improve if low-activity users disappear. Per-user mean, ratio of totals, mean of user ratios, and average of group averages are different estimands. Include sample rows and reconciliation identities so reviewers can test meaning without reading every query.

deepSections.title: Directionality, sensitivity, validity, and reliability
deepSections.body: Directionality asks whether an increase consistently represents improvement in the target objective. Validate with domain theory, known harmful and beneficial launches, long-term holdouts, and downstream outcomes. Sensitivity asks whether the metric detects decision-relevant changes with acceptable variance; estimate standard error, MDE, and experiment hit rate without favoring noisy false positives. Construct validity asks whether it measures the intended concept; criterion validity compares trusted outcomes. Reliability asks whether repeated equivalent measurement is stable. Robustness covers heavy tails, bots, missing data, seasonality, and implementation changes. An easy-to-move but weak proxy is dangerous; a perfect long-term outcome arriving too late may be unusable for iteration.

deepSections.title: Ratios, transforms, and composite scores
deepSections.body: For a ratio metric, state whether the estimand is total numerator divided by total denominator or average of unit-level ratios; they weight units differently. Denominator treatment effects can make relative movements hard to interpret. Use influence-function, delta-method, bootstrap, or unit-level analysis consistent with randomization. Winsorization and log transforms change the estimand and must be prespecified. Composite scores require direction alignment, scaling, weights, and missing-component rules; weights express value trade-offs, not statistical truth. A composite can hide a severe loss behind compensation, so preserve component reporting and keep true guardrails outside the compensating score.

deepSections.title: Gaming, drift, and metric lifecycle
deepSections.body: Goodhart's law warns that an optimized proxy can decouple from its target. Perform threat modeling: how could a feature increase the metric without helping users, exclude difficult cases, shift cost, or delay harm? Monitor component and population drift, metric correlation with long-term outcomes, missingness, event coverage, and conflicting movements. Use immutable versions for definition changes and dual-run old/new metrics through backfills and live experiments. Recompute historical series only under explicit version labels. Document known limitations and deprecation reasons. When a metric bug is found, identify affected experiments and decisions, publish corrections, and prevent silent dashboard rewrites.

lessons.math: A ratio-of-sums estimand is R=sum_i A_i/sum_i B_i, while a mean-of-ratios is n^{-1}sum_i A_i/B_i; they are equal only in special cases. For experiment arms, Delta=R_T-R_C and uncertainty can use the influence value psi_i=(A_i-R B_i)/E[B] at the randomization unit. A composite S=sum_j w_j s_j requires defined scaling s_j and weights w_j. Sensitivity can be summarized by standard error or MDE, while directionality is a substantive claim requiring external or longitudinal validation.

workedExamples.title: Replacing raw engagement with a value-and-health scorecard
workedExamples.body: Trace the proxy's gaming path, define a directionally stronger primary outcome, separate drivers from diagnostics, and make ecosystem and reliability harms noncompensable guardrails.

exercises.prompt: Why does average session duration sometimes rise after a bad change?
exercises.solution: If the change causes short-session users to leave, the remaining-session denominator selects longer sessions; the average can rise while total user value falls.

exercises.prompt: Give a ratio-of-sums example.
exercises.solution: Click-through rate as total clicks divided by total eligible impressions; preserve both components and define deduplication and attribution.

exercises.prompt: How do you validate directionality?
exercises.solution: Use product theory, known interventions, long-term holdouts or downstream outcomes, component analysis, and attempts to find changes that game the proxy.

visuals.title: Metric decision hierarchy
visuals.caption: Metrics have different evidentiary roles; a diagnostic movement does not automatically become a launch criterion.

visuals.title: Two plausible rate estimands
visuals.caption: Neither is universally correct; the contract must name which population weighting matches the decision.

lab.goal: Validate a semantic metric contract, compute a ratio of sums at user grain, and verify that aggregation, denominators, and pandas results reconcile.
lab.useIt:
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(rows)
pandas_metric=df['numerator'].sum()/df['denominator'].sum()
mean_user_ratio=(df['numerator']/df['denominator']).mean()
lab.shipIt: Version the complete metric contract and additive components, run grain/coverage/reconciliation tests, dual-run migrations, monitor proxy drift and guardrails, and freeze affected decisions when lineage or semantics fail.

sourceNotes.contribution: Provides the OEC, metric hierarchy, sensitivity, directionality, and guardrail framework from the canonical experimentation text.
Provides peer-reviewed lessons for data-driven metric directionality and sensitivity development.
Documents recurring metric interpretation failures observed across thousands of online experiments.
Provides platform-scale metric governance, alerting, and decision-practice context.

lessons.title: Funnels & Conversion Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: A funnel is a versioned sequence estimand, not just counts by event name. I define the eligible entity and entry cohort, strict or loose order, conversion window, repeat and re-entry rules, identity resolution, and whether conversion is unique entities or event completions. I deduplicate at the chosen unit, require complete follow-up or handle censoring, and reconcile cumulative counts so they cannot increase. I segment only with pre-step attributes for causal interpretation, inspect time-to-transition and alternative paths, and use experiments to test proposed causes. Drop-off shows where progression stops under the definition; it does not prove why.
keyPoints: Funnel definitions construct the population and path
Entity counts and event counts answer different questions
Conversion windows and maturity prevent unequal opportunity
Step drop-off is descriptive, not a causal explanation
Identity and event-contract quality dominate trustworthy funnel analysis
lessons.why: Onboarding, checkout, application, and activation flows are operationally sequential, so aggregate conversion can hide where a change occurred. But a user may skip steps, repeat them, switch devices, complete offline, or enter through another path. A dashboard can show a dramatic drop simply because one event was renamed or a recent cohort lacks time to convert. Funnel analysis is valuable when it turns a product theory into explicit state transitions and testable hypotheses. Interviews probe whether analysts define denominators and time correctly. In production, funnel metrics share instrumentation with experiments and can bias launch decisions if event loss differs by variant.
lessons.intuition: Imagine following each eligible person with a timestamped event ledger. A strict funnel asks whether the ledger contains step A, then a later B, then a later C, all within a clock that starts at A. Count each person once at the furthest qualified step. The narrowing bars are just an aggregation of these state-machine traces. If the last cohort entered yesterday and conversion allows seven days, its apparent failure is administrative censoring. If B is missing because an app version stopped logging, that is measurement loss, not user abandonment. Examine both the accepted path and what users did instead.
lessons.deepDive: A funnel is a temporal query over entity histories. Its scientific quality depends on state semantics, observation opportunity, identity, and the difference between descriptive transition rates and causal mechanisms.
lessons.workedExample: A checkout funnel shows 100,000 cart users, 70,000 payment-page users, and 45,000 purchases. After an app release, payment-to-purchase appears to improve, but entry-to-purchase falls. Investigation finds the new app creates a fresh anonymous ID after payment failure; the payment event is under the old ID and repeat purchase under a logged-in ID. A loose cross-device join matches only successful users, inflating the middle transition. The team repairs identity linkage, starts from assigned cart entrants, applies a seven-day maturity cutoff, and adds payment-error events. The corrected analysis shows increased failures, leading to rollback and a randomized fix.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting events as users
commonMistakes.correction: Repeated events can inflate downstream steps; deduplicate the defined entity or use explicit journey IDs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing immature recent cohorts
commonMistakes.correction: Require the full conversion window or use censoring-aware time-to-event analysis.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating drop-off as a cause
commonMistakes.correction: It locates an observed transition; errors, alternatives, selection, and experiments are needed to identify mechanisms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Joining only users with every step
commonMistakes.correction: That removes nonconverters from the denominator; begin with entry and left join later states.

followUps.question: What is a strict funnel?
followUps.answer: An entity must complete defined steps in order, typically within a conversion window; intervening events may or may not be allowed according to the contract.

followUps.question: Why can cumulative counts increase?
followUps.answer: They should not for a unique-entity strict funnel. An increase signals inconsistent populations, repeated-event counting, re-entry, identity, or query errors.

followUps.question: How do you compare funnel conversion in an A/B test?
followUps.answer: Use assigned eligible units or an assignment-invariant trigger as denominator, prespecify the end metric, and treat intermediate steps as drivers without post-treatment filtering.

lessons.production: Govern every step event with owner, schema, version, entity key, event-time semantics, and property tests. Build funnels from immutable entry cohorts and left-joined histories, using a versioned identity graph and late-data cutoff. Persist step counts, cumulative and transition rates, time distributions, window maturity, missingness, and alternate-path counts. Monitor monotonicity, event coverage, ordering violations, identity-link rates, transition shifts, and platform/version slices. Protect journey data and suppress small cohorts. Dual-log renamed events and reconcile before cutover. On instrumentation failure, freeze funnel-based decisions, publish the affected interval, backfill only under explicit versions, and roll back the metric or product change without rewriting prior definitions.

lab.goal: Build an ordered unique-user funnel from event histories, compare counts with pandas, and verify monotonicity, deduplication, and conversion-window semantics.
lab.useIt:
import pandas as pd
df=pd.DataFrame(events,columns=['user','event','time'])
entry_users=set(df.loc[df.event=='cart','user'])
pandas_entry=len(entry_users)
unique_event_users=df.groupby('event')['user'].nunique().to_dict()
lab.verifyIt:
assert counts==[4,3,1]
assert counts==sorted(counts,reverse=True)
assert pandas_entry==counts[0]
assert reached['u1']==3 and reached['u2']==1
assert unique_event_users['purchase']==3 and counts[2]==1
assert ordered_funnel(events,steps,20)[0]==[4,3,2]
assert counts[2]/counts[0]==0.25
lab.shipIt: Version entity, step, order, window and identity semantics; build from entry with complete opportunity; persist additive counts and transition times; monitor event parity and monotonicity; and freeze decisions when instrumentation breaks.

lessons.description: Funnel analysis measures how eligible entities progress through a defined sequence of product states or events and where they fail, branch, repeat, or take too long. A funnel is not an objective map of user behavior: step definitions, order rules, identity, attribution, conversion window, denominator, and re-entry policy construct the result. This chapter develops strict and loose funnels, unique-user versus event conversion, closed versus open cohorts, step and cumulative rates, time-to-convert, competing paths, censoring, segmentation, instrumentation, causal limits, and experimental use. You will learn how repeated events and inner joins inflate conversion, why recent entrants have incomplete opportunity, how to distinguish a product obstacle from selection, and when a state machine or journey analysis is better than a linear funnel. A worked checkout example exposes an identity and window bug. The lab implements a deterministic ordered unique-user funnel from raw events, compares it with pandas, and verifies monotonic counts, window rules, deduplication, and denominator reconciliation. Production guidance covers event contracts, late data, sessionization, privacy, monitoring, metric versions, and rollback. The goal is a reproducible behavioral estimand that guides hypotheses, not a decorative narrowing chart that implies causality.
learningObjectives: Define funnel population, entity, step events, ordering, window, attribution, repetition, and denominator semantics precisely.
Compute cumulative and step conversion without double counting entities or granting unequal observation opportunity.
Diagnose instrumentation, identity, time, competing-path, and selection explanations for apparent drop-off.
Implement and verify an ordered funnel while preserving raw counts, transition times, and alternative paths.

deepSections.title: Entity, entry, steps, order, and window
deepSections.body: Name the entity: user, account, order, application, device, or session. Define eligibility and entry event with source and version. A strict funnel requires step order; a loose funnel may allow intervening events while preserving order; any-order completion answers a different question. Define whether timestamps may tie, whether one event can satisfy multiple steps, and whether all steps must share an order or item property. The conversion window begins at a stated event and uses event time with a timezone and late-data policy. Closed cohorts fix entry membership; open funnels can mix changing populations. Version every semantic choice.

deepSections.title: Unique entities, repeats, and denominators
deepSections.body: Unique-entity conversion counts each entity once, usually using the earliest eligible entry and earliest qualifying next step. Event-total funnels can count repeated completions and may exceed entry entities; label them explicitly. Step conversion N_k/N_{k-1} differs from cumulative conversion N_k/N_1, and their product reconciles when definitions align. Decide whether users can re-enter after failure or complete multiple journeys; then use a journey identifier rather than accidental event pairs. Preserve numerator and denominator for every transition. An inner join of completed steps drops nonconverters and can make conversion appear 100%; start from the entry population and left join forward.

deepSections.title: Time to convert and observation maturity
deepSections.body: Report transition-time distributions, not only means, because latency is often skewed and long tails determine the window. A fixed window classifies no completion by its end, but entities entering near the data cutoff have not had equal opportunity. Restrict to matured entrants, use cohort-age tables, or apply survival methods when time-to-event is the target and right censoring assumptions are defensible. Calendar shocks and app releases affect cohorts differently. Sessionization adds an inactivity threshold that can split or merge journeys; document it and test sensitivity. Late events can revise earlier funnels, so publish a data-completeness cutoff.

deepSections.title: Drop-off, segmentation, and competing paths
deepSections.body: A large drop identifies a transition worth investigation, not its cause. Inspect errors, latency, validation messages, alternate events, support contacts, and qualitative evidence. Segment by pre-entry attributes such as platform or acquisition channel, while recognizing composition and multiplicity. Segmenting on a later step selects converters and can reverse interpretation. Users may reach the same value through a different sequence, so path or state-transition analysis can reveal false drop-off. Compare step rates on common cohorts and complete windows; decompose an aggregate change into entry mix, within-segment transition changes, and logging coverage.

deepSections.title: Causal tests and data-quality controls
deepSections.body: Funnel patterns generate hypotheses such as a form field causing abandonment. Randomize the proposed change and estimate ITT effects on prespecified end conversion plus transition drivers and guardrails. Do not declare causal impact from users who happened to complete a step. In experiment funnels, denominator should normally begin with assigned eligible units or an assignment-invariant trigger; treatment-dependent exposure filters bias comparison. Test event schema, uniqueness, ordering, property consistency, assignment coverage, and arm-specific missingness. Maintain synthetic journeys and expected counts. When a step event changes, dual-log and reconcile before migrating the metric.

lessons.math: Let E be entry entities and S_k the subset that satisfies ordered steps 1..k within window W. Cumulative conversion C_k=|S_k|/|E| and step conversion c_k=|S_k|/|S_{k-1}|, with C_k=product_{j=2..k}c_j when sets and denominators align. Drop-off at k is |S_{k-1}|-|S_k|. Time-to-step T_k=t_k-t_entry is censored at the data cutoff or window for incomplete entities. Compare arms at the randomization-unit level and retain additive counts for reconciliation.

workedExamples.title: An identity reset that turns failures into apparent success
workedExamples.body: Trace raw entity histories, detect cross-step identity loss, rebuild from entry with complete windows, and separate instrumentation repair from the randomized product fix.

exercises.prompt: Counts are 1000, 800, 600. What are step and cumulative final conversion?
exercises.solution: Step conversions are 80% then 75%; final cumulative conversion is 600/1000=60%, equal to 0.8*0.75.

exercises.prompt: Why can a 30-day window bias the newest cohort?
exercises.solution: Members have not all had 30 days of follow-up; restrict to mature entries or use censoring-aware methods.

exercises.prompt: A user completes B before A. Do they convert?
exercises.solution: Only under an any-order definition. A strict ordered funnel excludes that sequence; the contract must decide.

visuals.caption: Conceptual unique-user cumulative conversion; each stage is a subset of the prior stage under one identity and window contract.

visuals.title: Linear funnel versus journey view
visuals.caption: Choose the representation that matches product structure rather than forcing every behavior into one line.
