lessons.title: Entropy & Information Content
lessons.interviewAnswer: Entropy measures average uncertainty in a distribution: concentrated distributions have low entropy; balanced, unpredictable distributions have higher entropy.
lessons.why: Entropy is the language behind cross-entropy, decision trees, compression and language-model uncertainty.
lessons.intuition: A fair coin is harder to predict than a coin that is heads 99% of the time, so it carries more uncertainty per observation.
lessons.deepDive: For a discrete variable, entropy is expected negative log-probability. The logarithm makes information from independent events additive. Differential entropy for continuous variables has different interpretation and can be negative.
lessons.math: H(X)=-Σp(x)log p(x)
commonMistakes: Treating entropy as variance.
Assuming continuous differential entropy behaves exactly like discrete entropy.
followUps: Why use a logarithm?
How is entropy related to compression?
lessons.production: Use entropy as an uncertainty summary, but operational decisions still need calibrated probabilities and task costs.
lessons.workedExample: A fair binary variable has 1 bit of entropy; a 99/1 variable has much less.

visual.title: Entropy rises with uncertainty
visual.caption: Entropy is highest when outcomes are balanced and falls as one outcome becomes predictable.

lessons.title: Cross-Entropy & Log Loss
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cross-entropy evaluates a predicted probability distribution against the target. In classification it rewards high probability on the true class and heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions.
lessons.why: Cross-entropy is a core training objective in classification and language modeling.
lessons.intuition: Predicting 0.9 for the correct class is mildly penalized; predicting 0.001 is punished strongly because -log(0.001) is large.
lessons.deepDive: With one-hot targets, cross-entropy is the negative log probability assigned to the true class and corresponds to maximum likelihood for common probabilistic classifiers.
lessons.math: CE(p,q)=-Σp(x)log q(x)
commonMistakes: Calling cross-entropy an accuracy metric.
Applying softmax twice when a framework loss expects logits.
followUps: Cross-entropy vs KL divergence?
Why train on logits?
lessons.production: Monitor calibration and downstream decision metrics in addition to cross-entropy.
lessons.workedExample: True-class probability .9 gives loss ≈.105; probability .1 gives ≈2.303.

lessons.title: KL Divergence
lessons.interviewAnswer: KL divergence measures how poorly distribution Q approximates P. It is non-negative but asymmetric, so it is not a distance metric.
lessons.why: KL appears in VAEs, variational inference, distillation and policy optimization.
lessons.intuition: Think of P as what you care about and Q as your approximation; KL penalizes Q where it fails to represent probability mass used by P.
lessons.deepDive: D_KL(P||Q)=E_P[log P-log Q]. Forward and reverse directions produce different approximation behavior, especially for multimodal distributions.
lessons.math: D_KL(P||Q)=Σp(x)log[p(x)/q(x)]
commonMistakes: Calling KL symmetric.
Treating KL as bounded between 0 and 1.
followUps: Why does KL appear in VAEs?
Forward vs reverse KL?
lessons.production: Check support and numerical smoothing because zero probabilities can create infinite/unstable values.
lessons.workedExample: Approximating a bimodal target with one Gaussian can cover modes or concentrate on one depending on KL direction.

lessons.title: Mutual Information
lessons.interviewAnswer: Mutual information measures how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another and can capture nonlinear dependence.
lessons.why: MI connects probability, feature selection and representation learning.
lessons.intuition: If knowing X says nothing about Y, MI is zero; if X nearly determines Y, shared information is large.
lessons.deepDive: I(X;Y)=D_KL(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y))=H(X)-H(X|Y). Estimating MI in high-dimensional continuous data is difficult and estimator-dependent.
commonMistakes: Assuming zero correlation means zero MI.
Comparing biased MI estimators as if values were directly comparable.
followUps: MI vs correlation?
Conditional mutual information?
lessons.production: Use MI-based features carefully: leakage can look like strong information.
lessons.workedExample: Y=X² can have weak linear correlation for symmetric X while still having substantial MI.

lessons.title: Perplexity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Perplexity is the exponential of average negative log-likelihood. Lower is better on the same data/tokenization, but perplexity is not directly comparable across different tokenizers.
lessons.why: Perplexity links sequence-model evaluation to information theory.
lessons.intuition: It loosely represents the model’s effective uncertainty over next-token choices.
lessons.deepDive: With natural logs, perplexity=exp(mean NLL). Tokenization changes sequence length and token probabilities, so cross-tokenizer comparisons can mislead.
commonMistakes: Treating perplexity as human preference.
Comparing across tokenizers without care.
followUps: Bits-per-character?
Why can lower perplexity fail downstream?
lessons.production: Use task, safety, latency and cost metrics alongside perplexity.
lessons.workedExample: Two models using the same tokenizer can be compared on held-out perplexity; byte- and word-level perplexity should not be compared naively.

lessons.title: Information Bottleneck & Representation Learning
lessons.interviewAnswer: The information-bottleneck view seeks representations that preserve information useful for a target while discarding irrelevant detail.
lessons.why: It provides a useful conceptual lens for learned compression and representation learning.
lessons.intuition: A good representation should keep structure needed by the downstream task without memorizing every nuisance detail.
lessons.deepDive: The classical objective trades information retained about input against information retained about the target. Estimating these quantities in deep networks is nontrivial, so it is often a guiding principle rather than a literal measured objective.
commonMistakes: Assuming smaller latent means more semantic.
Claiming the theory is directly measurable in every deep model.
followUps: How does this relate to VAEs/VQ models?
Compression vs fidelity?
lessons.production: Choose bottlenecks by downstream quality, storage and latency trade-offs.
lessons.workedExample: A compressed image code may discard sensor noise while retaining boundaries needed for prediction.

lessons.title: Gaussian Processes
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Gaussian process defines a distribution over functions using a mean and kernel; conditioning on observations produces a posterior predictive distribution with both mean and uncertainty.
lessons.why: GPs are canonical nonparametric probabilistic models and useful for small-data uncertainty-aware regression and Bayesian optimization.
lessons.intuition: Instead of fitting one curve, a GP reasons over many plausible functions and narrows uncertainty near observations.
lessons.deepDive: Every finite collection of function values is jointly Gaussian; the kernel defines covariance. Exact training solves an n×n covariance system and scales roughly O(n³).
commonMistakes: Saying GP means Gaussian input features.
Ignoring kernel choice and scaling.
followUps: What does the kernel control?
How do sparse GPs scale?
lessons.production: Use GPs where calibrated local uncertainty matters and data size permits; monitor kernel fit and numerical conditioning.
lessons.workedExample: With an RBF kernel, uncertainty is narrow near data and widens far from observed inputs.

lessons.title: Bayesian Networks & d-Separation
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bayesian network is a DAG that factorizes a joint distribution into local conditional distributions; d-separation encodes conditional-independence relationships.
lessons.why: Graphical models represent complex joint distributions in a structured, interpretable way.
lessons.intuition: Each node only needs a conditional model given its parents rather than one giant joint probability table.
lessons.deepDive: p(x1,…,xn)=∏p(xi|parents_i). Graph structure determines independence properties, but a causal interpretation requires additional assumptions beyond probability factorization.
commonMistakes: Assuming every Bayesian network is causal.
Confusing graph reachability with d-separation.
followUps: Bayesian network vs MRF?
Exact vs approximate inference?
lessons.production: Use graphs to make assumptions explicit; dense networks can make inference computationally expensive.
lessons.workedExample: Rain→WetGrass←Sprinkler is a collider; conditioning on WetGrass can make Rain and Sprinkler dependent.

visual.title: A simple Bayesian network
visual.caption: A DAG factorizes a joint distribution into local conditional relationships.

lessons.title: Markov Random Fields & Factor Graphs
lessons.interviewAnswer: An MRF is an undirected graphical model whose joint distribution is expressed with local compatibility factors; it is useful when dependencies are symmetric rather than naturally directed.
lessons.why: MRFs underpin structured prediction and spatial/image models.
lessons.intuition: Neighboring pixels can prefer similar labels without one pixel causing the other.
lessons.deepDive: The joint density is proportional to a product of positive potentials and requires a partition function for normalization, which can make inference difficult.
commonMistakes: Treating potentials as normalized probabilities.
Reading causal direction from an undirected graph.
followUps: What is a factor graph?
Why is the partition function hard?
lessons.production: Large MRFs often require approximate inference; validate both quality and latency.
lessons.workedExample: Image segmentation can combine per-pixel evidence with pairwise smoothness between neighbors.

lessons.title: Hidden Markov Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: An HMM models a sequence with hidden states that follow Markov transitions and emit observations. Forward-backward computes marginals/likelihoods, Viterbi finds the most likely state path, and Baum–Welch learns parameters.
lessons.why: HMMs are foundational probabilistic sequence models used in speech, bioinformatics and state estimation.
lessons.intuition: You observe noisy outputs but assume an unobserved state evolves over time.
lessons.deepDive: The Markov assumption enables dynamic programming. Forward recursion sums over state paths; Viterbi replaces summation with maximization to recover the best path.
commonMistakes: Confusing state with observation.
Using Viterbi when marginal state probabilities are required.
followUps: Forward-backward vs Viterbi?
How is Baum–Welch related to EM?
lessons.production: HMMs are interpretable and efficient baselines, but their assumptions can be too restrictive for complex sequences.
lessons.workedExample: A machine can move through healthy/degraded/failing hidden states while vibration measurements are noisy emissions.

visual.title: Hidden-state sequence with observations
visual.caption: Latent states transition through time and generate noisy observations.

lessons.title: Variational Inference
lessons.interviewAnswer: Variational inference converts difficult posterior inference into optimization: choose a tractable q(z) and optimize it to approximate the true posterior, commonly by maximizing the ELBO.
lessons.why: VI is central to VAEs and scalable Bayesian models.
lessons.intuition: Instead of sampling indefinitely from a hard posterior, fit a simpler distribution that approximates it.
lessons.deepDive: The ELBO contains an expected data-fit term minus KL(q||prior) and lower-bounds log evidence. The approximation family itself can limit posterior quality.
commonMistakes: Calling ELBO exact log likelihood.
Ignoring approximation-family bias.
followUps: Mean-field VI?
Why reverse KL?
lessons.production: VI can be fast but may underestimate uncertainty; validate posterior predictive behavior.
lessons.workedExample: A VAE encoder outputs q(z|x) parameters and trains via an ELBO rather than computing p(z|x) exactly.

lessons.title: Aleatoric vs Epistemic Uncertainty
lessons.interviewAnswer: Aleatoric uncertainty comes from irreducible data noise; epistemic uncertainty comes from limited model knowledge and can often be reduced with better data.
lessons.why: Production systems often need to know when a prediction is uncertain and why.
lessons.intuition: A noisy sensor can remain ambiguous with infinite data; a model seeing a new population is uncertain because it lacks knowledge.
lessons.deepDive: The decomposition is model-dependent. Heteroscedastic likelihoods can model aleatoric noise; ensembles/Bayesian methods can approximate epistemic uncertainty.
commonMistakes: Equating softmax confidence with epistemic uncertainty.
Claiming all uncertainty disappears with more data.
followUps: How do ensembles help?
What happens under shift?
lessons.production: Use uncertainty to trigger abstention, human review or safe fallback.
lessons.workedExample: A medical model may be uncertain because the scan itself is ambiguous or because the patient population differs from training.

lessons.title: Proper Scoring Rules: Log Loss & Brier Score
lessons.interviewAnswer: Proper scoring rules reward honest probabilistic forecasts: in expectation, reporting the true probability minimizes expected score. Log loss and Brier score are common examples.
lessons.why: Accuracy ignores how good probability estimates are.
lessons.intuition: Predictions of .51 and .99 can yield the same class decision but represent very different probability quality.
lessons.deepDive: Brier score is squared error on predicted probabilities; log score punishes assigning tiny probability to events that occur.
commonMistakes: Using accuracy to judge probability quality.
Assuming one proper score determines every thresholded decision.
followUps: Brier vs log loss?
Calibration vs discrimination?
lessons.production: Use proper scores for probability quality and separate cost-aware thresholds for decisions.
lessons.workedExample: Two classifiers with equal accuracy can have very different log loss because one is overconfident on mistakes.

lessons.title: Conformal Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Conformal prediction wraps a predictive model to output sets or intervals with finite-sample marginal coverage under exchangeability; a calibration set determines the nonconformity-score quantile.
lessons.why: Conformal prediction is a practical way to add rigorous uncertainty to black-box models.
lessons.intuition: Instead of returning only a point estimate, return an interval calibrated to cover the target at a chosen long-run rate.
lessons.deepDive: Split conformal trains a base model, scores held-out calibration errors, selects a finite-sample corrected quantile and expands future predictions by that score. The guarantee is marginal, not automatically conditional for every subgroup.
commonMistakes: Saying each individual interval has a 90% probability guarantee after seeing x.
Using training examples improperly as calibration.
followUps: What assumptions are needed?
Conditional vs marginal coverage?
lessons.production: Monitor empirical coverage under distribution shift and use the sets to drive abstention/fallback when appropriate.
lessons.workedExample: Regression can use absolute calibration residuals to create prediction intervals around future predictions.

lab.goal: Build split-conformal regression intervals from held-out residuals.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
x=np.linspace(0,1,120); y=2*x+rng.normal(0,.15,len(x))
pred=2*x
cal=np.arange(80,100); test=np.arange(100,120)
scores=np.abs(y[cal]-pred[cal]); q=np.quantile(scores,.90,method="higher")
lo,hi=pred[test]-q,pred[test]+q
print(q,np.mean((y[test]>=lo)&(y[test]<=hi)))
lab.useIt: print(list(zip(lo[:3],hi[:3])))
lab.verifyIt: assert q>=0 and np.all(lo<=hi)

lessons.title: Selective Prediction & Abstention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Selective prediction lets a model abstain on uncertain cases, trading coverage—the fraction answered—against risk on the answered subset.
lessons.why: High-stakes automation should sometimes know when not to decide.
lessons.intuition: Answer easy cases automatically and escalate ambiguous cases instead of forcing a low-confidence prediction.
lessons.deepDive: A reject rule thresholds a confidence/uncertainty measure; as coverage falls, accepted-case error should usually fall. The fallback path and capacity are part of the system design.
commonMistakes: Optimizing coverage without tracking accepted-case error.
Assuming the same threshold remains valid after shift.
followUps: How do you choose the abstention threshold?
How does conformal prediction help?
lessons.production: Define fallback SLOs and monitor risk-coverage after deployment.
lessons.workedExample: OCR can accept clear forms and route ambiguous scans to manual review.

lessons.title: Empirical Risk Minimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: ERM minimizes average training loss; generalization theory asks when low empirical risk also implies low expected risk on unseen data.
lessons.why: ERM is the abstraction behind most supervised objectives.
lessons.intuition: Training optimizes the sample you have, but deployment cares about an unknown population.
lessons.deepDive: Population risk is an expectation over the data distribution; empirical risk replaces it with a sample average. Capacity, sample size and sampling assumptions affect the gap.
commonMistakes: Equating training loss with true risk.
Assuming ERM guarantees a global optimum for nonconvex networks.
followUps: What controls the generalization gap?
How does regularization modify ERM?
lessons.production: Validation must represent deployment; theory cannot fix a mismatched sampling process.
lessons.workedExample: A deep tree can drive training risk near zero while test risk worsens.

lessons.title: PAC Learning Intuition
lessons.interviewAnswer: PAC learning formalizes whether enough samples let a learner find, with high probability, a hypothesis whose true error is approximately small.
lessons.why: PAC provides a clean vocabulary for learnability and sample complexity.
lessons.intuition: The question is how much data is needed so a learned model is likely to be good enough, not whether it can be perfect.
lessons.deepDive: Bounds connect hypothesis complexity, desired error ε, confidence δ and sample size. Classical bounds can be loose but reveal qualitative dependencies.
commonMistakes: Treating PAC bounds as exact data calculators.
Ignoring IID-like assumptions.
followUps: Realizable vs agnostic PAC?
How does VC dimension enter?
lessons.production: Use theory for intuition and empirical validation for actual deployment decisions.
lessons.workedExample: A simpler class may need fewer samples to control generalization but can have more approximation bias.

lessons.title: VC Dimension & Capacity
lessons.interviewAnswer: VC dimension measures the richness of a binary hypothesis class via the largest set of points it can shatter; greater capacity usually requires more data for uniform generalization guarantees.
lessons.why: VC theory is foundational capacity theory.
lessons.intuition: A class that can realize every labeling of many points is extremely flexible.
lessons.deepDive: VC dimension yields uniform-convergence bounds for classification classes. Deep-network generalization is more nuanced, so VC dimension is a conceptual foundation rather than a practical tuning metric.
commonMistakes: Saying VC dimension equals parameter count.
Using VC dimension directly to tune deep nets.
followUps: What does shatter mean?
How does VC dimension affect sample complexity?
lessons.production: Use real validation for model selection; capacity theory explains tendencies.
lessons.workedExample: Linear separators in 2D can shatter some configurations of three points but not arbitrary labelings of four.

lessons.title: Margins & Generalization
lessons.interviewAnswer: A classification margin measures separation from the decision boundary; large-margin methods such as SVMs prefer a wider buffer while allowing controlled violations in the soft-margin case.
lessons.why: Margins connect geometry, regularization and generalization.
lessons.intuition: Two separators can classify training points correctly, but the one farther from the closest examples is less sensitive to small perturbations.
lessons.deepDive: Hard-margin SVM maximizes geometric margin; soft-margin SVM trades violations against margin size through C.
commonMistakes: Confusing weight magnitude with geometric margin.
Assuming margins solve overlapping/noisy labels automatically.
followUps: Hard vs soft margin?
How do kernels change geometry?
lessons.production: Margin robustness does not replace shift/feature-quality monitoring.
lessons.workedExample: For separable classes, support vectors determine the maximal-margin boundary.

lessons.title: Regularization as Capacity Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: Regularization penalizes or constrains effective model complexity, often trading a little training fit for better generalization when variance is high.
lessons.why: Regularization is a general principle spanning linear models, trees and deep networks.
lessons.intuition: When many solutions fit training data, regularization encodes a preference for ones expected to generalize better.
lessons.deepDive: Explicit penalties add λΩ(θ) to empirical risk; architecture, augmentation, optimization and early stopping can also create implicit biases.
commonMistakes: Equating regularization only with dropout.
Assuming stronger regularization always helps.
followUps: Explicit vs implicit regularization?
How does λ change bias/variance?
lessons.production: Tune against representative validation and reassess as the data distribution evolves.
lessons.workedExample: Ridge shrinks coefficients; Lasso can zero some coefficients.

lessons.title: Generalization Under Distribution Shift
lessons.interviewAnswer: IID test performance can fail under covariate, label or concept shift. Use time/geography/group-aware validation, shift diagnostics and post-deployment monitoring when future data differs from training.
lessons.why: Distribution shift is one of the most common reasons production performance differs from offline evaluation.
lessons.intuition: A model trained on one year, hospital or country may see systematically different deployment inputs.
lessons.deepDive: Different shifts change p(x), p(y) or p(y|x). Some shifts can be reweighted; concept shift usually requires adaptation/retraining.
commonMistakes: Calling every change concept drift.
Randomly splitting temporal data and claiming future generalization.
followUps: How do you detect shift?
When does importance weighting help?
lessons.production: Design validation to mimic deployment and monitor performance by important slices.
lessons.workedExample: Fraud strategies evolve after a detector is deployed, changing p(y|x).

lessons.title: Frequent Itemsets & Association Rules
lessons.interviewAnswer: Association-rule mining finds frequent item combinations and rules A→B. Support measures frequency, confidence estimates P(B|A), and lift compares the rule with B’s baseline rate.
lessons.why: This is a classic data-mining pattern for market baskets and co-occurrence.
lessons.intuition: Bread and butter appearing together is only interesting if the co-occurrence is frequent and stronger than what item popularity alone predicts.
lessons.deepDive: Apriori uses downward closure: if an itemset is frequent, its subsets must be frequent, which prunes the exponential search.
commonMistakes: Using confidence without lift.
Interpreting association as causation.
followUps: Apriori vs FP-Growth?
Why is support anti-monotonic?
lessons.production: Control combinatorial explosion and validate discovered rules with domain context.
lessons.workedExample: A rule can have high confidence because B is common; lift reveals whether A truly adds association.

lessons.title: MinHash & Jaccard Similarity
lessons.interviewAnswer: MinHash creates compact signatures whose collision probability equals Jaccard similarity, allowing approximate set similarity at scale.
lessons.why: MinHash is foundational for web-scale duplicate detection and sparse-set similarity.
lessons.intuition: Keep a small randomized signature instead of repeatedly intersecting huge sets.
lessons.deepDive: Under a random permutation, the probability that two sets share the same minimum element equals their Jaccard similarity.
commonMistakes: Confusing MinHash with cryptographic hashing.
Using it for arbitrary Euclidean distance.
followUps: How does MinHash connect to LSH?
How many hashes are enough?
lessons.production: Choose signature size by memory/accuracy requirements and validate candidate recall.
lessons.workedExample: Document shingles can use MinHash to detect near-duplicate pages.

lessons.title: Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH)
lessons.interviewAnswer: LSH intentionally hashes similar items into the same buckets with high probability, reducing candidates for approximate similarity or nearest-neighbor search.
lessons.why: LSH explains scalable approximate search before modern graph indexes such as HNSW.
lessons.intuition: Normal hashing separates inputs; LSH wants similar inputs to collide.
lessons.deepDive: Different LSH families match different similarity measures; banding/concatenation tunes collision probability.
commonMistakes: Assuming exact nearest-neighbor guarantees.
Using a hash family for the wrong metric.
followUps: LSH vs HNSW?
How do bands affect recall?
lessons.production: Benchmark recall, latency and memory together.
lessons.workedExample: Near-duplicate documents can be bucketed by MinHash signatures before exact checking.

lessons.title: Bloom Filters
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic set-membership structure: it can return false positives but not false negatives under normal insert/query use.
lessons.why: Bloom filters avoid expensive storage/cache lookups when a key definitely is absent.
lessons.intuition: They answer “definitely not present” or “maybe present.”
lessons.deepDive: Each inserted key sets k hash-selected bits; queries test those bits. Saturation raises false-positive probability.
commonMistakes: Saying Bloom filters have false negatives by design.
Deleting from a standard Bloom filter without a counting variant.
followUps: How do k and array size affect false positives?
Counting Bloom filter?
lessons.production: Size for expected cardinality and monitor saturation.
lessons.workedExample: A storage engine can skip disk reads for keys the filter says are absent.

lessons.title: Count-Min Sketch & Heavy Hitters
lessons.interviewAnswer: Count-Min Sketch approximates frequencies in streams with multiple hash tables; queries take the minimum counter and overestimate nonnegative frequencies within probabilistic error bounds.
lessons.why: Sketches estimate large-stream frequencies without storing every key.
lessons.intuition: Several compressed counters see each event; the minimum reduces collision inflation.
lessons.deepDive: Width controls additive error and depth controls failure probability.
commonMistakes: Treating estimates as exact.
Using the basic sketch for arbitrary negative updates.
followUps: How do you recover heavy-hitter keys?
Count-Min vs hash map?
lessons.production: Use when approximate counts are acceptable and throughput/memory dominate exactness.
lessons.workedExample: Telemetry can estimate popular URLs across billions of requests in bounded memory.

lessons.title: HyperLogLog & Distinct Counting
lessons.interviewAnswer: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct elements from hashed leading-zero statistics, giving low relative error with very small memory and easy merging.
lessons.why: Unique-user and cardinality queries are common analytics operations that become expensive with exact sets.
lessons.intuition: A long leading-zero run is unlikely unless many distinct hashes were observed; many registers stabilize the estimate.
lessons.deepDive: Distributed HLL sketches can merge register-wise without exchanging raw identifiers.
commonMistakes: Expecting exact counts.
Using poor hashes.
followUps: Why is HLL mergeable?
How does memory affect error?
lessons.production: Use exact counting for small sets and sketches when scale justifies approximation.
lessons.workedExample: Services can estimate global daily active users by merging local sketches.

lessons.title: PageRank & Link Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: PageRank scores nodes by the stationary distribution of a random walk with teleportation: links from important nodes contribute more than raw in-degree alone.
lessons.why: PageRank is a foundational web/graph-mining algorithm and distributed iterative-computation example.
lessons.intuition: An endorsement from an important page should count more than one from an isolated page.
lessons.deepDive: Teleportation prevents sinks and makes the chain well-behaved under standard conditions; repeated sparse matrix-vector multiplication converges to rank scores.
commonMistakes: Equating PageRank with in-degree.
Omitting teleportation/sink handling.
followUps: PageRank vs HITS?
How does damping affect ranking?
lessons.production: Large graphs require sparse/distributed iteration and resistance to adversarial link manipulation.
lessons.workedExample: Citation networks can use PageRank-like centrality to rank influential nodes.

lessons.title: Vector vs Raster Spatial Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vector data represents discrete geometry as points, lines and polygons; raster data represents space as a grid of cells. The correct representation depends on the phenomenon and operations.
lessons.why: Spatial representation determines storage, joins, visualization and modeling choices.
lessons.intuition: Roads and administrative boundaries are naturally vector; satellite imagery and elevation are naturally raster.
lessons.deepDive: Vector analysis uses geometry/topology; raster analysis uses aligned grids. Converting between them can lose detail or introduce resolution assumptions.
commonMistakes: Treating longitude/latitude as ordinary Euclidean x/y.
Assuming higher raster resolution always means higher information quality.
followUps: When would you rasterize polygons?
How do vector indexes work?
lessons.production: Choose formats/resolution based on query, model and scale.
lessons.workedExample: Store shops as points and land cover as raster, then aggregate nearby raster cells around each shop.

visual.title: Vector and raster representations
visual.caption: The representation changes which spatial operations are natural and efficient.

lessons.title: Coordinate Reference Systems & Projections
lessons.interviewAnswer: A CRS defines how coordinates map to Earth. Longitude/latitude is angular; projected CRSs map locations to a plane for meaningful distance/area calculations over a suitable region.
lessons.why: CRS mistakes can produce plausible-looking but numerically wrong spatial analysis.
lessons.intuition: One degree of longitude is not the same ground distance everywhere.
lessons.deepDive: Every map projection preserves some properties and distorts others; choose based on spatial extent and measurement needs.
commonMistakes: Computing kilometer distances directly in degrees.
Assigning a CRS label instead of transforming coordinates.
followUps: What is EPSG:4326?
Which projection for area?
lessons.production: Store CRS metadata and make transformations explicit/reproducible.
lessons.workedExample: Before buffering points by 5 km, reproject EPSG:4326 coordinates to an appropriate projected CRS.

lessons.title: Spatial Joins & Predicates
lessons.interviewAnswer: A spatial join combines rows based on geometric relations such as within, contains, intersects or nearest instead of equality on a key.
lessons.why: Spatial joins are the geographic analogue of a core relational data operation.
lessons.intuition: Infer a region from whether a customer point lies inside a polygon instead of requiring a region_id.
lessons.deepDive: Predicates have different boundary semantics and can create one-to-many matches; distance joins require compatible coordinate systems.
commonMistakes: Using intersects when within is required.
Ignoring duplicates or CRS mismatch.
followUps: sjoin vs nearest?
How do indexes accelerate joins?
lessons.production: Validate geometry, CRS, cardinality and boundary rules before downstream aggregation.
lessons.workedExample: Attach neighborhood demographics to store locations with a point-in-polygon join.

lessons.title: Spatial Indexes, Geohash & H3
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spatial indexes reduce expensive geometry comparisons by pruning candidates. R-trees organize bounding boxes; hierarchical grids such as geohash/H3 encode locations into cells.
lessons.why: Without indexing, many spatial queries become expensive all-pairs operations.
lessons.intuition: Use a cheap spatial partition to find candidates before exact geometry checks.
lessons.deepDive: Tree and grid indexes optimize different workloads; grid resolution controls aggregation/detail and partition size.
commonMistakes: Treating cell distance as exact geodesic distance.
Using one grid resolution for every task.
followUps: R-tree vs H3?
How does indexing help kNN?
lessons.production: Choose index/resolution based on workload and update pattern.
lessons.workedExample: A ride-sharing system can aggregate demand by H3 cell while an R-tree accelerates polygon queries.

lessons.title: Geodesic Distance & Spatial kNN
lessons.interviewAnswer: Global spatial distance should respect Earth geometry or use an appropriate projection; raw Euclidean distance on latitude/longitude can be misleading.
lessons.why: Distance choices affect clustering, nearest-neighbor features, logistics and service areas.
lessons.intuition: One degree longitude represents different distances at different latitudes.
lessons.deepDive: For regional work, a suitable projection often makes planar distance practical; global work needs geodesic formulas or libraries.
commonMistakes: Using Euclidean distance on lon/lat globally.
Ignoring road/travel-time distance when it is the real objective.
followUps: Geodesic vs routing distance?
How would you accelerate spatial kNN?
lessons.production: Use the metric that matches the physical/business process.
lessons.workedExample: Choose the closest warehouse by projected/geodesic distance rather than raw degree difference.

lessons.title: Spatial Autocorrelation & Moran’s I
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spatial autocorrelation asks whether nearby observations are more similar than expected. Moran’s I is a common global measure; local indicators identify spatial clusters/outliers.
lessons.why: Geography often violates the independence assumption behind ordinary statistics.
lessons.intuition: Nearby house prices or disease rates often move together.
lessons.deepDive: A spatial weights matrix defines neighborhood structure; Moran’s I compares neighboring deviations with overall variance and commonly uses permutation inference.
commonMistakes: Calling visual clustering statistically significant.
Choosing weights after seeing the desired result.
followUps: Global vs local Moran?
Effect on regression?
lessons.production: Define neighborhoods from domain logic and account for spatial dependence in inference/validation.
lessons.workedExample: A high-high cluster can identify adjacent regions with consistently elevated values.

lessons.title: Spatial Cross-Validation & Geographic Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Random splits can overestimate geospatial model performance because nearby samples are correlated; spatial blocking or leave-region-out validation better measures transfer to new areas.
lessons.why: Spatial data can make test examples near-duplicates of training examples.
lessons.intuition: If deployment is a new city, validation should mimic a new city—not random points from the same streets.
lessons.deepDive: Block scale should reflect autocorrelation range and deployment scope; performance can be reported by region and distance from training support.
commonMistakes: Randomly splitting spatially correlated rows.
Using blocks too small to break dependence.
followUps: How choose block size?
Spatial vs temporal leakage?
lessons.production: Design validation around geographic deployment and monitor regional performance.
lessons.workedExample: Hold out whole farms/regions for crop prediction instead of random pixels from each farm.

visual.title: Spatial validation holds out coherent regions
visual.caption: Conceptually, geographic blocks separate train and test instead of randomly mixing neighbors.

lessons.title: Causal Masks vs Bidirectional Attention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Causal masks prevent tokens from attending to future positions for autoregressive next-token prediction; bidirectional encoders can attend to both sides under different objectives.
lessons.why: Masking determines what information a token is allowed to use.
lessons.intuition: A next-token model cannot peek at the answer to its right.
lessons.deepDive: Causal attention sets future logits to -∞ before softmax; padding masks solve a different batching problem.
commonMistakes: Confusing causal and padding masks.
Training autoregressive objectives with future leakage.
followUps: How does BERT differ?
How does masking interact with KV cache?
lessons.production: Mask bugs can silently leak labels or break variable-length serving.
lessons.workedExample: When predicting “sat” in “the cat sat”, the model can attend to “the cat” but not future tokens.

lessons.title: Cross-Attention
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cross-attention uses queries from one sequence and keys/values from another, letting one representation retrieve information from a different encoder or modality.
lessons.why: Cross-attention is fundamental to encoder-decoder, multimodal and conditioned generative systems.
lessons.intuition: The decoder asks questions while another representation supplies keys and values.
lessons.deepDive: The same scaled dot-product operation is used, but Q and K/V come from different tensors/sequences.
commonMistakes: Calling every attention block self-attention.
Ignoring Q/K/V sequence-shape differences.
followUps: Cross-attention vs concatenation?
Where does diffusion use it?
lessons.production: Long conditioning contexts can dominate memory/latency; profile them.
lessons.workedExample: Image latents can query text embeddings in text-conditioned generation.

lessons.title: RoPE & Modern Positional Encoding
lessons.interviewAnswer: RoPE rotates query/key feature pairs according to token position so relative position affects attention scores without simply adding a fixed position vector.
lessons.why: Many modern LLMs use rotary or related positional mechanisms.
lessons.intuition: Position changes the orientation of Q/K vectors, so dot products encode relative offsets.
lessons.deepDive: RoPE applies frequency-dependent rotations; context-extension tricks rescale frequencies but can change quality.
commonMistakes: Saying RoPE is one-hot absolute position.
Assuming arbitrary context extension is free.
followUps: RoPE vs ALiBi?
Why Q/K rather than V?
lessons.production: Benchmark long-context quality as well as maximum length and memory.
lessons.workedExample: Identical tokens at different positions interact differently because their Q/K rotations differ.

lessons.title: Mixture-of-Experts Transformers
lessons.interviewAnswer: MoE layers route each token to a small subset of expert feed-forward networks, increasing total model capacity without activating all parameters per token.
lessons.why: MoE explains how some large models scale capacity more cheaply than dense models.
lessons.intuition: A router sends each token to only a few specialized sub-networks.
lessons.deepDive: Top-k routing reduces arithmetic but introduces load-balancing, expert-capacity and distributed communication problems.
commonMistakes: Assuming all MoE parameters run for every token.
Ignoring communication/load balance.
followUps: Dense vs MoE inference cost?
What is expert collapse?
lessons.production: MoE can become network-bound; topology and routing balance are system-design concerns.
lessons.workedExample: Different token types may statistically route to different experts, though expert semantics are not guaranteed.

lessons.title: LLM Training Lifecycle: Pretraining → SFT → Preference Tuning
lessons.interviewAnswer: Modern LLM development commonly starts with next-token pretraining, then supervised instruction fine-tuning, and may add preference optimization such as RLHF or DPO. Each stage serves a different purpose.
lessons.why: This prevents mixing up pretraining, fine-tuning and alignment.
lessons.intuition: Pretraining learns broad language structure; SFT teaches task formats; preference tuning shifts behavior toward preferred outputs.
lessons.deepDive: Pretraining uses broad corpora and next-token likelihood; SFT uses curated prompt-response examples; preference stages optimize rankings/rewards.
commonMistakes: Calling LoRA a training objective.
Assuming preference tuning reliably adds factual knowledge.
followUps: SFT vs continued pretraining?
RLHF vs DPO?
lessons.production: Dataset provenance and regression evaluation matter at every stage.
lessons.workedExample: A base model may autocomplete text, while an SFT model follows instructions more reliably.

lessons.title: Topic Modeling & LDA
lessons.interviewAnswer: Latent Dirichlet Allocation is a probabilistic topic model where documents are mixtures of latent topics and topics are distributions over words.
lessons.why: Topic models remain useful for interpretable exploratory structure in corpora.
lessons.intuition: A document may combine several themes rather than belong to one hard cluster.
lessons.deepDive: LDA uses Dirichlet priors over document-topic and topic-word distributions; inference estimates hidden topic assignments.
commonMistakes: Confusing topic-model LDA with Linear Discriminant Analysis.
Treating topics as objective ground truth.
followUps: How choose number of topics?
LDA vs embedding clustering?
lessons.production: Check topic stability and human usefulness; embeddings can capture richer semantics but have different interpretability.
lessons.workedExample: Customer feedback can be summarized into recurring themes before labels exist.

lessons.title: Text Classification & Encoder Fine-tuning
lessons.interviewAnswer: A pretrained text encoder can be fine-tuned with a classification head or used as a frozen embedding extractor. Fine-tuning adapts more strongly but costs more and can overfit small data.
lessons.why: Text classification is a common practical NLP task and a strong baseline before generative solutions.
lessons.intuition: Reuse broad language representations instead of learning linguistic features from scratch.
lessons.deepDive: A classifier consumes a pooled/token representation; training updates only the head or the full encoder with a smaller learning rate.
commonMistakes: Using a generative LLM for every classification problem.
Ignoring class imbalance/calibration.
followUps: Fine-tune vs embeddings + linear model?
Which metric for imbalance?
lessons.production: Benchmark simple models for latency/cost and use batch/quantized inference where appropriate.
lessons.workedExample: Route support tickets into categories using a fine-tuned encoder.

lessons.title: Feature Stores: Offline vs Online
lessons.interviewAnswer: A feature store manages reusable feature definitions and provides historical point-in-time-correct features for training plus fresh low-latency values for online inference.
lessons.why: Feature stores address consistency and reuse problems in real-time ML.
lessons.intuition: Training needs historical values as they existed at prediction time; serving needs the freshest values quickly.
lessons.deepDive: Feature definitions can feed offline analytical stores and online key-value stores; point-in-time retrieval prevents future leakage.
commonMistakes: Calling a feature store just a feature database.
Joining current values into historical training rows.
followUps: When is a feature store overkill?
Batch vs streaming features?
lessons.production: Use one when reuse, real-time freshness or training/serving consistency justifies the complexity.
lessons.workedExample: A fraud model uses historical 30-day transaction counts in training and fresh counts at authorization time.

visual.title: Offline and online feature paths
visual.caption: A feature platform keeps semantics consistent while optimizing different access patterns.

lessons.title: Training–Serving Skew
lessons.interviewAnswer: Training-serving skew occurs when feature or preprocessing semantics differ between offline training and live inference because of code, time, freshness or source differences.
lessons.why: Skew can destroy live quality while offline evaluation still looks good.
lessons.intuition: If training computes a feature in SQL and serving computes it differently in application code, model semantics diverge.
lessons.deepDive: Prevent skew with shared definitions, point-in-time datasets, schema contracts and parity checks between offline and online values.
commonMistakes: Calling any distribution shift training-serving skew.
Retraining without fixing the feature contract.
followUps: How test offline/online parity?
How does point-in-time correctness help?
lessons.production: Continuously sample parity checks and treat feature definitions as versioned APIs.
lessons.workedExample: A recommender trained with end-of-day popularity accidentally sees future clicks unavailable at request time.

lessons.title: Data, Model & Experiment Lineage
lessons.interviewAnswer: ML lineage records which data snapshot, feature definitions, code commit, configuration, environment and artifact produced a model version so it can be reproduced and audited.
lessons.why: Without lineage, rollback and debugging become guesswork.
lessons.intuition: A file named final_v7.pt is not enough to explain how it was created.
lessons.deepDive: A reproducible run pins source commit, data/version identifiers, preprocessing schema, hyperparameters, environment and metrics. Exact floating-point reproducibility may still vary on GPU hardware.
commonMistakes: Equating a random seed with complete reproducibility.
Versioning model weights but not data/preprocessing.
followUps: What belongs in a model registry?
How do containers help?
lessons.production: Capture lineage automatically through pipelines and define retention for audit/rollback needs.
lessons.workedExample: When v42 regresses, lineage lets you compare it with v41 rather than reconstruct history manually.

lessons.title: ML Testing & Quality Gates
lessons.interviewAnswer: ML systems need software tests plus data/model checks such as schema invariants, leakage tests, slice metrics, baseline comparison, latency bounds and deployment gates.
lessons.why: Many ML failures are data/interface failures rather than architecture failures.
lessons.intuition: A service can be healthy while receiving impossible feature values, so API tests alone are insufficient.
lessons.deepDive: Promotion gates can require schema compatibility, baseline improvement, minimum critical-slice metrics and system constraints before a model becomes deployable.
commonMistakes: Testing only model code.
Promoting because one aggregate metric improved.
followUps: Unit vs integration tests?
How test nondeterministic training?
lessons.production: Run cheap deterministic checks in CI and heavier validation inside train/deploy pipelines.
lessons.workedExample: Block a new model if aggregate AUC rises but recall on a critical rare-event slice falls below policy.

lessons.title: Kernel Methods & the Kernel Trick
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kernel methods replace an explicit nonlinear feature map with a kernel that computes inner products in that feature space, enabling algorithms such as SVMs to learn nonlinear boundaries without materializing all transformed features.
lessons.why: Kernels are a classic bridge between linear methods and nonlinear function spaces.
lessons.intuition: If a linear separator fails in original coordinates, map inputs into richer features—but compute only pairwise inner products through a kernel.
lessons.deepDive: A valid kernel corresponds to an inner product in some feature space. The RBF kernel creates a very rich space controlled by gamma/bandwidth; regularization still controls effective complexity.
commonMistakes: Saying kernels simply “add dimensions” with no mathematical constraint.
Using RBF gamma without scaling/tuning features.
followUps: What makes a kernel valid?
RBF vs polynomial?
Why do kernel methods scale poorly with n?
lessons.production: Kernel matrices can be O(n²) memory/time; use approximations or other models at large scale.
lessons.workedExample: Two concentric classes can become separable under a suitable nonlinear kernel even though no straight boundary works in input space.

lessons.title: Perceptron & Online Learning
lessons.interviewAnswer: The perceptron is an online linear classifier that updates weights only when an example is misclassified. Under linear separability it has a finite mistake bound tied to the margin.
lessons.why: The perceptron is a simple foundation for online learning and linear decision rules.
lessons.intuition: Process one example at a time: if the current separator is wrong, nudge it toward the correct class.
lessons.deepDive: For labels ±1, update w←w+ηyx when y(w·x)≤0. The classical convergence theorem assumes separability; noisy data can cause ongoing updates.
commonMistakes: Assuming convergence on nonseparable data.
Confusing perceptron probabilities with logistic regression.
followUps: Perceptron vs logistic regression?
What is the mistake bound?
lessons.production: Online updates require drift handling, learning-rate/version controls and protection from bad/adversarial labels.
lessons.workedExample: A streaming spam classifier can update after each newly labeled message rather than retraining from scratch.

lessons.title: Factor Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Factor analysis models observed variables as linear combinations of a smaller number of latent factors plus variable-specific noise, focusing on shared covariance structure.
lessons.why: Factor analysis is a classic latent-variable model distinct from PCA.
lessons.intuition: Several measured variables may move together because of a smaller hidden cause, while each retains its own measurement noise.
lessons.deepDive: The model x=Λz+ε assumes latent factors z and diagonal/specific noise ε; maximum-likelihood or Bayesian methods estimate loadings and uncertainty.
commonMistakes: Calling factor analysis identical to PCA.
Interpreting rotated factors as uniquely determined truths.
followUps: Factor analysis vs PCA?
What is factor rotation?
lessons.production: Use domain interpretation and stability checks; latent factors can be non-identifiable up to rotations/signs.
lessons.workedExample: Survey questions about similar behaviors may load on a small number of latent traits.

lessons.title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
lessons.interviewAnswer: ICA decomposes observed mixtures into latent components that are statistically independent, typically relying on non-Gaussianity; unlike PCA, the objective is independence rather than just uncorrelated variance directions.
lessons.why: ICA is a classic blind-source-separation method and deepens understanding of latent representations.
lessons.intuition: Multiple microphones record mixtures of the same speakers; ICA tries to recover the original independent sources.
lessons.deepDive: After centering/whitening, ICA optimizes a measure of non-Gaussianity or independence. Components are identifiable only up to permutation and scale/sign under standard assumptions.
commonMistakes: Equating independence with zero correlation.
Assuming ICA can separate Gaussian sources uniquely.
followUps: ICA vs PCA?
Why is non-Gaussianity important?
lessons.production: Check component stability and physical interpretability; preprocessing strongly affects results.
lessons.workedExample: Separate mixed audio signals recorded by several sensors without knowing the mixing coefficients.

lessons.title: Time-Series Foundation Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: Time-series foundation models pretrain on large collections of sequences and adapt or zero-shot forecast new series. They can reduce per-series modeling work, but still need comparison with strong naive/statistical baselines and careful domain-shift evaluation.
lessons.why: Foundation-model ideas have moved into forecasting and are increasingly relevant to modern applied ML.
lessons.intuition: Instead of fitting one model from scratch for each SKU or sensor, pretrain broad temporal patterns and adapt to new series.
lessons.deepDive: Architectures vary—tokenized patches, transformers or pretrained probabilistic decoders—but evaluation must preserve time order and account for horizon, scale and domain mismatch.
commonMistakes: Assuming a foundation model automatically beats statistical forecasting.
Evaluating with random splits or mismatched horizons.
followUps: Global model vs local model?
How would you fine-tune without leakage?
lessons.production: Benchmark latency/cost, calibration and per-segment accuracy; keep simple fallback forecasts for failure cases.
lessons.workedExample: A global pretrained model can forecast a newly introduced product with little history, then be compared against seasonal-naive/ETS baselines.
